# Chapter 1: Introduction to Humanities

Overview

In this chapter, we will shortly discuss the basis of humanities and share a brief summary of what is expected throughout the learning experience of humanities. 

Objectives 

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- learn about the experiences of humans throughout time

- understand other cultures

- think about your own world experiences

## A. What are the Humanities?

The Humanities are the study of the creative processes that humans have historically used to express themselves. These include, but are not limited to, arts such as paintings, sculptures, dance, music, and literature. It involves studying how people document the human process, especially through creative outlets like art and literature. Each generation learns from the previous yet finds a new way to express their own experiences as humans. 

Additionally, you must be aware of the different period markers. Originally, terms such as **Before Christ (BC)** and **Anno Domini**  (**AD**; Latin for “in the year of our Lord”) were used to note years and timelines. However, in this Study Guide, we will use **Before Common Era** (**BCE) **and **Common Era (CE)** instead of BC/AD. BCE and CE are the **more secular terms** and the current international scientific standard and are also used in the CLEP exam. The table below illustrates their differences.

To determine the year, we** count down the closer we get to 0 BCE** and **count up the further we get from 0 CE**. Also, as there was no “0th century,” we refer to the years 0-100 CE as the “first (1st) century,” 100-200 as the “second (2nd) century” and so on, which means we are in the 21st century now (2000–2100 CE). Lastly, you may also come across “c.” or “**circa**” which means “approximately.” Hence, “c. 3rd century BCE” simply means “approximately in the 3rd century BCE.”

Lastly, this Study Guide will first give you an overview of art. After which, you will look back into the **Visual Arts** from Prehistoric times until the present times. Next, the same pattern will be used to discuss **Literature** and **Performance Arts**.

# Chapter 2: Overview of the Arts

Overview

This chapter will discuss the modes of expression and reflection in art, the elements of different art forms, and steps taken in evaluating art.

Objectives*** ***

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- identify the modes of expression and reflection in art and the elements of different art forms

- understand the different steps in evaluating art

## **A. ****Modes of Expression and Reflection**

The humanities have several **modes of expression**. One of them is **Visual Art**, which includes sculpture, painting, photography, architecture, and film. Another one is **Performing Arts** (dance, theater, and music), and lastly, **Literary Arts **(poetry and prose). When analyzing these, one must look into the influence of philosophy, religion, and history and reflect on “what is the truth?” and “what is the meaning of the past?” 

Moreover, when studying humanities, we have five essential terms to remember when speaking about art: values, taste, artistic form, perception, and conception. **Values**, which can vary from person to person, are objectives and events we care about. **Taste**, on the other hand, is someone's personal preference. This can be anything from ice cream to music to perfume; it's what that individual likes. An **artistic form** is an artistic composition or structure that conveys meaning. Think of why an author or artist has chosen to create a novel rather than a play or an oil painting rather than a sculpture. **Perception** is, as it sounds, anything you can observe. Finally, **Conception** is what you already know about the work or the context. We will use these terms throughout the course to refer to the art we are studying. 

Analyzing Art

Taken altogether, the analysis of artwork may be **objective** (or visual), which describes the elements as they are viewed, or **subjective** (or symbolic), which often describes our feelings when viewing the work of art. It can also be analyzed from a formal point of view (or aesthetic) that analyzes all the visual syntax  or the composition, which includes its historical context, theme, and organization of the elements, which involves a more comprehensive search. Certain common** criteria** need to be taken into account:

- Time

- Technique

- Theme

- Resources used by the artist, etc.

To analyze an artwork, all the parts and features work together as a whole. The step of analysis requires how the elements of the artwork work together in terms of the principles of art, for example, balance, contrast, emphasis, or movement. An analysis does not interpret or evaluate the work. However, a thorough study will set the stage for interpretation and assessment. 

Approach

Appropriate research is the first step towards analyzing art and giving our first impression. Anything observable in the work of art is noteworthy and gives a reason for the analysis. Remember that we must always justify our findings so that others can relate to them and thus understand them. 

- **Gather data on the author:** such as date of birth and death, social origin, training, and other works

- **Recognise the subject: **religious scene, historical, mythological, allegorical, portrait, landscape, etc.; if it is part of an exhibit, and what was its first public appearance, etc.

- **Analyze the subject:** a description of what is represented, settings, frames, characters, actions, etc. You can also add data relating to its location, creating a brief caption: author, title, date of production, support/material, dimensions, and place of storage/display.

Additionally, we can establish comparisons between several works,  even between artists, and consider alternatives that the artists could have chosen. We can dwell on what might have affected the artist’s choices in the particular work.

Evaluating an Artwork

Part of analyzing art is ***art criticism***, which is the analysis and evaluation of works of art that involves the effort to understand a particular work of art from a theoretical perspective and to establish its significance in the history of art. It is based on facts, not opinions.

Similarly, art criticism in light of historical evidence or based on the context in which a work was created, includes facts about the artist’s life and the historical and social circumstances when the work was done. While understanding the physical properties and visual experience of art is important, it is also important to focus on the significance of works as cultural artifacts.  There are** four main steps **to reflect on a work of art: 

- Descriptive criticism 

- Analyzing criticism

- Interpretive criticism

- Evaluative criticism

Descriptive Criticism

In ***descriptive criticism,*** the focus is on the form, including important parts and characteristics. Various elements constitute a description:

| Form of art:** **architecture, sculpture, painting | Medium of work: clay, stone, steel, paint, etc. | Technique:  tools used | Description of color and texture |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Size and scale of work: relationship to the person and/or frame and/or context | Elements or general shapes: architectural structure, painting with several figures lined up in a row | Description of axis:  vertical, diagonal, horizontal, etc. | Description of line: thick, thin, variable, irregular, intermittent, indistinct, etc. |
| Contour: soft, planar, jagged, etc. | How line describes shape and space: distinguish lines of objects and composition | Relationships between shapes: large and small, overlapping, etc. | Context of object: original location and date |

Analyzing Criticism

***Analyzing criticism ***focuses on the merits of a work. It is used to determine what the features suggest and conclude what the artist wants to convey. Elements for analysis include:

| Determination of subject matter through naming iconographic elements: historical events, allegory, mythology, etc. | Identification of most distinctive features or characteristics: line, shape, color, texture, etc. | Analysis of the principles of composition: stable, repetitious, rhythmic, unified, symmetrical, harmonious, geometric, varied, chaotic, horizontal or vertically oriented, etc. |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Determine how elements contribute to the appearance of an image or function | Analysis of the use of light and color:** **contrast, shadow, illogical, warm, cool, symbolic, etc. | Treatment of space and landscape: both real and illusionary, e.g. compact, deep, shallow, naturalistic, random |
| Portrayal of movement and how it is achieved | Effect of medium(s) used | Perceptions of balance, proportion, and scale: relationships of each part of the composition to each other and as a whole |

Interpretive Criticism

The focus for ***interpretive criticism*** is on the content or the subject matter. It establishes a broader context for the type of art based on facts. The various elements that comprise interpretation include:

- Main idea behind the work 

- Why did the artist create it, and what does it mean?

- The evidence within and outside the artwork that supports the interpretation 

To interpret, it is helpful to know about other artworks by the same artist or other artworks from the same style or art movement.  It provides valuable insight into the reason for the artwork.

Evaluative  Criticism

Evaluative criticism is judging a piece of work about other works by considering its originality. It determines the effectiveness of an artwork according to specific criteria that are established by its style and the art movement. A good evaluation is based on the description, analysis, and interpretation for support. 

As part of analyzing artworks, the elements of each mode of expression must be considered. Hence, the succeeding section will discuss the principles and elements of different forms of visual art, performance art, and literature.

Historical Context

Historically, art was **representational**, meaning early artists from the ancient times to the 19th century portrayed the world in which they lived in their artwork. They painted what they saw, like people and landscapes. With time how the artists portrayed these figures, or other elements changed gradually. There are various historical approaches to creating art from ancient times to the Italian Renaissance, which ended around the mid-1500s. 

Golden Mean

The **golden mean **is the age-old principle and one of the earliest approaches to creating art. Also called the **golden ratio** or the **divine proportion** was the idea that a specific ratio of smaller elements to larger elements resulted in art and architecture appealing to the eye. It has influenced many areas, including architecture, math, design, and art. 

A mathematical equation with a **specific ratio of 1 to 1.618 that can be repeated indefinitely—****also represented by the Greek letter phi Φ**. It was used to describe how elements can be placed in the most aesthetically pleasing way.  

It was extensively used by the notable painter **Leonardo Da Vinci** for constructing his masterpieces using the proportions set forth by the golden ratio. In his painting, ***The Last Supper***** (c. 1498)**, every key dimension of the room, the table, and the ornamental shields were based on the golden ratio, and in the Renaissance period, it was known as the **Divine Proportion**.

It can also be seen in **Michelangelo’s** *The Creation of Adam* (c. 1512) in the Sistine Chapel and **Edward Burne-Jones’s ***The Golden Stairs *(1880).** **Though it is hard to tell where it first developed, it is evident in the artwork of the ancient Egyptians, and the ancient Greeks used it when building classical structures like the *Parthenon *(447–432 BCE). 

Hierarchical Proportion

**Hierarchical proportion**, also known as a **hierarchical organization**, is a technique where the importance of figures is depicted through their size. Art portrayed who was the most powerful or important figure in the composition. Important figures like kings or saints were larger to depict their importance or hierarchy. Not only the size of the figures but also the individual parts of the body like the head could be enlarged compared to the rest.

Present in Egyptian art and Roman art, they are found in the reliefs of the Arch of Constantine, where the sovereign is larger than the subjects. As it merged into Byzantine art, it can be seen in Christian stylization, with Jesus and the Virgin being the main subjects with secondary figures, such as angels.

Linear Perspective

In the early Italian Renaissance, artists started to consider ***Perspective*** or ***Linear Perspective***. This new technique was used to visualize three-dimensional forms in space to represent them more realistically. The principle is that objects closer to the viewer appear larger than the objects that are further away; in other words, objects that are away are portrayed as smaller so that they appear far. 

The key essential components to achieve linear perspective in a painting: 

- Orthogonal (parallel lines)

- Vanishing point

- Horizon line

Artist places a horizontal line across the surface of the picture, known as the “horizon line.” Orthogonal then converge as they recede and meet at the vanishing point on the horizon line.

Hierarchical proportion vs. Linear Perspective

* **Maesta* (1308–1311) by Duccio, Italy with Hierarchical Proportion

*    **Adoration of the Magi *(1481) by Leonardo da Vinci  with Linear Perspective

## B. Elements of Paintings

One of the major forms of visual art is painting. When analyzing a painting, it is important to record the details of the painting, like the name of the painter, the title of the work, the stylistic period, the date, and the medium and materials used. Several elements have to be kept in mind as below:

- Media/Medium

- Lines and Shapes

- Color and Light

- Patterns and Texture

- Composition/ Narrative / Symbolism

- Time and Period

Medium

The **medium** of a painting is the material being used and the choice of medium can help convey a message like the period or the type of artist, etc. Medium is usually applied to a base with a brush or other materials like knives.

Nearly all colors come from nature, like plants, which comes down to **pigment**, the actual color. It gives an effect to the painting and highlights the subject. A **binder** or a substance is applied to a canvas (or other material) to apply the paint. The binder separates the acrylic from encaustic (or wax), watercolor, or oil paints. Artists use a combination of pigment and binder to form a colorful liquid or gel-like substance.  

**The most common media used in paintings are:**

- Tempera

- Fresco

- Oil

- Watercolor

- Acrylic

- Ink

- Gouache

- Mixed Media

Lines and Shapes

**Lines** are the most basic element of a drawing, which is used to control our eye and create unity and balance. Lines are narrow marks created where two things meet to help construct meaning. There are different types of a line, and each has different functions.

- **Horizontal and vertical lines** help separate elements neatly in a picture

- **Diagonal lines **often convey tension or movement

- **Curving lines **convey softness and are usually more flowing

- **Axis lines **are imaginary lines that determine the basic visual direction of a painting.

Color and Light

Color is considered one of the most basic components or building blocks of painting or art in general. It can be used to represent emotions and bring life  Every color has three elements to it:

- Hue: The color

- Value: The amount of lightness and darkness in the painting

- Saturation: The degree of purity of color

Oftentimes, colors are mixed. For instance, **c****omplementary colors** are pairs of colors that, when combined or mixed, cancel each other out by producing a grayscale color.  Complementary colors are also called **opposite colors **of each other on the color wheel. Mixing complementary colors in small amounts can change the value, saturation, and hue.  They produce the sharpest contrast between the two colors when put side by side.

The Influence of Light

Light helps to create depth and controls the art's composition and storytelling. Darkness and light can help show contrast and emphasis in a picture. **Reflecting light **in art bounces off objects, whereas **Glowing light** is the light source as depicted. The technique to capture light has evolved, like chiaroscuro, sfumato, shading, etc. Arts in various periods like **Renaissance, Baroque, and Impressionism **have emphasized it and created some of the most notable art pieces.

Patterns & Texture

The repetition of elements like shapes, lines, or images creates **patterns**. It doesn't always have to be an identical repetition of a component. When implied, it suggests the roughness or smoothness of objects in the composition. Artists use patterns as a composition technique for a particular subject or an entire artwork piece. They are diverse and valuable as a tool that grabs a viewer's attention, whether it is subtle or very apparent. 

The **texture** is the feel of something, which can be an actual or simulated texture. It is used to define the tactile quality of a three-dimensional object. In two-dimensional work, such as painting, it may refer to the** visual ****"****feel****"**** of a piece**. 

For example, a natural rock might feel rough or smooth, and hard when touched. A painter depicting a rock would create illusions of these qualities through other elements of art, such as color, line, and shape. Artists can play with texture by manipulating the medium and materials they use to create art. 

Composition, Narrative & Symbolism

**Composition** is typically the organization of elements or the arrangement of visual elements like color, shape, space, texture, etc., in a painting or other artwork. These elements are composed according to the principles of art and design  (balance, contrast, emphasis, movement, pattern, rhythm, unity/variety) to give the painting structure and convey the artist's intent. There are various elements of composition to note:

| Balance | The equilibrium of opposing visual forces |
| --- | --- |
| Gradation | The changes in details and regions |
| Movement and Rhythm | The way the painting controls the pace of the viewer’s vision |
| Proportion | The emphasis on items due to scaling |
| Unity | The togetherness of the elements in a painting |
| Variety | The contrast of details and regions |

Composition-Balance

Balance refers to how the artwork "feels right" and isn't heavier on one side. Having a **symmetrical balance** adds a sense of calm, whereas an **asymmetrical balance** creates a more dynamic feeling. When there is an imbalance, it generates a sense of uneasiness. 

**Types of Balance:**

- ***Symmetrical***: Such artwork has symmetry throughout it. The image appears to be a mirror image, such as a painting with two identical pictures with equal distances from each side. 

- ***Asymmetrical***: Such artwork is weighted as well, but it is not in an obvious way. 

- ***Radial***: It focuses on a central point and radiates outward. For instance, a wagon wheel's spokes extend outward from the center. 

In the figures below, you can see the differences between Symmetrical and Asymmetrical artwork. 

Composition-Gradation

***Gradation*** is a smooth visual transition or a process of subtle or gradual changes in elements like hue, value, shade, texture, etc. Artists use various methods to create this gradation, like **blending**, **scribbling**, **hatching**, **cross-hatching**, **shading,** and many more. The process used depends on the art medium used by the artist. 

Composition-Movement & Rhythm

The arrangement of objects, figures' position, and river flow can give a **sense of movement **in a painting. Also, certain shapes and repeated colors can make us **see art at a certain pace**.

Composition- Proportion

Through ***proportion,*** we can analyze how things fit together and relate to each other in size and scale, whether big or small, nearby or distant. This is usually emphasized through scaling to draw attention to a subject or object in art, rather than the other smaller objects.

Composition-Unity

This composition element raises questions like whether all the parts of the composition feel as if they belong together or if something is out of place.

Although there is a lot of contrast in the entire composition of Picasso’s** *****Guernica*** (1937), the artist has created an overall picture that gives a sense of this art.

Composition-Variety

Paintings with ***variety*** have a different feel, and it draws a viewer’s attention to the artist's creation, focusing a lot on the entire composition. Great differences between light and dark in a painting play a vital role in the entire texture of the art as compared to a painting with minimal contrast in light and dark. Other contrasts can be differences in shape, color, size, texture, type of line, etc. 

Abstract Paintings

When we picture great paintings in our minds, we typically picture the elements discussed above or those with clearly defined subjects, like women, ducks, or ponds. When we lose sight of what we are looking at, it can be easy to dismiss the work for something childish or not worthy of prestige. This concept would break a lot of abstract artists' hearts. **Abstract** or **non-representational paintings **typically have no subject, but they emphasize lines, color, and texture. Abstract art represents the qualities and elements that stimulate our vision or sense. By appealing to our **senses**, abstract art frees us from our human habit of only seeing subjects and not diving into our emotions. Another aspect of abstract art is **presentational immediacy** or awareness of something all at once, not piece by piece. For example, this would be like looking at a painting and seeing the artwork while recalling a memory or dreaming of a new place. 

## C. Sculpture

Unlike paintings, sculptures are objects we usually picture as being three-dimensional (3D). ***Sculpture*** is the art of making 3D representation forms and is one of the main types of  both visual and fine art. One of the most common subjects of sculptors is the human body and its various forms. Typically, they are **either representative or abstract**. 

The four traditional methods to create a sculpture were:

- Stone carving

- Bronze casting

- Wood carving

- Clay firing

The vital **elements that define a sculpture and other 3D artworks** are:

| Line | Space | Mass or Volume | Shape |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Value | Color | Rhythm or Repetition | Continuity |
| Emphasis | Balance | Texture | Proportion |

Four Types of Sculptures

The first sculptures we will discuss are **sunken reliefs**; sculptors typically carve into a rock for these works. They project inwards and are dependent on light and touch to be experienced. **Low-relief sculptures***** ***also project inwards but are not as prominent as sunken. The depth of the sculpture or raised parts is minimal. **The high-relief sculpture***** ***refers to art carved into a material, and while some remain connected to the source, a protruding portion is emphasized. **Full-round***** ***sculptures are free-standing and usually more difficult to create. These are the three-dimensional sculptures that we picture in our brains.

 Sculpture Materials

Sculptures can be made of almost any material. For example, **s****tone and wood **sculptures are made by chipping, while** the plaster** is used to layer and build. **Metal** is used to bend and beat, or it can be melted. Other popular materials are **rubber, glass, clay,** and **wax**. All these materials can be carved, molded, cast, welded, sewn, or assembled. Recently, modern sculpture often uses **“found” objects.**

Processing Sculpture

Although there are many sculpture materials, there are generally only two ways for an artist to create sculptures.  The first way is the **subtractive process** or removing material to create the work of art. Usually, this is done with stone or wood, and the artist chips away, sands, and takes off layers until they are finished. Meanwhile, the **additive process***** ***creates sculptures by layering materials one on top of another. This process is common with plaster, clay, wax, and sometimes metal. The artist's process is unique to them and can be altered however they choose; these are merely examples of the most common techniques. 

Other elements that add to sculptures are **texture, movement, and location**. Although statues in formal settings are discouraged from being physically touched, our minds still understand what it would feel like to touch them. This concept is related to the **sculpture's texture **as it can convey meaning. For example, Michelangelo’s *David *(1501–1504)* *is made of smooth marble, which appears flawless; this makes the statue feel perfect, pristine, and almost inhuman. Similarly, metal can feel industrial and harsh, and wood feels rustic and primitive. These are subjective and dependent on your personal taste, but critics agree that a material conveys meaning. 

Additionally, the way the sculptor places the body or subject can give off a feeling of **movement***.* Some positions imply stagnation, while others can make you feel like you are in mid-step by the foot placement. **Freed sculptures **are pieces of art that move. This type of sculpture has become more prevalent in modern times, especially after the creation of the mobile in the 20th century. 

Lastly, the **location***,**** ***where the sculptor places and intends for the sculpture to be, is often part of the artwork. Many sculptures are made to be placed in temples, churches, and nationalist locations, while others are in parks or select areas that influence the inspiration of the art itself. Some sculptures go “on tour” to new cities and are available for the public to interact with. People use all these elements and traits to evaluate sculptures.

## D. Architecture

Another form of art is **architecture**, which is the shaping of buildings and space. Since buildings require more money and resources, great architecture is usually associated with power and money. Architecture is composed of **three essential elements**—design, material, and function. All three elements must be strong for the building to work.

First, **design** is the way a building uses space. One type is **centered space**, the arrangement of things around a large, central axis. Next is **living space**, the arrangement of objects to create comfort. Lastly, the **configurational center** is the gathering point at which life is centered (like city buildings or churches). Many of these can be seen in ancient and classical structures, such as post-and-lintel, stylobate, columns, entablature, and pediment. A detailed discussion of these will be explained in the succeeding chapters.

Meanwhile, the **materials** used are essential to determine how long a structure will last. They can be decorative as well as functional. To ensure safety, architects and engineers must design buildings that can withstand the forces of nature. They often consider the exterior and interior of buildings. The **exterior** is the outside of a structure and is where the building presents itself. The **interior** is the inside of a structure and revolves mostly around function. These two parts can either complement each other in design or have different principles of design. Thus, when evaluating architecture, one must ask the following:

- What is the purpose of the building?

- What materials were used?

- What is the design like?

- How does the building employ other arts?

- What is the correlation between the interior and exterior?

## E. Music

Unlike the previous sections which talk about visual arts, music is a type of **performance art**. Music is sound organized in time and abstract art created by performers. Unlike other art forms that can be physically touched, music only exists in time or the fourth dimension. Given its abstract nature and the vast array of music that exists today,  did you know that there are only four properties that make sounds vary from one another? 

These **four properties** are as follows:

- **Duration**: This describes how long a sound or a quiet lasts and where one sound is followed by another.

- **Rhythm**:** **This is the beat or a unique combination of accents and duration of notes.

- **Timbre**:** **It refers to the musical sound's source, the instrument, or the type of voice that is creating the song.

- **Frequency: **It identifies the pitch and counts the regular vibrations each second.

Apart from these properties, music also has four elements:

- **Tone**:** **This refers to the musical sound or what is being sung or played.

- **Scale**: It is a predetermined sequence of notes, such as The Sound of Music's do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, si, do.

- **Color of music**: This is how tones sound, such as bright, dark, and raspy.

- **Pitch**: This refers to how low or high a sound is.

Lastly, there is also **melody**. This is a series of notes that take center stage in the audience's ears. The typical arrangement of melody in songs follows an A-B-A format. For instance, an initial melody (A) is followed by a slightly different melody (B) and then the restatement of the first melody (A). Melody is also known as **form**, statement, variation, or restatement.

Other useful terms are as follows:

- **Key**:** **This is an agreed-upon scale consisting of certain intervals between notes, which also plays the melodies.

- **Meter**: This tells the musicians how many beats one musical note gets.

- **Chords**:** **These are notes that, when played together, can represent an entire musical key.

- Consonance is the sound that two notes make that is usually appealing to the ear. 

- Dissonance is when two or more notes do not sound "good" to the listener and create a contrast or variation in the sounds of the music.

- **Rondo**: This is an instrumental musical style that starts with an A-section refrain and switches between episodes (B and C). 

- **Sonata form (or sonata-allegro form)**:** **A musical structure typically consisting of three main sections: an exposition, a development, and a recapitulation.

- **Scherzo**: A piece of music that has a trio section, is frequently quick-paced, and in 3/4 time and is often compared to its predecessor, **minuet**.

- **Minuet: **This is a piece of music that is more formal than the scherzo and frequently uses slower tempos.

- **Trio Section**: A B-theme placed between two outer statements of the A theme, which is intended to feel like a different theme.

- ** Libretto: **The text for an opera or musical.

Given these various terms and elements, music typically evokes an emotion or sets a mood. Tonal differences and tempo changes can allow music to tell a story. Hence, the structure, form, and composition of a piece are all important when evaluating music. Don’t worry if these are still unclear as this will be discussed further in the upcoming sections. Later on, we will see how these are used by composers and musicians in operas, orchestras, or other musical pieces. 

## F. Dance

Closely linked to music, **dance **is also a performance art and is often difficult to evaluate. Dance is defined as the moving body shaping the space around it. It is considered an ancient art that has been found in all cultures.  The focus remains on the visual patterns the body makes that draw the audience's attention. Dance is typically performed on a stage and contains some similarities to theater, such as music and a narrative. 

While some dancers improvise or make it up on the spot, most perform a choreographed piece. A **choreographer** is someone who designs and coordinates a dance, usually with multiple dancers involved. Most popular dances are trying to tell a story or evoke an emotion from the spectator. They may use a technique called **mimetic**, where they imitate real-life motions to convey their story. The art form of dance includes rhythm and a pattern that the dancer's body follows. Oftentimes the musical style and dance moves have the same name (hip-hop, disco, etc.). Typically, dances are categorized as follows: 

- **Ballet**: The art form that highlights leaps, poses, and turns, with the intent to tell a story set to music.

- **Popular dance**: Includes traditional dances performed at ceremonies, social events, or religious services

- **Modern dance**: A dance that focuses on freedom and self-expression.

To evaluate dances, one must pay attention to the following:

- Movements to better understand the emotion and story a dancer is trying to convey

- Repeated movements

- Lack of repetition

- How the stage/area is used

- Number of dancers and the role each play

- Significance of the clothing worn by the performers

## G. Literature

While the previous sections talked about visual and performing arts, you will now learn about literature. **Literature** refers to written works, such as novels, plays, poems, and short stories, that are considered to have artistic merit and cultural significance. It can take many forms and can be written in a wide range of styles, including fiction, non-fiction, drama, and poetry.

There are many different** types and styles of literature**, including:

- **Fiction**: This includes works of imagination, such as novels, short stories, and plays, that are not based on real events.

- **Non-fiction**: This includes works that are based on real events or factual information, such as biographies, histories, and essays.

- **Drama**: This includes plays and other works that are intended to be performed on stage or screen.

- **Poetry**: This includes works written in verse, such as sonnets, haikus, and free verse.

- **Epic poetry**: This includes long, narrative poems that tell the stories of heroic figures and their deeds.

- **Lyric poetry**: This includes shorter, emotional poems that express the thoughts and feelings of the poet.

- **Prose**: This includes written works that are not written in verse, such as novels, short stories, and essays.

- **Mystery**: This includes works that focus on solving a crime or puzzle.

- **Romance**: This includes works that focus on love and relationships between characters.

- **Science fiction**: This includes works that explore the potential consequences of scientific, technological, and societal innovations.

Nonfiction

Literary nonfiction, also known as **creative nonfiction**, is writing that is based on reality but uses techniques more typically seen in fiction, such as tone, figurative language, descriptive imagery, plot, setting, and characters. Literary nonfiction can take the following forms: 

- **Nonfiction essays**: These can be **expository** (explaining a subject), **personal** (sharing experiences or thoughts), or **persuasive **(persuading the reader of a position); these texts are often succinct and deal with a particular subject.

- **Personal narrative nonfiction**:  This is written about the experiences of the author and includes **autobiographies** (the life story of the author), **memoirs** (which focus on one theme, era, or experience), **diaries**, **journals**, **letters**, and **biographies** (the only personal narrative written by a third party)

- **Science writing**: This is communicating scientific ideas and facts through imaginative writing.

- **Narrative journalism**: Journalism that uses a narrative style and an informal tone to report on current events, travel, sports, or food.

- **Narrative history**: Factual historical events are told in a story-telling manner.

Major Literary Periods and Movements

Additionally, literature has a long and varied history and has evolved and changed over time. Some **major literary periods and movements **include:

- **Ancient literature**: This includes works from ancient civilizations, such as the Epic of Gilgamesh from ancient Mesopotamia and the works of Homer from ancient Greece.

- **Medieval literature**: This includes works from the Middle Ages, such as the tales of King Arthur and the works of Geoffrey Chaucer.

- **Renaissance literature**: This includes works from the period of cultural revival in Europe known as the Renaissance, such as the plays of William Shakespeare and the poetry of John Milton.

- **Romantic literature**: This includes works from the Romantic movement of the late 18th and early 19th centuries, which focused on emotion, nature, and the individual.

- **Victorian literature**: This includes works from the Victorian era in England, characterized by a focus on social issues and moral values.

- **Modernist literature**: This includes works from the early 20th century, marked by a break with traditional forms and an emphasis on individual experience.

- **Postmodern literature**: This includes works from the late 20th and early 21st centuries, characterized by a questioning of traditional narrative structures and a focus on language and form.

These are just a few examples of the many different periods and movements in literature. Each period has its unique characteristics and themes and has contributed to the rich and diverse history of literature. Thus, in analyzing poetry or prose, readers must:

- Discuss how the author uses rhetorical devices to communicate a message to readers.

- Address the time period the work is from to provide additional context.

- Look for a deeper meaning or theme to understand the message the author was trying to convey.

In writing poetry or prose, authors or poets often use literary devices, techniques, and elements to convey their meaning. 

Literary Devices

- **Allegory**: An allegory is a work that uses symbolism to convey a deeper meaning or message. The symbolism in an allegory is often used to represent abstract ideas or concepts.

- **Allusion**: An allusion is a reference to a person, place, or event from literature, history, or culture. Allusions can be used to add depth and complexity to a work by providing additional context and meaning.

- **Anaphora**: It is the recurrence of a word or phrase at the start of subsequent clauses or sentences.

- **Antithesis**: It is the usage of opposing concepts, words, or expressions to strike a balance or establish contrast. It is often used to emphasize the difference between two ideas or to create a sense of tension.

- **Euphemism**: A euphemism is a mild or indirect word or expression that is used in place of a more direct or harsh one. It is often used to avoid offending or upsetting someone.

- **Hyperbole**: It is an exaggeration used for emphasis or impact. It is often used for comedic or rhetorical purposes.

- **Imagery**: It is the use of descriptive words to give the reader a feel. It can include descriptive language related to sight, sound, touch, taste, and smell.

- **Irony**: Irony is a contrast between what is expected and what happens. There are three types of irony: verbal irony, situational irony, and dramatic irony.

- **Personification**: Personification is the attribution of human characteristics to non-human things. It is used to give inanimate objects or abstract concepts a human-like quality.

- **Metaphor**: A metaphor is a comparison between two unlike things using the verb "to be." It is used to describe something more imaginatively or expressively.

- **Simile**: A simile is a comparison between two unlike things using the words "like" or "as." It is similar to a metaphor but uses these specific words to signal the comparison.

- **Symbolism**: Symbolism is the use of symbols to represent ideas or concepts. These symbols can be objects, characters, or events that have a deeper meaning within the context of the work.

- **Theme**: The theme is the central idea or message of a story.

Elements of Literature

- **Tone**: The tone of a work is the overall feeling or attitude that is conveyed by the author. It can be serious, playful, formal, informal, or any other mood or emotion.

- **Mood**: The mood of a work is the atmosphere or emotional feeling that is created by the author. It can be happy, sad, creepy, eerie, or any other emotion.

- **Characterization**: Characterization is the process of creating and developing characters in a work of literature. It can be done through the characters' thoughts, words, actions, and appearance, as well as through the way they are described by the narrator or other characters.

- **Static characters**: Static characters are characters who do not change or develop significantly throughout a story. They remain the same from the beginning to the end.

- **Dynamic characters**: Dynamic characters are characters who change or develop throughout a story. They may undergo significant personal growth or transformation.

- **Direct characterization**: Direct characterization is when the narrator or another character directly tells the reader about a character's traits or personality.

- **Explicit characterization**: Explicit characterization is when a character's traits or personality are clearly stated or shown through their actions and words.

- **Indirect characterization**: Indirect characterization is when the reader infers a character's traits or personality based on the character's thoughts, words, actions, and appearance. This is a more subtle way of characterizing a character.

- **Implicit characterization**: Implicit characterization is similar to indirect characterization, but involves even more subtle hints and clues about a character's traits and personality. It requires the reader to carefully interpret and infer information about the character.

Literary Techniques

- **First-person point of view**: First-person point of view is when the story is told from the perspective of a character who is participating in the events of the story. The narrator uses the pronouns "I," "me," and "my" to refer to themselves. Although using this allows the author to easily connect with the reader, it limits the author to writing only one perspective.

- **Second-person point of view**: Second-person point of view is when the story is told from the perspective of a character who is addressed directly by the narrator. The narrator uses the pronoun "you" to refer to the reader or the main character.

- **Third-person point of view**: Third-person point of view is when the story is told from the perspective of a narrator who is not a character in the story. The pronouns "he," "she," and "them" are used by the narrator to identify the characters.

- **Omniscient and limited views of the third-person point of view**: The omniscient view is when the narrator has access to the thoughts and feelings of all of the characters in the story. The limited view is when the narrator only has access to the thoughts and feelings of one or a few characters.

- **Conflicts**: Conflicts are problems or challenges that characters face in a story. There are two types of conflict: internal conflict, which is a struggle within a character's mind, and external conflict, which is a struggle between a character and an external force or obstacle.

- **Internal and external conflict**: Internal conflict is a struggle within a character's mind, such as a conflict between their desires and their values. External conflict is a struggle between a character and an external force or obstacle, such as another character or nature.

Apart from these, the theme is also an important aspect of literature. The **theme** is the message the author is trying to convey; it is not a cliché or moral. Finding a story's topic needs the reader to infer, which is a higher-order skill. To help you derive the theme of a particular literature, try the following:

- When you finish reading, ask yourself to sum up the reading in a single word or phrase. For example, in the fable *Three Little Pigs*, this could be about thinking ahead.

- Stretch that single word into a message. In the previous example, this can be stretched as those who fail to plan will often find disaster.

## H. Poetry

Unlike prose which is formed by paragraphs that follow traditional grammar rules, **poetry** is work that uses stanzas to arrange words into a free-flowing piece. When we analyze poetry, we are looking at how a poet arranges a poem on paper. We consider how many stanzas are present, the punctuation, the breaks in the lines, and whatever other details we can see. **Diction **is the word choice that the author makes; the informal or formal phrases and words can change the tone, characterization, and theme of the poem. 

Moreover, poets often employ **sonic devices** to convey and reinforce the meaning or experience of their writing through the skillful use of sound. These are especially important for poets. After all, poets are trying to use a concentrated blend of sound and imagery to evoke an emotional response. Understanding sonic devices is crucial both for analysis and for one's writing. One sonic device is **alliteration**, which uses a stream of words that all start with the same first phoneme. For example, "someone sang a song" uses alliteration since four of the words begin with the same "s" sound. The use of alliteration can suggest a humorous or even a threatening tone.** **

Another sonic device is **assonance**, the repetition of a similar set of vowel sounds, typically used to emphasize intensity, mood, and imagery. Examples of assonance include "go and mow the lawn" or "here and there and everywhere." A** cacophony** is defined as a harsh mixture of sounds. In poetry, a cacophony is the use of words with harsh consonants, usually at the beginning of a word. A poet might use cacophony to set a mood of negativity and unhappiness. 

Lastly, an **onomatopoeia** is a word that attempts to emulate a sound such as a bang, zoom, crash, or smack. Poets use onomatopoeia to make their writing enjoyable and to provide variety in their poems. A combination of all these elements can determine the heart and intention of a work of literature. 

Furthermore, there are **three types of poetry**: haiku, elegy, and euphony.

- **Haiku**: A haiku is a traditional form of Japanese poetry consisting of three lines. It consists of 17 syllables; the first and third lines contain five syllables, while the second line has seven syllables. Also, haikus do not need to rhyme, and they are typically written with a nature theme and often convey a moment of insight or beauty.

- **Elegy**: An elegy is a type of poem or song that is written to express grief or lamentation, often for someone who has died. The word "elegy" comes from the Greek word "élegos," which means "lament." Elegies are typically written in a formal and somber tone, and they may include themes of loss, memory, and the passage of time. An iconic example is Thomas Gray’s “Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard.”

- **Euphony**: It is the quality of being pleasing or harmonious to the ear, particularly in terms of the sounds of words and phrases. It is the opposite of **cacophony**, which refers to harsh or discordant sounds. Euphony is often created through the use of vowel sounds, consonant sounds, and the rhythms and inflections of language. In literature, euphony is often used to create a sense of beauty, flow, and musicality in writing. It can be achieved through the use of rhyme, alliteration, and other sound devices, as well as through the choice of words and their arrangement in a sentence or phrase. An example of this is long vowel sounds like in “**Ode to Autumn**” by John Keats.

Types of Verses

Not all poems are written in the same way. Some rhyme, while others do not. For instance, there is **free verse**. Unlike other forms of poetry, the free verse does **not **use rhyming lines nor adhere to any meter. Meanwhile, **b****lank verse**** **is a writing style using the typical metrical but non-rhyming lines, usually in iambic pentameter. **Iambic pentameter**,** **the most common meter in English poetry, is the meter of the line or the number of stressed and unstressed syllables. Although the blank verse is often seen in poems, plays can also be written using it. Some of the pieces of literature using iambic pentameter can be seen in the following:

- Geoffrey Chaucer's *The Canterbury Tales (*c. 14th century)	

- John Milton's *Paradise Lost *(1667)

- William Shakespeare's sonnets

- Phillis Wheatley's poems

- Emily Barrett Browning's sonnets

- Percy Bysshe Shelley’s “Mont Blanc” (1816)

- John Keats’ “To Autumn” (1820)

- Alfred, Lord Tennyson’s “Ulysses” (1842)

- William Wordsworth's "The Prelude" (1850)

- Christopher Marlowe’s plays

Moreover, there’s the **heroic couplet**,** **a traditional form of English poetry pioneered by Geoffrey Chaucer and is often seen in epics and narrative poems. A frequently-cited example is  John Denham’s description of the river Thames in “Cooper's Hill”:

	O could I flow like thee, and make thy stream

My great example, as it is my theme!

	Though deep yet clear, though gentle yet not dull;

	Strong without rage, without o'erflowing full.

Note also that poems have rhyme schemes such as the **terza rima**. It is a rhyme scheme introduced by Dante Alighieri and contains several **tercets**, or three-line stanzas, throughout the poem, and uses the pattern ABA BCB CDC DED and several variations to connect its stanzas. 

Here’s an example from Dante’s *The Divine Comedy:*

Midway on our life's journey, I found myself

In dark woods, the right road lost. To tell

About those woods is hard – so tangled and rough

And savage that thinking of it now, I feel

The old fear stirring: death is hardly more bitter.

And yet, to treat the good I found there as well

# Chapter 3: Prehistoric Era (290,000–5,000 BCE)

Overview

This chapter will trace the earliest examples of visual art from more than 40,000 years ago or even before recorded history began (**prehistory**). It will cover how early humans attempted to control their surroundings by, for example, painting lifelike animals on the walls of caves as seen in Paleolithic art. After which, we’ll discuss mesolithic and neolithic artworks to see how art representations changed throughout prehistory.

Objectives 

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- state the key artworks per prehistoric era

- discuss the speculations of why experts think these artworks were created

## A. Paleolithic Era Art (40,000–10,000 BCE)

Paleolithic artists painted graceful and realistic animals on the walls of caves and carved stone statuettes of females as symbols of fertility to master their environment. Caves in southwest Europe hold some of humanity's most ancient paintings and engravings Images often show animals and may have been ritual worship sites. Often these sculptures showed pregnant women or exaggerated female sexuality. The **Paleolithic **sites of Lascaux in France and Altamira in Spain have yielded some of the most famous examples of this type of art. Additionally, early humans carved stone statuettes of females, which were likely meant to symbolize fertility. The "Venus" figures of Willendorf, Lespugue, and Lausell are some of the best-known examples of this type of artifact.

Cave Art - Lascaux Cave (17,000–15,000 BCE)

Lascaux Cave is situated in **southwestern France** and is a **Paleolithic **cave. This means that the cave contains some of the earliest prehistoric drawings that humans have discovered. In total, there are nearly 600 paintings and 1,400 etchings have been found within Lascaux Cave.

The Lascaux Cave drawings are mainly of **animals**, including bulls, aurochs, horses, stags, and felines. **Horses **are the most commonly depicted animal in the cave, though the reason for this is unknown. Scientists believe that the cave may have been used to** record hunting successes** or to **perform ceremonies**. Additionally, the paintings may have served as a way for ancient humans to make sense of the world around them.

Other drawings found in the cave depict** human figures **alongside animals. It is interesting to note that no plant life or vegetation is depicted in the other drawings. Artists in the past used **minerals and ores** to create their pigments for paintings. Some examples of these materials are hematite, iron, manganese, clay, and charcoal. The most commonly seen colors throughout these artworks are red, yellow, and black. The paintings look to have been painted **by hand**.

Sculpture - Venus of Willendorf (c. 22,000–24,000 BCE)

The Venus of Willendorf is an important statue from the **Paleolithic **era. It is thought to date back to 22,000-24,000 BCE, making it one of the oldest examples of Paleolithic art. It was discovered on the left bank of the Danube in Willendorf II, Lower Austria on August 7, 1908, during excavations led by Josef Szombathy and supervised by Hugo Obermaier and Josef Bayer. The statue is remarkably well-preserved, providing valuable insights into the art and culture of this early period.

This ancient sculpture, sometimes called the **Woman of Willendorf** or **The Goddess of Willendorf**, is made from oolitic limestone. Its original meaning is not clearly understood, but there are several theories about what it might represent. 

**1**. The **religious **symbol of a goddess can represent **fertility** or a good hunt.

**2**. A **fertility **symbol may overemphasize female sexual characteristics, but it can also be a good luck charm for men.

**3**. An aspirational totem is a** lucky charm** that is believed to bring **prosperity**.

The statue is an important archaeological discovery because it depicts a woman with exaggerated features, such as large breasts, stomach, and thighs. The statue is faceless, which has led archaeologists to believe that it was not meant to represent any one specific individual. The stone it is made out of is not found in the area where the statue was discovered, leading researchers to believe that it was brought to the area by nomadic people from another location. One of the most interesting things about the Woman of Willendorf statue is that it is just one of many similar statues that have been uncovered at other European archaeological sites.  They may never know for certain the actual reason why this statue was created and what it meant to the people who lived in the society that made it.

## C. Neolithic Era (10,000–4,500 BCE)

Neolithic people erected megalithic structures of huge stones to create an environment for religious ritual and the sophisticated measurement and tracking of celestial bodies. The earliest monumental structures were stone circles and soil mounds. It is believed the structures were used to commune with the powers people felt governed their lives. Some of these structures are Göbekli Tepe in Anatolia, Turkey (c. 9500 CE) and Stonehenge in Salisbury Plain, Southwest England.

Stonehenge (c. 3000–1600 BCE)

Stonehenge is a prehistoric **Neolithic **structure found in Wiltshire, England. The structure consists of a circle of large stones surrounding a smaller circle of stones. The stones are believed to have been erected between 3000 and 2000 BCE. Two types of stones are used in the construction of Stonehenge: **bluestones **and **sarsen **stones. The sarsen stones are the largest stones making up the structure and are considered **megaliths**. Megalithic structures are typically massive stone structures that have been used for a variety of purposes throughout history. While the purpose of Stonehenge is still largely debated, it is widely believed that the site was used for **burial purposes**, as numerous human remains have been found on the location. Others believe that it served as a religious or astronomical site for early people in the area.

# Chapter 4: The Ancient World (5000 BCE–500 CE)

Overview

This chapter will explore the different civilizations in the Ancient World from Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Asia, highlighting their notable visual art. 

(Note: We will sometimes be using the term “Ancient Near East” in this Study guide. “Near East” and “Middle East” essentially mean the same thing, but “Near East” is what the “Middle East” was called in the 19th century by early archaeologists when describing the ancient world in that area – the term stuck and so you will sometimes encounter it in the material we will be studying here.)

Objectives

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- identify the renowned artworks or architecture of each ancient Near Eastern civilization

- explain how the religion and culture of each civilization shaped their artworks and architecture

## A. Civilizations of Mesopotamia

One of the main areas referred to as the Near East is Mesopotamia, which is often considered the birthplace of civilization. It is often called part of the "Fertile Crescent" because of the natural water resources available for agriculture in the crescent-shaped area. It is located between the Tigris River and the Euphrates River to the northeast of Egypt. Major ancient civilizations like Sumer, Babylon, and Assyria resided in ancient Mesopotamia.

The Sumerians (4500–1900 BCE)

Mesopotamian culture and civilization began with the Sumerians, who settled in the South near the Persian Gulf. They were the first major civilization and created various city-states for 2000 years, located along the region's rivers. Each city-state had its ruler, army, and ziggurat. Ziggurats were ancient Mesopotamian temples that were shaped like flat pyramids with steps to each side. Each ziggurat was dedicated to a different deity and served as a seat of government for a city-state as well as a visual reminder of the king's power.

Photo: An ancient Sumerian Ziggurat

The **most famous Sumerian city-states **were:

- **Uruk**, **the oldest** city in Mesopotamia

- **Ur**, home to the **legendary Gilgamesh**

- **Eridu**, the city the Sumerians **claimed to be** the oldest

| **Study**** Note****:** What is a City-State? A city-state is an** ****independent nation whose capital city governs the surrounding countryside.** One of the first types of administration was the city-state, which emerged as the first agricultural settlements developed into cities. The city-states of ancient Greece are perhaps the most well-known. The two most notable are Sparta, a rigidly controlled militaristic civilization, and Athens, one of the world's earliest democracies. |
| --- |

The Babylonians (1895–539 BCE)

Babylon was a small city-state in central Mesopotamia founded in 1894 BCE in central Mesopotamia. From 1792 to 1750 BCE, under the reign of king Hammurabi, things changed. He was an effective monarch and established an organized bureaucracy with taxation. Following his conquest of southern Mesopotamia, Hammurabi liberated Babylon from foreign domination, bringing stability to the region.

One of the most significant creations of this First Dynasty of Babylon was the creation of the **Code of Hammurabi** around 1754 BCE, a **collection of laws** built upon earlier written laws from Sumer, Akkad, and Assyria. The Code was written on **clay tablets and stone steles** (slabs) and consisted of **282 laws with scaled penalties based on social standing**. For example, if a member of the noble class broke the arm of a slave, they would have to pay a fine, but if a member of the noble class damaged the arm of another aristocrat, that noble would have their arm broken in turn. 

| **Study Note:** The Code of Hammurabi’s historical influence This law is the origin of the famous biblical phrase "an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth," which was paraphrased from The Code.  It also established the right to a trial by jury, the presumption of innocence, and the right to submit evidence in court to support one’s case. |
| --- |

The Babylonian Empire persisted for 260 years until foreign armies stormed Babylon in 1531 BCE, sacking it. Eventually, the nation recovered, and the Neo-Babylonian Empire was established. Babylon once more took control of the area from 626 to 539 BCE. However, the Persians overthrew this new empire in 539 BCE and dominated the area until Alexander the Great's reign in 335 BCE.

## B. The Assyrians (1500–612 BCE)

When the Babylonians ruled southern Mesopotamia, the Assyrians were a small civilization located in northern Mesopotamia on the Tigris River. Their capital city of Assur (or Ashur), named after the head god of the Assyrian pantheon, was built around 1900 BCE. Led by **aggressive warrior kings**, the Assyrians expanded their control over Mesopotamia around 1300 BCE, conquering all of northern Mesopotamia and parts of southern Mesopotamia, including Babylon, amassing vast wealth in the process.

**King Ashurbanipal **(685–631 BCE) is known as the last great king of Assyria and is chiefly remembered today for his **patronage of artwork and literature**. Throughout his long reign, he collected texts and documents of various genres, amassing them in the **Library of Ashurbanipal**. Comprising over 100,000 texts, it was only surpassed by the construction of the Library of Alexandria over 400 years later.The Assyrians were also renowned for their **narrative relief sculptures** that decorated the walls of their palaces and temples, and none were finer than those found at King Ashurbanipal’s North Palace at Nineveh. ***The Lion Hunt of Ashurbanipal*** (645–635 BCE) is the most notable carving, depicting a formalized ritual hunt of lions by King Ashurbanipal himself. 

| **Study Note:**** **Assyrian narrative reliefs Assyrian reliefs were originally painted and had a** narrative structure similar to modern comic books** where the story starts at a panel on one end and follows along the walls to the concluding panel at the other end. |
| --- |

By around 700 BCE, the Assyrian empire had expanded to cover all of ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt. Major cities such as Assur, Nineveh, and Nimrod served as **cultural and trade hubs** in the empire. The Assyrians controlled this for almost a century. However, the Assyrian Empire came to an end in the late 600s BCE as a result of pressure from multiple different groups.

## C. The Ancient Persians (550–331 BCE)

During its reign, the Persian Empire grew into the **world's first superpower**, expanding its territories from India to Europe. Their **culture, art, and architecture were rich with aspects from different civilizations**,** **such as Mesopotamia, Greece, and Egypt, due to their military conquests and commercial trades. Their economic achievements, such as the development of the **Royal Road**, led to the spread of their culture and their ability to learn from other civilizations. They are thought to have influenced future movements for **human rights** due to their well-known tolerance of other customs, traditions, and religions. Future Middle Eastern, Central Asian, and European civilizations would go on to greatly benefit from the Persian cultural legacy. 

Persian architecture and art **merged elements from other cultures with particularly Persian elements**, resulting in ornate palaces, intricate reliefs, and other influential works of art. Generally, they feature elaborate palaces, detailed reliefs, sculptures, and textiles, Persian architecture and art combined features from other cultures with distinctly Persian aspects.  One of the most **potent symbols of art, taste, and beauty in Persian societies** was and is the **traditional woven carpet**, also known as the **Persian Rug**. This originated in areas of present-day Iran and Turkey. These rugs are handmade, hand-knotted works of art that follow a tradition that dates back many thousand years. Persian rugs are high-end luxury objects that are meticulously produced, thus they frequently have a heavy price tag. 

| **Study Note:** The Persian Rug’s cultural heritage Persian rugs have long been valued for their **distinctive artistry, sturdiness, and intricate patterns and imagery.   **They are traditionally woven by expert weavers from high-quality materials, such as fine silks. They use natural colors extracted from plants and animals to weave detailed and beautiful pattern work. |
| --- |

Eventually, though, the Persian empire began to decline, and under the leadership of Alexander the Great, Persia was conquered, and power was seized in Mesopotamia by the Greeks in 323 BCE.

## D. Ancient Egypt  (4300–30 BCE)

Ancient Egyptian civilization lasted for more than **3,000 years** and represents one of the most remarkable ancient cultures that is still being studied in the present era.  It had a wealth of resources since it was situated where the **Nile River** drains into the Mediterranean Sea. The Nile River's **yearly flooding** created incredibly productive agricultural land, enabling the Egyptians to produce enough food to feed a rapidly expanding population and fuel their territorial conquests.  Egyptian civilization placed a **high value on art and architecture**, **which had close links to religion**. Temple complexes built in ancient Egypt, such as those at Karnak and Luxor for example, frequently had **distinct religious motivations for their architecture**.

Ancient Egyptian Architecture

Their society consisted of intricate social structures, and they produced significant architectural achievements that dot the landscape of their ancient realm to this day. Four key architectural structures, in particular, were of great importance to Egyptian society: **Mastabas, Pyramids, Temples, and Obelisks**.

- **Mastabas **are the earliest type of **funerary building **created by the ancient Egyptians and were initially **for the aristocratic elite of society**.

- **Pyramids **were constructed to house **pharaohs' tombs** as well as act as **temples to the gods**. The ancient **pyramids of Giza**, which were constructed more than **4,000 years ago** and are still standing today, are regarded as one of the seven wonders of the ancient world.

The Giza Pyramid Complex consists of The Great Pyramid of Giza (center), the Pyramid of Khafre (right), and the Pyramid of Menkaure (left)

- **Mortuary temples **were constructed to **honor pharaohs**, whereas **cult temples** were constructed to **pay homage to gods**. The **Karnak temple complex** is an example of an enormous Egyptian religious hub.

Interior of the Karnak temple complex

- **Obelisks **are **pointed stone pillars** that the **pharaohs, and other notable Egyptians,** **erected as monuments to their great accomplishments**. They also acted as places of **worship for the sun god Ra**, and as a form of **magical protection** for Egypt's tombs, temples, and kingdoms.

Ancient Egyptian obelisks outside Karnak temple

Ancient Egyptian Art

Three key artworks of Egyptian civilization are hieroglyphics, tomb paintings, and sculptures. First, **hieroglyphics**, the ancient Egyptian **pictorial writing system** (and one of the oldest writing systems in the world), **represented words and sounds using images and symbols** and are found on the walls of every Egyptian obelisk and pyramid chamber. They range from **telling historical narratives of kingly conquests to religious tales and evocations of their gods**.

Hieroglyphics painted on papyrus (paper made from reeds) depicting Queen Nefertari's coronation before the goddess Hathor (right)

Aside from hieroglyphics, **tomb paintings, sculptures, and reliefs** often filled the **burial chambers** of wealthy Egyptians. The paintings were richly colored and detailed with images showing the **dead's journey to the afterlife**, and sculptures often represented their idealized forms or represented specific gods and goddesses. It was believed that these paintings and smaller sculptures would become real and join the dead in the afterlife to serve them. 

A pharaoh buried in his tomb with everything he’ll need for the afterlife

| Study Note: Size matters - hierarchical proportions **D****oll-sized figurines,** called **shabtis, **represented everyday people and were kept in small, intimate burial spaces.  Whereas **enormous statues**, like the **Colossi of Memnon,** which feature two identical figures representing pharaoh Amenhotep III, were often found in highly visible areas to propagate the myth of god-kings in Ancient Egypt. |
| --- |

Shabti family (left), Colossi of Memnon (right)

As these paintings and sculptures portrayed the **perfect world of the gods** rather than the imperfect real world, art (and much of Egyptian society) was predicated on the idea of **perfect equilibrium** - using **binary concepts** such as good/evil, beautify/ugliness, life/death to inform their rituals and laws. 

Even though it lasted longer than other nearby civilizations, the Ancient Egyptians would eventually decline. Soon, they found themselves conquered by other empires over time, including the Assyrians, Persians, Alexander the Great, the Romans, the Turks, the French, and finally, the British. 

Even so, their cultural legacy was so strong that all these civilizations, and more besides, felt **strongly influenced by the accomplishments of the Egyptians**, even paying homage to them through famous architectural landmarks, such as the **Washington Monument**  (an obelisk) in Washington DC, USA and the **Louvre Art Museum** (pyramid) in Paris, France.

Washington Monument obelisk (left), Louvre Art Museum pyramid (right)

The Giza Pyramids were constructed in 2570 BCE, more than 2500 years before her rule (and more than 4500 years ago for us), which means she is 500 years closer to us than the pyramids! ## E. Asia: India, Myanmar, and China (5000 BCE–1000 CE)

Asian art and architecture are known for their beautiful fusion of culture and religion. Major art forms are heavily influenced by Hinduism and Buddhism, which are reflected in their architecture throughout Asia. Historically, because of the trade routes between various Asian countries and other parts of the world, there has been an exchange of various cultures and communities influencing Asian art and architecture.

Around the 700s CE, there were some religious establishments throughout Asia where religious heads like Hindu Brahmins and Buddhist monks started to bring forth their religious practice and imagery. Some Hindu religious imagery included idols of animals and various gods, while the statue of Buddha became popular because of the Buddhist monks, all of which influenced the structures and architecture throughout Asia. 

| **Did You Know?** **Silk Roads **were **trade routes **that were significant in facilitating economic, cultural, political, and religious interactions between the East and West.  Its name comes from the extremely profitable trade in **silk textiles**, which were almost entirely made in China. |

Asian Architecture: Pagodas

As Buddhism was spreading throughout Asia and the far east, Buddhist monks started to erect **large Buddha statues** around the 7th century in temples. The interior often contains an altar or a smaller **pagoda** with a series of staircases for the visitor to ascend and witness the view from an opening on one side of each tier. 

A **pagoda** is a towerlike, multistory, solid, or hollow structure made of stone, brick, or wood, usually associated with a Buddhist temple complex. It is where Buddhist monks and nuns gather to teach and practice the tenets of Buddhism. Most have between three and 13 tiers and usually have an odd number of tiers with the classic gradual-tiered eaves. They are common to Nepal, India, China, Japan, Korea, Myanmar, Vietnam, and other parts of Asia.The origin of the pagoda can be traced to the **stupa** (3rd century BCE) in India, which is a domed-shaped monument. With time, the architecture of Chinese towers blended with the Pagoda style which gradually spread to other parts of Asia. Moreover, the style of pagodas in different places varies from one another as they all derive from different styles of architecture. Like the pagodas in Thailand, Myanmar differs from the Japanese Pagodas.

Types of Pagoda

Stupa

The most common temple design erected by the Buddhists was called a **stupa,** which means pile or heap in Sanskrit. The stupa was a dome-shaped structure constructed of shaped stone that formed a hemisphere when complete. The main function of the stupas was to **preserve relics and different religious objects and offer the believers a place to meditate and pray**. The dome shape of the stupa originated with the burial of great Buddhist monks who died and were consequently buried under a heap of rocks. Later on, the heap was modified architecturally and turned into the great stupas.

Shwedagon Pagoda

The **Great Golden Mountain Stupas (c. 6**th**–10**th** CE),** or the **Shwedagon Pagoda,** is believed to house relics from four of the Buddhas. It stands out for its beauty and is ornately decorated with marble, gold, and precious gems. The main pagoda complex is circular, with four entrances, all guarded by marble and gold lion statues called Chinthes. 

The summit of the main stupa is entirely encrusted in gold and has diamonds, rubies, and emeralds. Smaller shrines and stupas surround it. The eight small shrines encircling the Pagoda are dedicated to the seven days of the week, with Wednesday split into morning and evening, which makes a total of eight shrines. 

The main stupa of Shwedagon Pagoda

Porcelain Tower of Nanjing

**The Porcelain Tower of Nanjing,** is a historic site on the south bank of the external Qinhuai River in Nanjing, China. The original pagoda  was mostly destroyed in the 19th century during the Taiping Rebellion. What remains is the modern life-size replica.

It was an octagonal tower with a base of about 97 feet in diameter and a height of 260 feet. It was one of the largest buildings in China, with nine stories and a staircase in the middle of the pagoda, which spiraled upwards for 184 steps.

The tower was originally built in the 15th century during the Ming dynasty with **white porcelain bricks** **and at night as many as 140 lamps were hung from the building to illuminate the tower**. It was decorated with numerous Buddhist images and glazes; stoneware was worked into the porcelain creating a mixture of green, yellow, brown, and white designs of animals, flowers, and landscapes on the sides of the tower.*                 *

Horyuji Temple Pagoda

The **Horyuji Temple Pagoda in Nara** is one of the oldest Buddhist complexes in Japan (607 CE) and was declared a world heritage site in 1993. Unlike Chinese pagodas, Japanese pagodas are mainly made of wood, have bigger roof overhangs, and are viewed as secondary structures.
