# Chapter 5: The Classical Age

Overview

This chapter will review and highlight the innovative art and architecture of Ancient Greece—from the Archaic, Classical, and Hellenistic periods—as well as from Ancient Rome and their revolutionary engineering marvels. 

Objectives 

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- state the key artworks and architecture of the Ancient Greeks and Romans

- identify the three main elements of Greek architectural relief and three orders of columns

- describe the key elements of Roman architecture and engineering

Classical art spans the cultures of Greece and Rome and has served as the foundation of Western civilization for centuries. Classical Art, which included advancements in painting, sculpture, decorative arts, and architecture, sought ideals of beauty, harmony, and proportion, even as those values altered and changed with time. The human figure, human experience of space, and their relationship with the gods were important to Classical Art, although often also used for political propaganda. Philosophy, science, music, theater, and literature were all also very important to the cultures of this era and helped shape the world around them as much as their civilizations. However, despite all the advancements in the arts, the expansions of empires and outbreaks of war were regular occurrences, ironically leading to both spheres influencing one another.

## A. Ancient Greece: Archaic, Classical, and Hellenistic (2700–30 BCE)

Greek art styles are broken into **four distinct periods** that reflect the changes in the history and culture of Ancient Greek society. The works of the Greeks also vary depending on specific periods in history. The following section attempts to discuss some of their prominent works. Note, however, that the terms “Ancient” or “Archaic” period is a separate era from the Classical and Hellenistic periods. Nonetheless, “Ancient Greece” is sometimes used even when talking about the Classical and Hellenistic periods as “Ancient Greece” is often used to refer to the whole period and the people anyway. 

| **Geometric (900–700 BCE)** Primarily painted pottery and clay work made from terracotta clay, metalwork from bronze, and other metals. Lines, patterns, geometric shapes,  images of people, animals, and chariots. |  |
| --- | --- |
| **Archaic (600–480 BCE)** Carved large freestanding sculptures of humans from stone. Male nude statues, called kouros, and clothed female statues, called kore. **Black-figure pottery** became popular. |  |
| **Classical (480–323 BCE)** **Early Classical Greek Art (480–450 BCE)** Subjects were more accurately proportioned with more motion and emotion. Attention to detail in the body, hair, and clothing. The red-figure painting on vases and other pottery replaced the black-figure painting. **High Classical Greek Art (450–400 BCE)** Marble sculptures of human figures (mostly nude males or the "heroic nude") with a focus on youth and emotions. This period is known for the famous temple built in Athens: the Parthenon. |  |
| **Hellenistic (323–31 BCE)** The death of Alexander the Great in 323 BCE marks the beginning of this period. Diversity of art in terms of styles, subjects, and medium. E.g. grotesque, children, elderly, and non-Greek peoples. | "*Boxer at rest*," bronze (c. 330 to 50 BCE) |

## B. Ancient Greece (2700–750 BCE)

Ancient Greece is known for several important cultural developments, including:

- Being the birthplace of **Western philosophy** (Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle) and **democracy**

- Classical **literature **(Homer and Hesiod) and **theater **(Sophocles, Euripides, and Aristophanes)

- Logical **mathematics **(Pythagoras and Euclid)

- Early **historiography **(Herodotus)

- The **Olympic Games**

- And many more contributions including the foundations of the **scientific method** and the **Latin alphabet**.

Ancient Greece began as a collection of civilizations spread across the Aegean Sea region. While we know about the Greek contributions to the world, it is also important to learn about the two most influential foundational **Ancient Greek civilizations**: the **Minoans **and the **Mycenaeans**.

## C. The Minoan Civilization (2700–1500 BCE)

The Minoan civilization emerged on the island of Crete around 2700 BCE during the Bronze Age, spreading across the Mediterranean and gradually forming a complex society by 3000 BCE. The Minoan society was rich in trade, art, and writing. Many were artists, seafarers, and traders, and they traveled the Mediterranean, exchanging language, arts, and goods with people from around the ancient world, particularly ancient Egypt. The most important **trade goods** for the Minoans seem to have been **saffron **and **tin**.

It was Sir Arthur Evans who discovered the evidence of their existence in 1900 on the island of Crete, which helped us understand the world of Minoans and their civilization.

| **Did You Know?** A **labyrinth-like palace **was discovered in **Knossos**. Analysis of pottery shards revealed that these Minoan palaces were massive storehouses where raw food was processed and stored. |
| --- |

Minoan Art

Minoan art tells us about their culture, yet as we cannot read Minoan records, it is difficult to know the exact meaning behind their art. Though there are various interpretations, it is safe to say that the story behind each of these arts is unknown.  Most Minoan paintings take the form of frescoes, which can be seen in homes, palaces, and even in the throne room in Knossos.

| Bull-leaping fresco, c. 1400 BCE | **Bull-leaping fresco** from the east wing of the palace of **Knossos **is 78 cm high. It is not known if it was a sport, a rite of passage, or some religious ceremony. The people are color-coded like in the Egyptian style. |
| --- | --- |

Minoans seemed to favor nature scenes in their art, like landscapes, with frescoes depicting the natural world, animals, and sea creatures. Humans are depicted jumping over bulls, a famous Minoan subject. However, it is unclear if the people did it or not. 

Minoan Sculptures

For their sculptures, Minoans used stone and bronze, sometimes other materials. Some of the bronze works portray women in skirts, with at least one exposed breast,  men in loincloths, and some animal figurines were also found.  

**The snake goddess**, created around 1600 BCE, is a nearly **30 cm tall **figure of a **woman holding a writhing snake in either hand**.  Intricate refined details of her clothing (**layered skirt**, **exposed breasts**) and **intense glare staring straight ahead**.When creating human figures in sculpture, the Minoans stuck to the same tall, slender figures similar to their paintings. Some of the almost life-size nude sculptures are carved from stone and layered with ivory and gold, very similar to later Greek sculptures, hinting that the Minoans may have been the early influencer or originator of the style *chryselephantine*.

The Decline of Minoan Civilization 

So, what caused the decline of Minoan civilization in the 15th century BCE? The  Minoan civilization started to decline sharply around 1450 BCE, though the exact cause is still debatable, and nothing has been proven.

Many believe that the advent of the Iron Age played a major role as people no longer needed so much bronze, leading to the decline of the Minoan in the market. Others believe that the rise of Mycenaean civilization and their dominance of the island of Crete a few decades later contributed to the decline of Minoan civilization. The other explanation is the catastrophic explosion of the volcanic island of Thera, modern-day Santorini, which could have produced a tsunami of epic proportions and destroyed the island of Crete.

## D. The Mycenaeans Civilizations (1600–1100 BCE)

During the Late Bronze Age, the ***Mycenaeans ***were at their height in the Peloponnese Peninsula of southern Greece between 1600 and 1100 BCE. They were a warrior society that conquered their neighbors and raided settlements by both land and sea, gradually building their wealth and power. They controlled more than one hundred city-states across the Peloponnese and were the most powerful Aegean civilization before the rise of ancient Greece. **Mycenae **was the most dominant among Mycenaean city-states. 

A categorized society was developed with royalty, priests, and warriors forming the upper classes with regional differences; however, the common Mycenaean culture characteristics were art and architecture. Mycenaeans were also known to trade with neighbors like Anatolia (modern-day Turkey), Egypt, and Mesopotamia, further accumulating their wealth.0

Mycenaean Art and Metalwork

Mycenaeans adopted many traditions from the Minoans and excelled at creating frescoes, pottery, jewelry, armor, and sculptures. While Minoan art is known for being more natural, Mycenaean art is **more stylized and has more abstract** forms and images. Like Minoans, they decorated the walls of palaces, private homes, and other buildings with massive frescoes.

At first, the Mycenaeans imitated Minoan designs that decorated the whole surface of the vessel which evolved over the years in different shapes and sizes. Mycenaean pottery shows Minoan plant and animal life and the Mycenaean fascination with warrior scenes and warfare. They added more patterns and designs and left open space in their jars. While plain clay vessels were affordable to everyone, decorated jars catered to an elite clientele.

The Mycenaean warrior elites were buried with death masks—a funerary representation of the deceased. The **Death Mask of Agamemnon**, a 16th-century BCE gold funerary mask named after the **legendary king of Mycenae** from Homer's The Iliad, is the most famous death mask.

Mycenaean Fortifications

Because of their warrior culture, the Mycenaeans built walls of massive rough-cut stones stacked tightly together with no binding agent. The fortifications of Mycenae were known as ***Cyclopean walls******,**** *and they measured about 45 feet tall and at least 20 feet thick.

The Mycenaeans also excelled at the corbelling technique to create archways called the **corbel arch. **In the** corbel arch **rows of stones extend slightly past the one under it, forming a relieving triangle, an open space that keeps weight off the lintel. The **corbel vault** is a series of corbel arches placed together to make an open space or walkway.

The Decline of Mycenaean Civilization

With the Bronze Age Collapse of the 12th century BCE began the decline of Mycenaean Greece, but it laid the foundation for the rise of Western Civilization. The vibrant material culture, art, and architecture of the Mycenaeans influenced the ancient Greeks.

Ancient Greek pottery was crafted by potters with their bare hands. The potters created vessels from regional clay, known as **keramos**, which was easily available in the nearby countryside. The most popular are *Corinthian clay *(pale and buff-colored) and A*ttic clay* (deep red).  Potters developed vessels mainly for utilitarian reasons, such as transporting or storing water or food.

## F. Classical Greece

Subsequently, after the end of the Mycenaean civilization around the 12th century BCE, the people and territories of Ancient Greece slowly emerged anew. The trade exchanges with their Mediterranean neighbors allowed for the movement of goods and ideas, which set the stage for later political and artistic revolutions on the Greek mainland.

Classical Greek Sculptures: Discobolus (460–450 BCE)

Most of the early Greek sculpture was inspired by Egyptian and Eastern style art, especially in their renditions of the human form. Greeks were the first culture to portray the most realistic and accurate figures possible. Ancient Greek sculpture is known for portraying lifelike figures later inspiring others in the field of sculptors. 

***Discobolus*** by Myron of Eleutherae is believed to introduce greater boldness of pose and a perfect rhythm, subordinating the parts to the whole. The sculptor was an Athenian from the mid-5th century BCE. He worked almost exclusively in bronze and was popular for his work on representations of athletes.

| **Study Note: **Discobolus  (460-450 BCE) Myron's *Discobolus*, or "discus thrower,"  was the first piece to successfully portray a moment of balance and harmony. The original *Discobolus*, crafted in bronze, has been lost to history and is known only through its Roman marble copy. |
| --- |

Classical Greek Architecture: Elements of Design

Greek architectural styles remained consistent over large periods because they were constructed with precise mathematical and scientific approaches. The **three main elements of architectural relief** are entablature, capital, and pediment. First, an **entablature** is a horizontal element that is on top of the columns of Greco-Roman Classical style buildings or similar structural supports in non-Classical buildings. The entablature is divided into three sections:

- **Architrave: **The bottom horizontal base

- **Frieze: **The decorative element that may include relief sculptures.

- **Cornice: **The decorative horizontal element below the roofline.

Second is the **capital, **the structural columns, and the upper base of the column is called the capital, and it supports the entablature.

| Lastly, **the pediment **is a triangular gable—a wall that extends to fill the space underneath the two slopes of a pitched roof—which is an element of Classical and Neoclassical architecture. |  |
| --- | --- |

| **Study Note:**** **Classic Greek column The ratio between the diameter of the shaft at the base of the column and its height is used to determine the height of the column. |
| --- |

Classical Greek Architecture: Orders of Columns

Moreover, the Greeks developed three orders—the Doric, the Ionic, and the Corinthian. It became a fundamental part of Rome’s architecture and, subsequently, much of Europe and the United States. These were developed in different parts of Greece and at different times. The difference between the columns, their capitals, and the entablature above them define the distinction between the orders. 

**The Doric Order**

The simplest of the orders is the Doric order which has smooth or fluted columns with circular capitals. Above the simple columns, the entablature elements add a more intricate decorative accent. 

**The Ionic Order**

The Ionic column has **volutes** (Latin for scroll), as a decorative element at the top of the capital. A narrative frieze is intended to run the length of the structure thanks to the entablature's design.  

**The Corinthian Order**

## H. Ancient Rome: Kingdom, Republic, and Empire (753 BCE–476 CE)

Rome, founded in **753 BCE** by brothers Romulus and Remus (so legend has it), has been the site of some of the most significant events in human history. It was a center of power and influence for centuries and the world's largest city during the Roman Empire at its height that included the entire Italian peninsula, much of Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. Historically, the Roman Empire is divided into **Republican Rome** (509–27 BCE), when Rome was governed by the aristocracy, and** Imperial Rome** (27 BCE–476 CE) when Rome was ruled by emperors.

During the** Republican Rome**, archaic culture continued and the conquest of Greece becoming a part of the Roman province led to the blend of Greek and Roman art and culture. Under Roman general Sulla (82–79 BCE), Roman artworks began to appear, ultimately leading to identifiable Roman artistic culture. 

Meanwhile, during **Imperial Rome**, each leader’s reign emphasized different art forms. For instance, under Augustan (27 BCE–14 CE), the fusion of the Greek styles and Italian naturalism prevailed. Meanwhile, the Julio-Claudian (14–68 CE) dynasty is characterized by extravagance, and imperial portraiture was used for propagandistic purposes. Lastly, during the period of Flavian (69–98 CE), Rome underwent major rebuilding, including the construction of new aqueducts and canals.

Eventually, the influence of Roman art is seen in the Italian Renaissance and on contemporary art forms. Roman Architecture and Engineering

Brick and Mortar Masonry

The Roman Arch

The Romans are considered the first builders in Europe, perhaps the first in the world, fully to appreciate the advantages of the arch, the vault, and the dome. The Dome

# Chapter 6: An Empire Divided - Rome and Byzantine (272–1453 CE)

Overview

This chapter will explore how the spread of Christianity led to the division of the Roman Empire into the Western Roman Empire and the Eastern Roman Empire (called the Byzantine Empire). Additionally, it will show the notable artworks and architecture of the two empires, starting from when Christianity was illegal until it was legalized.

Objectives 

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- explain why Rome and Byzantine split

- describe the key characteristics of artworks and architecture from Rome and Byzantine

Spread of Christianity (40–600 CE)

In the first century CE, the **Apostle Paul **actively spread Christianity to the Greek and Roman cities of the ancient Mediterranean world. He encountered the religious and cultural experience of the Greco-Roman world in cities like Ephesus, Corinth, Thessalonica, and Rome, which played a major role in the formation of Christianity. Christianity was then eventually adopted as the official religion of the Roman Empire by **Emperor Theodosius **in 380 CE, thereby ensuring its spread across the Western world and beyond. However, this adoption led to religious and political division in the Roman empire between East and West. The Western empire declined, but the East grew into the Eastern Byzantine Empire.

Aside from Emperor Theodosius, another prominent figure in the spread of Christianity is **Emperor Constantine. **He was a patron of the arts and built many churches. He was also the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity in 312 CE. In 313 CE, he issued the Edict of Milan officially legalizing the Christian religion in the Roman Empire. Lastly, in 330 CE, he moved the capital of the Roman Empire from Rome to Byzantium (Constantinople).

## A. Christian Rome  - The Western Empire (380–476 CE)

During the early Christian days, Christianity was considered illegal, and anyone found guilty would be punished by seizing their property or even getting killed. Because of the punishment by death afforded to people discovered to be Christian, several Christian artworks were kept a secret.

| **Did you know?** The first known Christian artworks are the ichthys. These were depictions of fish with an acrostic for the Greek words meaning, ''Jesus Christ, God’s Son Savior. '' |
| --- |

Roman Christian Art (Before Edict of Milan)

Christianity was illegal before the Roman emperor Constantine issued the Edict of Milan. Before the Edict of Milan, Christian artwork could be found in the catacombs or hidden underground tombs. In Rome, many people would cremate their loved ones and keep the remains. However, as Christians believed in the resurrection of the body, they needed a place to bury them. They did so in the catacombs built into the soft volcanic stone underneath the city.Frescos, or art written directly into plaster, were common in the catacombs and were described as crude. Early depictions of Christ in the catacombs portrayed him as “The Good Shepherd.”  *The Good Shepherd *is an image of Christ as a shepherd who lays down his life for his sheep

Roman Christian Art (After Edict of Milan)

In 313 CE, the emperor Constantine issued the Edict of Milan, which legalized Christianity, removing the persecutions previously leveled on Christians. This meant that they could practice their religion openly. Christian artists could now use their faith in their art forms, including artistic sarcophagi, sculptures, mosaics, and illuminated Bibles.

Sarcophagi  

In the 4th century, early Christians no longer had to hide their dead in the catacombs. Now, they could bury them in sarcophagi or stone caskets. The earliest ones included traditional Roman images, but later examples include depictions of Biblical scenes rather than life-sized human figures that showed wishes for the afterlife. Over 2000 of these sarcophagi exist today.Mosaics 

After the Edict of Milan, under Constantine’s rule, Christian churches began to develop. Glass mosaics were used in these churches differently than how they were used before. Instead of just using them to decorate floors, they used them everywhere, including on walls and ceilings. They were made of bright, colorful glass and used on floors, ceilings, and walls.

Illuminated ManuscriptsElaborate artwork could not be entailed in scrolls because the paintings would get ruined when the documents were rolled up. During the early Christian period, written documents slowly moved from being on papyrus scrolls to vellum or parchment, which could be stored flat. These pieces of papyrus could be collected together in a book, “codex,” thus leading the world to artistic documents. Early Christians started to add new illustrations called illuminated manuscripts to their Bibles. These illustrations were used to accompany a text.

Vienna Genesis is one very well-known illuminated Bible and also one of the earliest surviving Bibles of its type. Instead of creating a single image, the Vienna Genesis contains a whole sequence of events, much like a comic strip.

While the Edict of Milan was an important development in the history of Christianity, it was not a total replacement for traditional Roman beliefs. Roman religious beliefs changed slowly over time. The Roman Empire did not become Christianized overnight. Christianity was still growing when the Western Roman Empire fell in 476 CE. It emerged from Jewish traditions and was influenced by Roman cultural and political structures for many centuries.

Roman Christian Churches: St. Peter's Basilica

Early Christian worshippers gathered in house churches that would have a baptistry with frescoes of the Good Shepherd on the wall along with Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden. Early Christian house churches often used symbolism. For example, mosaics with the art of Bacchus, the Roman god of wine, with scenes of vines and grapes could be seen from a Christian viewpoint as an homage to the Eucharist,  which is a ceremonial portion of the Mass in which bread and wine are thought to become the body and blood of Christ.

| **Did You Know?** The oldest house church that is now known to survive is in **Dura-Europos**, Syria, a town that was once ruled by the Romans. |

With Christians being allowed to practice publicly, there was no longer a need to disguise their houses of worship. They moved into Roman basilicas and later began building churches on the basilica plan. 

A Roman basilica is characterized by a row of pillars supporting a roof that encloses a long, open space called the nave. Often, the basilica had a semi-circular area called an apse at the far end of the nave. Romans often used basilicas as official, secular meeting spaces, while Christians devoted this architectural style to their churches incorporating elements from pre-Christian religions. 

The **Old St. Peter's Basilica** is one of the best examples of the basilica plan in early Roman church architecture. It was built over the burial place of St. Peter, the first pope of Rome, in the 4th century CE. Its interior was shaped like a **cross** and was structured in a way that visitors and worshippers travel across the building on a sacred journey from outside the building to the altar, where the mystery of the Mass was made visible to those who had been baptized. Additionally, ***The Pieta**** *(1498–1499) by Michelangelo is one of the most well-known artworks in the Basilica of St. Peter.

## B. Byzantine - The Eastern Empire (395–1453 CE)

The Eastern Roman Empire that existed after 395 CE was referred to as the Byzantine Empire by Historians. The term “Byzantine“ derives from the original name for the capital of the empire, Constantinople. The city was originally known as Byzantium until the Roman Emperor Constantine moved the capital city to Byzantium and renamed it Constantinople, which is modern-day Istanbul, Turkey. The Western Roman Empire was declining, and the eastern half was getting richer and more politically stable, which was one of the reasons he moved to the capital city. 

After the death of Constantine, the split between the East and West became permanent and was governed by separate emperors. The Western Roman Empire finally fell in 476 CE, but the Eastern Roman Empire continued for nearly 1,000 years.

Byzantine Visual Arts & Iconography

The Byzantine Art period (330–1453 CE) is divided into three parts: **Early** (330–730), **Middle **(843–1204), and **Late** (1261–1453). The Byzantine Empire contributed various forms of art, including paintings, iconography, statues, and mosaics. The characteristics of Byzantine art forms continued into early Christian art forms, mainly Christian artwork which can be found in Christian churches throughout the world. Byzantine art had heavy Greek Christian themes blended with Byzantine imperial religious advocacy. Unlike Christian art which is mostly religious, Byzantine art mixes religion with politics. We can witness religious-secular combinations in Byzantine art because of many reasons:

- Some emperors tried to unite their empires with the Christian religion. 

- In the Byzantine Empire, its emperor had authority over the Church.

- Roman-style imperialism stayed in the East much longer.

Byzantine Paintings

The major form of Byzantine painting was **frescoing**, especially on basilicas. Byzantine artists were not equipped to create three-dimensional paintings as they did not have any techniques to illustrate shadows; however, they used complicated patterns to intricately illustrate religious figures.

**Wood panels** were also painted so that people could bring images of religious figures with them while they traveled. Scriptures and other religious artifacts were also painted, and paintings in this medium mixed themes of religion with secular life by pairing sacred characters with secular activities.

Eastern Orthodox religious icons had a **gold background with distinct halos **and a cartoonish look.  Most icons were religious, and a handful of them included numerous pictures that symbolized a different religious or secular story. Today St. Catherine's Monastery has the largest collection of Byzantine icons.

Byzantine Iconography & Iconoclasm

Byzantine iconography is a form of artwork rather than a medium, and it significantly impacted Christian artwork. An icon is a symbol of a religious person, especially of Christ, made for worship. Icons were typically painted on wood or made with mosaic tile. The majority of Byzantine icons were painted wood panels and, no matter in what form they were created, were seen as direct representations of the figures they represented. Icons became extremely important as some members of the Catholic Church at the time believed that images of religious figures carried the same spiritual effects as if those people were directly interacting in their lives. Their backgrounds were often solid gold or solid colors to prevent inadvertently placing these religious figures in any earthly context.

In the Byzantine Empire by the 8th century CE, there was a conflict about the role of an icon in the church. There were **iconophiles **in favor of the icons, while the **iconoclasts **wanted all icons destroyed saying that they violated the second commandment on idolatry. 

Emperor Leo III started a movement called Iconoclasm in the 8th century CE and prohibited the use of icons and persecuted the creators.  He ordered that icons portraying the deity, the saints, and religious stories be removed and destroyed. Icons were considered to amount to the worship of additional gods and hence were ordered to be destroyed. This order was ended by Empress Theodora, widow of Emperor Theophilus, in 843 and allowed the return of icons to places of worship. Today, Eastern Orthodox churches remain rich sources of icons.

Byzantine Mosaics

A **mosaic** is an artwork made by combining small cubes of stone, glass, ceramic, or another material to create a pattern or image. The ancient Romans used mosaics to decorate floors like the Baths of Neptune in Ostia. Sometimes they used small, colored tesserae that enabled them to appear almost like paintings. Later, the Byzantines frequently used mosaics **to decorate the walls and ceilings of churches**. Mosaics were the costliest form of monumental decoration in Byzantium and were generally favored by imperial and other elite donors.

Like early Christians, the Byzantines created their mosaics out of colored glass. The first Byzantine mosaics were created by Roman craftsmen who had previously created Greek mosaics celebrating the **Pantheon of Greek deities**. Their techniques and use of materials like glass, stone, and ceramic were used in work assigned by Emperor Constantine I. This style of mosaic work became popular in the Christian church, and as it spread through Europe and the Middle East, **gold and precious stones** were added to the mosaics.

The imperial mosaics in the church of San Vitale in Ravenna depict the 6th century. Byzantine empress Theodora across from her husband, the emperor Justinian.

Byzantine Architecture

With heavy influence from Classical Roman architecture and Early Christian architecture, Byzantine period architecture is famous for its grandeur in church design. One of the most influential Byzantine emperors,  **Justinian I** (r. 527–565 CE), was influenced by Constantine's Early Christian style architecture, such as the use of mosaics in the walls, ceilings, floors, and panels, a focus on the apse at the end of the nave where the altar is located, and the use of high windows called a clerestory above the ground floor of the nave to let light into the church. In sum, Byzantine architecture is characterized by religious structures that utilized **domes**, **pendentives**, composite order **capitals**, **mosaics**, an **apse**, **clerestories**, and a **central-plan design**. However, the difference between Early Christian architecture and Byzantine architecture was that the **Byzantine churches were grander, bigger, and more awe-inspiring**; everything was more—more windows, more columns, more mosaics, and more domes.

|  | The interiors of Hagia |

The most famous example of Byzantine architecture is the **Hagia Sophia **in Istanbul, commissioned by Emperor Justinian I. The Hagia Sophia, which means Holy Wisdom in Greek, was originally built as a Greek Orthodox church of the then-Byzantine Empire, in the city of Constantinople. The earliest structure started in 360 CE, but burned down twice, and then was rebuilt a third time in 537 under the rule of Byzantine Emperor Justinian. It was converted into a mosque by 1453 when the Ottomans conquered the region. The building has endured significant damage as well as changes in the empire and in power.

# Chapter 7: The Middle Ages (500–1500 CE) 

Overview

This chapter will introduce you to the Middle Ages, including the historical events that preceded it as well as the characteristics of art and architecture from the Early Middle Ages until the High Middle Ages and the Gothic Awakening.

Objectives 

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- explain how Charlemagne, feudalism, and monasticism shaped the art and architecture of the Middle Ages

- discuss the key characteristics of Islamic, Romanesque, and Gothic art and architecture 

The Middle Ages

What we call the “Middle Ages'' in Europe began soon after the collapse of the Roman Empire in 476 CE and lasted from c. 500 to 1500 CE. This was a dangerous and chaotic time characterized by famine, plague, ignorance, a lack of scientific and cultural development, and war which is why the first five hundred years of the Middle Ages are sometimes called the “Dark Ages.” However, most scholars discourage the use of this term as it is pejorative and does not accurately describe the period. Hence, “Middle Ages” refers to the time, whereas “Medieval” (Latin for “middle age”) is used to describe the people, places, and things of that time. Additionally, this period is divided into:

- The Age of Charlemagne and Feudalism (800–900 CE)

The Middle Ages in Europe occurred between the fall of the Roman Empire (476 CE)  and the start of the modern format of European countries (c. 1500 CE). Despite the wars and plagues, the Middle Ages would not last forever, and soon the Western world would be slowly but surely reformed through a series of revivals in learning, culture, and technology that would eventually see the Middle Ages end and the Renaissance begin in earnest.

## A. The Early Middle Ages (476–1000 CE)

As mentioned earlier, the Early Middle Ages was a **time of war **(the Crusades 1096–1291) and **plague **(the Black Death 1346–1353). Due to the collapse of the Roman Empire, and the stability it established across Europe and the Mediterranean, various warlords rose in prominence to fill the power vacuums left behind, leaving death and destruction in their wake. Simultaneously, the **Christian church** became far more influential and proceeded to ban certain religious and cultural practices across parts of Europe, as well as destroying advanced Roman knowledge sources, including architecture, medicine, literature, philosophy, and engineering, claiming it to be of pagan origin and heretical. 

Moreover, the hierarchical order of Heaven and Hell in society was expressed via **feudalism**, a social system establishing a ranking system from peasants to royalty. Likewise, **pagan cultures **were blended with Christian cultures helping to spread the arts, religion, and new learning methods.

Feudal Europe

The system of feudalism gained popularity across Europe after the Fall of the Roman Empire as a way to establish peace and order and to protect against barbarian invasions and Viking raids. As war and the Vikings conquered populated cities, small estates, and manors began to develop. They were owned by nobles and were communities that operated with a small government. An aristocratic landowner would have peasants who lived and worked on the land but were bound by a military oath to serve the landowner in battle.

As feudalism became more widespread, it shaped early medieval art and led to more elaborate homes for wealthy landowners. Stone castles were built to better protect the land. Similarly, arts at this time centered around feudal values, including romanticizing the heroic deeds of someone fighting for the landowner.

Early Medieval Art

Early medieval artists combined techniques from Byzantine Christianity with those from ancient Rome and Greece, with the decorative style of the northern pagans, which are characterized by curving forms and exaggerated features. By including familiar artwork and cultural elements from non-Christian (pagan) groups, the Christian church made it easier for non-Christians to relate to and eventually convert to Christianity.

Specifically, art in this period featured ornate patterns, bright colors, and Christian-themed symbolic imagery (religious iconography). Notable artworks from this period are mosaics in the apse of the Basilica of Sant'Apollinare in Classe, Ravenna, Italy (600 CE) and the *Golden Madonna of Essen* (990 CE).

Also, **metalworkers** were in high demand to craft elaborate armor decorations, book covers, chalices, jewelry, and more.  Two of the most important kinds of metalwork created during the early medieval period were the **reliquary** and the **chalice**. This kind of art was created by  heating various metals, usually bronze or silver, molding them into various designs as well as in-laying them with precious metals and jewels. They were popular with the Church because of their sturdiness and long-lasting nature.  

Reliquaries

The veneration of saints was a fundamental feature of medieval Christianity, which led to the worship of relics (the physical remains of holy persons).

A **reliquary** is an object containing a sacred relic, often a piece of cloth, hair, or bone from a saint. They were typically constructed of precious materials and often depicted scenes from the saint's life and Biblical history.  During the Middle Ages, reliquaries were of  incredible importance and led some people to go on long pilgrimages to pay homage and pray to them, in the hopes of receiving a miracle in return. Some of the significant reliquaries are the *Reliquary of St. Elizabeth* and the silver reliquary casket found in Italy.

Chalices

Meanwhile, a chalice is a cup that traditionally holds the sacramental wine used during the Christian Eucharist ceremony. These cups were often made of precious metal and sometimes decorated with jewels. The gold goblet symbolizes family and tradition. During the early Middle Ages, the iconic status of these cups increased significantly.

This ceremonial usage dates back to the early days of the church. Many iterations of the chalice have been used in the Eucharist since Jesus ordered his disciples to "Do this in remembrance of me." (Luke 22:19). It is also related to the apostle Paul's account of a typical Eucharistic rite in 1 Corinthians 11:24–25.

Early Medieval Architecture

Architecture from the early Middle Ages is known for its immense **westworks**, usually western-facing front entrances to larger churches. It also included high towers and many slightly pointed arches. Also, mosaics, frescoes, and relief sculptures were often placed in churches or monasteries to be used as a visual aid for regular church-goers as well as monks or nuns studying the Bible. Also, hand-written, **illuminated manuscripts** were also created in these monasteries. The religious texts had more sophisticated and intricate designs that differentiated them from earlier manuscripts. 

| **Did You Know?** Many art pieces were also portable to allow them to be taken on “tour” to other towns and churches, as well as to make them easy to remove and escape with if the church or town were to be attacked by marauding armies. |

The Age of Charlemagne (800–900 CE)

Apart from the influence of feudalism, Emperor Charlemagne (747–814 CE), a Frankish king, is also credited with promoting early medieval art and architecture. Charlemagne started on 25 December 800 CE when Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne as the new Roman Emperor, officially reviving the title in Western Europe over 300 years after the Western Roman Empire fell in 476. In doing so, the Pope formed a powerful political bond between the Roman Catholic Church and the secular “Roman” emperor, thus establishing the new Holy Roman Empire which would last from 800 to 1806 CE.

In this empire, Charlemagne became the first emperor. He made various institutional changes that culminated in the Carolingian Renaissance, a period of cultural flourishing characterized by advances in the arts and Latin literacy. To his credit, Emperor Charlemagne was intent on restoring this reborn Roman Empire to its former glory, which included the implementation of several reformations that led to new advancements in the arts, philosophy, law, music, literature, architecture, and engineering. 

He also opened several schools for boys, headed by monks and clergymen, to increase literacy rates and increase public education, even ordering the consistent creation of illuminated manuscripts from monasteries (one of the few places regularly producing written work). His royal court emphasized the value of education, and those that could read were held in higher esteem. Likewise, he oversaw the production of books depicting his life.

Though he passed only 14 years after becoming Emperor, the trend he began led to a widespread resurgence in art and literature across the empire. This would come to be known as the **Carolingian Renaissance**, and though it only lasted 100 years it contributed directly to the end of the Dark Ages and marked the beginning of new artistic and educational initiatives across western Europe.

Carolingian Illuminated Manuscripts

Until the invention of the printing press in 1440 CE, all texts were laboriously handwritten and some people would spend their entire lives meticulously copying one text or another. In the early middle ages, nuns and monks of monasteries trained in reading and writing and would hand-copy the Bible (or other religious texts) and paint ornamental designs on the pages with elaborate borders and miniature illustrations, and often with burnished silver and gold paints.

These texts are called illuminated manuscripts (“illuminated,” from the Latin “illuminare,” which means “lighted up,” referring to colorful paintings and designs) and they became popular collectible art pieces for the nobility and high-ranking clergy in the later Middle Ages.

The Rise of Islam (610 CE)

As the Byzantine Empire grew and the western Roman Empire declined, the Islamic faith developed in Arabia and spread across Afro-Eurasia. Like Christianity and Judaism, Islam was monotheistic, and it is the third of the Abrahamic religions. It has **five pillars**:

- **Shahada**: The essential declaration of faith ("There is no God but God (Allah), and Muhammad is His Messenger" is made three times in front of a witness to become a Muslim.

- **Salah**: It is the ceremonial prayer directed toward Mecca five times a day.

- **Zakat**: It is an obligatory donation to charity.

- **Sawm** is the obligatory fasting during Ramadan month.

- **Hajj: **It is a five-day pilgrimage to Mecca that must be done at least once in a Muslim’s lifetime. Doing so is thought to cleanse each pilgrim's sins before God.

Moreover, Islam was founded by Prophet Muhammad in 610 CE, in what is now Saudi Arabia. Islam started to quickly spread from 632 until the middle of the 8th century, following mass conversions and successful conquests by Muslim rulers, controlling many areas in the  Middle East, India, North Africa, and Spain. They beat two of the most powerful empires back then, the Byzantines and the Sassanids, to establish an empire that extended from Central Asia in the east to Spain in the West. After the 8th century, they expanded further into sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia. Still, its growth often created tensions and conflicts between Jews and Christians. 

Islamic Art 

As Islam is practiced all over the world, Islamic art covers a diverse range of styles. It depicts abstract forms rather than recognizable figures or objects and is mostly dominated by geometric shapes and calligraphic patterns. Calligraphy, which is the use of stylized letters, can be seen in Islamic architecture and illuminated books. Patterns drawn from nature such as leaves and plants can be seen in the art forms in mosques, buildings, and textiles.

| **Did You Know?** The most unique trait of Muslim art is the non-representation of human figures. It is in line with Islamic teachings that are a manifestation of aniconism (the belief that human beings should not be reproduced in art). |

Islamic MosaicsThe most popular Islamic mosaics can be found in mosques, which are places of worship for Muslims. Complex works of mosaics decorate these mosques which are adorned with towers called minarets. Such unique styles and patterns are also witnessed at madrasahs where they learn about law and theology.

Islamic Paintings

Islamic art forms can also be found as miniature paintings in illuminated books on poetry and other subjects. As these paintings were so small and could not be displayed in public they were not deemed to violate Islamic rules against idolatry which stopped them from making images of human figures. This type of Islamic art developed in Persia which came about after cultural exchanges with China and thrived in Persia and South Asia. 

Islamic Rugs and Textiles

Persian carpets are known for their beauty and elaborate construction for more than a thousand years. They contain typical Islamic art design patterns with geometric forms and are also known to contain human figures. It was an important source of trade and cultural exchanges and also became a very important economic activity in the Ottoman Empire. 

Islamic Architecture

The most popular examples of  Muslim architecture are mosques and **madrasahs**. However, there are many other structures including tombs, palaces, forts, and city government buildings. Though with the spread of Islam across the continents their architectural style became more diverse some characteristics remained consistent in Islamic architecture including domes, arches, minarets, Muqarnas vaulting, and girih tiles. The domes, arches, and tilework are some of the influences of Christian architecture.

Islamic architecture focuses more on the interior structure. From the outside, the exterior, especially of homes, looks simple and typically similar. The interior may have bright colors with details. Usually, the architecture from the outside does not display the signs of wealth, which is reserved for the family inside as it is intended to promote privacy and minimize social tension.

## B. The High Middle Ages (1000–1300 CE)

Monasticism

For the majority of the population of Medieval Europe, religion, and Christianity in particular, was a central component to their lives, often dictating the laws and norms of their societies. It was so important that many people joined monasteries to dedicate themselves to religious piety and worship. Monasteries are religious institutions that house monks and nuns who live by a set of religious vows that are often specific to the monastery itself and are called monastic orders. Furthermore, Christian monasticism is based on the desire to live within a structure and severe self-discipline to bring oneself closer to God. Consequently, monastery architecture reflected their minimalist approach  to life. Abbeys were constructed for monks to live in. They often had cloisters, which were arched walkways leading to a courtyard.

As monasteries grew in wealth and influence they became centers for learning (akin to early universities) and, subsequently, brought advancements to art, architecture, medicine, technology, and more. With this growth came the desire to demonstrate their devotion even further through ever more impressive religious art pieces and larger churches to hold them. Eventually, they copied and furthered techniques from the Ancient Romans to meet the needs for the kinds of churches and monasteries they required, thus beginning what would be called the Romanesque Period.

| **Did You Know?** Christian monasticism is based on the desire to live within a specific social structure with strict self-discipline to maintain a constant awareness of God's presence. |

The Influence of Pilgrimage on Romanesque Art & Architecture

The increase in **pilgrimages** (journeys to sacred destinations) significantly impacted the arts. More visitors meant larger churches were needed which promoted building innovations and the return of Roman architectural techniques (Romanesque) like arches and barrel vaults that dispersed weight and allowed for larger, more open structures. The rise was, in part, due to the Christian belief that the world would end in the year 1000, which caused people to travel far and wide to seek solace in their faith at sacred sites. When the world did not end, the pilgrimages continued but this time in gratitude that the world did not end. Such journeys were seen as significant acts of faith and were encouraged by the church.	

Eventually, the influx of funds from pilgrims led to an abundance of jobs for artists and architects alike as demands for **more reliquaries and bigger churches** to accommodate pilgrims increased. As a result, art and architecture of the period flourished, incorporating Roman characteristics with Medieval styles. Likewise, romanesque churches also introduced side chapels for pilgrims to view relics in, which gave the churches new, elaborate layouts.  For instance, the **Basilica of Saint-Sernin, Toulouse, France **(1096 CE) is an important stop on the pilgrimage road through southwestern France to Spain.

## C. Romanesque Art and Architecture

The Romanesque period, as the name suggests, refers to a point in the middle ages when art and architecture took on Roman-like characteristics. This change came about for two reasons: 1) a rise in monasticism and the monasteries needed to accommodate the religiously dedicated, and 2) a boom in early Christian religious tourism where pilgrims would travel vast distances to see sacred religious artifacts. 

As such, **Romanesque art** is the art of Europe from c. 1000 CE to the rise of the Gothic style in the 12th century. It was greatly influenced by** Byzantine art** (especially in painting) and the stylizations of the** Insular art **of the British Isles. ***The Bayeux Tapestry***** **(c. 1070 CE), for instance, is a 20-foot-tall and 230-inch-long Romanesque embroidery artwork, which illustrates these characteristics.

Architecture-wise, Romanesque churches rivaled the beauty and size of Gothic churches from the Holy Roman Empire. Romanesque architecture was also commonly used for medieval Christian religious structures and is identifiable as stark, heavy, and monumental in size. The period's architecture is directly linked to the major Romanesque art characteristics that focus on visual storytelling through painting, sculpture, and architecture.

In sum, what makes Romanesque Art distinct is the:

- Monumental size with sturdiness and weight

- Small windows, thick walls, round arches, and symmetrical layouts

- Religious themes

- Striking primary colors with decorative narration

- Human forms, animals, landscapes, and depth in abstract

- Compositions in tight spaces

During early Christianity, idolatry was avoided, hence early Romanesque architecture lacked ornamentation, but with time, many religious structures were incorporated for visual storytelling in the form of artwork.

Romanesque Style

In terms of painting, the style of Romanesque paintings exhibits abstract figures, flat, symmetrical, and rigid. They are found in an architectural setting, on illuminated manuscripts, on a tapestry, or on a framed panel depicting religious themes or scenes.  Romanesque walls and ceilings became a popular place for Romanesque painting because of the large space and flat walls seen in religious buildings like churches, monasteries, and abbeys.

Meanwhile, Romanesque sculpture was used to adorn columns, pilasters, reliefs, capitals, panels, niches, and moldings. Figurative sculpture focused mainly on biblical themes and appeared abstract, flat, and lacked a sense of depth and realism. The sculpture adorned churches, monasteries, and abbeys to educate the people by depicting biblical scenes. Also, churches back then had distinct features as shown in the images below.

Church, monasteries, and abbeys were popular, and eventually, the style spread into all types of buildings in Medieval Europe.

## D. The Gothic Awakening

The Gothic art period began when Gothic architecture spread out of France and its ideas and innovations spread throughout Europe from the 12th CE to the 15th CE when the early Renaissance began. It enlarged the ideas of the Romanesque period to a grand scale. Initially, the Gothic period of art focused on architecture, but as the movement spread throughout Europe, sculpture, painting, stained glass windows, illuminated manuscripts, and frescoes were also created in the Gothic style. 

Moreover, the design, layout, and decoration of churches built during the Gothic period revolutionized buildings throughout Europe, and these buildings were notable for their ornate decoration, their height, and the delicate appearance of both their interiors and exteriors. 

Gothic Art & Architecture

Gothic architecture was notable for its ornate decoration, its massive height, and the appearance of delicate work on their exteriors and interiors. It adopted the rounded arches and vaulted ceilings of the  Romanesque style of building and enlarged and executed them on a grand scale.  The advancement of Gothic architecture was also, in part, due to **Abbot Suger** (pronounced soo-jay), the Abbot of the abbey of St. Denis. He was a revolutionary architect and the inventor of the gothic flying buttress, one of the elements of gothic architecture.Elements of Gothic Architecture

The main characteristics of Gothic architecture are:

- Stained glass windows

- High and pointed arches

- Ribbed vaults

- Flying buttresses

- Ornate decoratio

# Chapter 8: The Renaissance and Reformation

Overview

In this chapter, we will discuss the various ages of the Renaissance, including  the Italian, Early, High, Late, and Northern Renaissance, and the events preceding this era. We will define the characteristics of this period and detail elements of Renaissance art and architecture.

Objectives 

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- identity the painters dubbed as the Early Masters and Renaissance Trio

- match the Renaissance paintings to the correct artists 

- describe the key characteristics of Italian, Early, High, Late, and Northern Renaissance art and architecture

Key Events Leading to the Renaissance

The advent of the Renaissance in Florence depended on some key events that took place over a period of centuries and eventually contributed to defining this era as the Renaissance Period.

1) **The Crusades **(1096–1204) - there were holy wars between Christians and Muslims throughout the Middle ages which exposed much of Europe to new learning from **Arabic** scholars including art, math, and architecture.

2) **The devastation of a widespread plague** called the **Black Death** (1347–1351) which killed over 25 million people (a third of the entire population of Europe at the time)

3)** The influx of wealth and resources** from **furthering the trade routes **established by the Roman Empire that connected to the Silk Road throughout Asia, as well as the initiation of the **Age of Discovery** which opened trade and colonization across much of the world.

A Cultural Revival

The Renaissance is known as a period of great artistic creation and intellectual and cultural renewal. Many artists attempted to create their paintings and sculptures as realistic as possible making this era one of the most important and artistic eras in history. The Renaissance centered on the rediscovery of** Ancient Greek and Roman philosophy, sculptures, and architectural techniques** that contributed to a revival in art, science, and engineering in parts of Italy. The innovations during this period are linked to various events that happened before and during the late 14th century to the early 17th century. 

Historically, the Renaissance was the period in European history that came after the end of the *Black Plague* in the **Middle Ages**. The period right before the Renaissance is called **Proto-Renaissance (1300–1425)** or pre-Renaissance, which transpired from the Late Middle Ages to the beginning of the Renaissance. During that time, France and England were going through the **Hundred Years' War**, and Italian artists like **Giotto** and **Donatello **moved away from Medieval artistic forms and created more realistic forms of art.

Moreover, the Renaissance overlapped with the periods of **Reformation, the Age of Exploration, and the Elizabethan Era**, which led to political and religious upheavals and advances in arts and sciences. Similarly, the invention of the **Gutenberg printing press** in Germany was a major innovation made during this era. It helped to spread innovations all over Europe and beyond. 

The philosophy of **humanism** also shaped culture and arts during the Renaissance. This  Greco-Roman-inspired secular philosophical movement encouraged the study of the Classics and what it meant to be human. As a result, artworks often exhibited mythological themes from Greece and Rome, and Christian and secular themes were depicted as human-like figures rather than larger-than-life beings. This was in contrast with medieval art where God and the supernatural were at the center of their art forms.

For instance, the subjects of paintings usually have calm, simple faces (but there are exceptions, such as in Michelangelo’s *The Last Judgment*, 1536–1541). In Early Renaissance art, the subject’s feet are not firm on the ground, giving the illusion of floating forms (e.g., Botticelli's *The Birth of Venus, *c. 1484–1486) - but High Renaissance art becomes more realistic. 

Given the spread of innovations, analysis of the Renaissance period is often divided into four:

- Italian Renaissance (1400–1600 CE)

- Early Renaissance  (1400–1490 CE)

- High Renaissance (1490–1527 CE), including Mannerism (1520–1620 CE)

- Late Renaissance (1520–1620 CE)

## A. The Italian Renaissance (1400–1600 CE)

After the key events that transpired over a period of centuries, the Renaissance centered in **Italy**, primarily around the city of **Florence **circa 1400 CE before spreading further through Italy and eventually around the rest of Europe. Florence was a major center of trade and commerce during the Middle Ages. At the time, Italy was a collection of independent and wealthy city-states. Each city-state was governed in its own way—some were ruled by hereditary nobles and others were republics, with elected leaders. However, the real power in the city-states rested in the hands of wealthy merchant families, who served as bankers to the rich and powerful. Competition between city-states often caused political and economic conflict.

One of the prominent wealthy merchant families is the **Medici family**. They engaged in politics, built churches and hospitals, and commissioned several prominent artists. Other wealthy leaders in Italy’s city-states also spent huge amounts of money on the arts and learning as a show of wealth, power, and influence and as a dedication to the growing philosophy of  **humanism**. This is an ideology that placed man, not religion, at the center of intellectual inquiry and artistic production. Nonetheless, religion was not excluded by Renaissance humanism; rather, it was given more human characteristics in religious depictions.

Renaissance Culture and Art

The philosophy of humanism also shaped culture and arts during the Renaissance. This  Greco-Roman-inspired secular philosophical movement encouraged the study of the Classics and what it meant to be human. As a result, artworks often exhibited mythological themes from Greece and Rome, and Christian and secular themes were depicted as human-like figures rather than larger-than-life beings. This was in contrast with medieval art where God and the supernatural were at the center of their art forms.

For instance, the subjects usually have **calm**, **simple faces** (but there are exceptions, such as in Michelangelo’s *The Last Judgment*, 1536–1541). In Early Renaissance art, the **subject’s feet are not firm on the ground**, giving the illusion of floating forms (e.g., Botticelli's *The Birth of Venus, *c. 1484–1486) - but High Renaissance art becomes more realistic. Some of the most well-known artists from this period were **Raphael**, **Donatello**, **Michelangelo**, and **Leonardo da Vinci**.

Vitruvian Man (1490)

**Leonardo's** observation of natural phenomena, his understanding of science, and his sense of mathematical proportion were very influential. His seminal ink drawing **Vitruvian Man **(1490) depicts a nude man in ideal human proportions inspired by the architectural proportions advanced by the Roman architect **Vitruvius** in his* De **A**rchitectura* (30–15 BCE).

| Vitruvian Man | The drawing is filled with Leonardo's writing that illustrates his deep scientific inquiries into anatomy. For example, "the length of the outspread arms is equal to the height of a man." It holds a unique distinction in aligning art, mathematics, science, classicism, and naturalism |

Elements of Renaissance Art 

Renaissance art can be categorized into three media:

- **Sculpture: **The creation of three-dimensional figures made out of marble, bronze, wood, clay, etc.

- **Painting: **Producing two-dimensional images on canvases, walls, and ceilings

- **Architecture: **The creation of buildings, including churches.

Each of these media had unique techniques that flourished during the Renaissance, such as chiaroscuro, fresco, linear perspective, and sfumato.

Chiaroscuro

The term **Chiaroscuro** comes from  the Italian ''light-dark,'' where the words “chiaro” means ''bright'' and “oscuro” means ''dark.'' It is an artistic technique that was first developed in the Renaissance and is a term used in art to describe the **interplay of light and shadow**. Chiaroscuro paintings typically have high contrast between light and dark, **highlight human anatomy **to give figures weight and proportion, **emphasize important figures**, and focus attention on the painting's subjects. 

| Early Chiaroscuro *The Tribute Money* (1420) by Masaccio | Late Chiaroscuro *St. John the Baptist in the Wilderness* (1605) by Caravaggio |

Chiaroscuro provides a sense of drama and intensity that is striking. During the Renaissance, **oil paints took over tempera **which was the Medieval technique of combining egg yolk, water, and a pigment to make paint. Although it is often used in painting, chiaroscuro can also be applied in woodcuts, drawing, photography, and film. Along with chiaroscuro, many artists used techniques like:

- **Linear perspective:** objects appearing smaller the further away they are 

- **Sfumato: **a smoky-shadowy way of modeling to make their works more three-dimensional and detailed.

**There are 2 types of Fresco:**

- **Buon Fresco** “true fresco” – paint applied while the plaster is still wet

- **Fresco Secco** – “dry fresco” – painting on dried lime plaster

## B. The Early Renaissance (1400–1490 CE)

Many works honoring the vitality of the human body, spirit, and mind were produced in the early Renaissance. Early Renaissance artists conveyed their philosophy of **humanism** through their realistic depiction and adoration of the human forms in visual art, sculpture, and architecture. These can be seen in their use of chiaroscuro, naturalism, linear perspective, and religious subject matter. Some of the prominent artists in this period are Filippo Brunelleschi, Donatello, and Sandro Botticelli, who are all dubbed as the early masters.

Characteristics of Early Renaissance Art

**Chiaroscuro**: Early Renaissance painters made many of their works true studies in contrast between dark and light shades making subjects appear more three-dimensional than before.

**Naturalism**: The Early Renaissance artists reached back to Greek and Roman sculpture to make their subjects look as true-to-life as possible.

**Perspective**: Early Renaissance artists used linear perspective to give an illusion of depth to their art. 

**Religious subject matter**: Artists of the Early Renaissance sought to humanize religious figures like the biblical Magi or the Virgin Mary (or the Madonna) in new ways along with inspiration from Greek and Roman mythology.

The Early Masters

Filippo Brunelleschi (1377–1446)

Filippo Brunelleschi was the first great architect of the Renaissance period. His most notable work is designing the** dome of the Florence Cathedra**l, which was considered a Renaissance engineering marvel. 

For centuries the technology to create large domes was not used anymore until Brunelleschi reinvented it to create such a structure with the utilization of the advancements in both mathematics and engineering.

Donatello (c. 1386–1466)

**Donato di Niccolò di Betto Bardi**, or simply **Donatello**, was the **first great Renaissance sculptor**. He was a master sculptor who worked in **bronze** and **marble **and is also known for his relief work and wooden sculptures. He played a key role in differentiating Renaissance sculptures from the late Gothic style. His work was not only classically inspired and realistic but highly theatrical and full of psychological undertones. He portrayed his subjects with realism, in a highly realistic manner.

**Statue of David (1430–1440 CE)**

His most famous **sculpture is David**, a statue of the biblical hero created for the Medici family in the 1430s. It was the first free-standing bronze statue of the Renaissance and the first nude sculpture of a male since antiquity.

Aside from the Statue of David, Donatello is also known for ***St. George***, a marble sculpture. This sculpture was commissioned by the Guild of the Armorers and Sword Makers, the Arte dei Corazzai e Spadai, to decorate the external niches of the Orsanmichele church in Florence. St. George was a Roman soldier who was martyred because of his Christian faith. 

Sandro Botticelli (1445–1510)

**Alessandro di Mariano Filipepi**, known as Sandro Botticelli, was an Italian Renaissance artist from Florence who became known for his paintings depicting **religious and mythical themes** of classical antiquity.

A favorite of the Medicis, he painted many Madonnas, as well as humanist allegories of classical inspiration such as* ****The Birth of Venus *****(1486 CE)**.** **It is unique in that it is not religious and was one of the first Renaissance paintings to show **a nude figure in a non-religious context**. This painting displays Botticelli's talent for depicting graceful human forms. 

It draws characters from ancient Greek and Roman mythological stories, like **Zephyr** (the god of wind), the **nymph**, and **Venus** (the Roman goddess of love and beauty). Since Venus is a goddess, she is the literal embodiment of divine beauty and love, and Botticelli seemed to be suggesting that celebrating the physical beauty portrayed in this painting is one way to contemplate the divine. 

## C. High Renaissance (1490–1527 CE)

Artists during this time utilized and perfected various techniques from Early Renaissance artists including the use of **linear perspective **to create **extreme depth, highly accurate **and** scientifically correct depictions of human anatomy**. They used  foreshortening of figures and subjects in the elevated paintings and sculptures to provide an authentic viewing experience and stage effects to seamlessly incorporate architectural elements into a work of art. The presentation of works with the utmost aesthetic, symmetrical, and compositional excellence was the main goal of the High Renaissance painters. Three of these prominent artists are Leonardo, Michelangelo, and Raphael. 

The Trio of Renaissance Masters: Leonardo, Michelangelo, & Raphael

**Leonardo da Vinci**, **Michelangelo,** and **Raphael** are undoubtedly the period's most notable legends. Many new styles arose that were groundbreaking for the time like **sfumato** which revolutionized the blending of tone and color with a glazing effect and ceiling paintings that drew the gaze of viewers up into heavenly features.

Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519 CE)

**Lionardo di ser Piero da Vinci**, aka **Leonardo da Vinci**, was not only a noted renaissance-era artist, and sculptor, but also a polymath who has been called the father of architecture, ichnology, and paleontology, among other fields. 

He was also an engineer, scientist, cartographer (mapmaker), inventor, philosopher, urban planner, and anatomist. His observations and findings, written in his notebooks, were added to other collections, including the *Codex Leicester *(1510) and the *Codex Arundel* (1480–1518

His intellectual curiosity led him to make scientific considerations and sketch out **inventions such as flying machines** and **armored vehicles** based on observed reality. His work epitomizes his artistic approach: strange and metaphysical, covered with mysterious light, the technique of sfumato, chiaroscuro, and accurate distance perspectives. He is also known for introducing a perspective of clarity in his artwork which was similar to linear perspective but showed distant objects as less distinct. His most notable works are ***The Mona Lisa*** and ***The Last Supper***.

Michelangelo (1475–1564 CE)

**Michelangelo di Lodovico Buonarroti Simoni**, or **Michaelangelo** was a versatile man who found success in many fields. He was a poet, painter, and architect but considered himself a **sculptor** first and foremost. His most famous architectural  achievement is the **redesign of St. Peter’s Cathedral in Rome**, where he added an enormous dome and completed the work previously planned by Bramante and Raphael.

He  is still considered by many to be the greatest sculptor of all time. His sculptures depict powerful and heroic, bodily perfection that portrays a perfect combination of the human and the divine, which was the epitome of the **Humanistic philosophy of the Renaissance**: the body expresses the spirit. 

The models from classical antiquity inspired his works, which greatly influenced Western art.

Michelangelo's David (1501–1504)

Michelangelo's ***David*** is notable for its detail–realism, and mannerism. It is a 17 ft. tall marble sculpture depicting the biblical David, the killer of Goliath, holding the slingshot over his shoulder. It was commissioned by the Opera del Duomo for the Cathedral of Florence.

Michelangelo’s The Battle of Cascina (1504)

Aside from *David, *Michelangelo is also known for ***The Battle of Cascina,*** a never-completed painting in fresco. Historically, *The Battle of Cascina* (1364) was a famous Florentine military victory over Pisa which Michelangelo attempted to represent in this image.

The Sistine Chapel Frescoes

His paintings on the ceiling of **The Sistine Chapel frescoes** in the Vatican in Rome are his masterpieces. He created some of the world’s most artistic images of complex  dynamic figures full of raw human power and divine spirit. These paintings are unforgettable and inspired the later Mannerist period of art. 

Raphael (1483–1520)

**Raffaello Sanzio da Urbino**, simply known as "**Raphael**," was a very successful High Renaissance painter and architect. He is popular throughout modern-day Italy and the Vatican for the masterpieces he created - altarpieces, various depictions of the *Madonna* paintings, portraits, and Christian-related scenes often built into arches and chapels, such as the *Mond Crucifixion* (1503). He was later appointed as Chief Architect of the Vatican in 1514 by Pope Leo X, which was the beginning of his career as an esteemed architect.

He was a leading figure of Renaissance classicism and used the artistic style of classical ideas and figures in the form of natural interaction with one another. His work is known for its realistic features and incredible clarity of form and light. His work has influenced many artists and his later works even helped usher in the Baroque period.

The School of Athens (1509–1511)

His first work at the Vatican was in the **Stanza della Segnatura** where his famous masterpiece ***School of Athens***** **was created. 

It is a massive composition of figures and architecture with elements of major Renaissance paintings.

The School of Athens has portraits of ancient philosophers, and likenesses of Leonardo, Michelangelo, and himself.

Transfiguration (1516–1520)

Raphael's last painting was **Transfiguration**, which was finished by his apprentices due to his death in 1520. It is notable for its dramatic lighting, the mixture of heavenly and earthly spheres, and floating figures in clouds which is ideal Renaissance period art and a blueprint for the pictorial elements used in Baroque art. Many consider this painting to be the critical moment in the **Mannerist movement **that took over realism.

## D. Mannerism (1520–1620 CE)

**Mannerism in art** means the style of painting, sculpture, and architecture that began in Europe at the end of the High Renaissance. It was originally set in Rome and Florence marking the **end of the High Renaissance** and the **beginning of Baroque**. Among the great Mannerists, **Michelangelo** is considered the founder of Mannerism even though he started as a High Renaissance artist. Some of the other greatest Mannerists include **Titian**, **El Greco**, **Giambologna,** and **Parmigianino**. 

Characteristics of Mannerism

Many Mannerism artworks often display the following unique characteristics:

- **Decentralized composition **- Human figures in the art were not in perfect proportions and were twisted.- **Tense poses **- Elongated limbs, and heads were smaller than the bodies and stretches of the stylized face. Usage of peculiar positions made their tense poses seem difficult and artificial.

- **Artificial Look **- Mannerism paint was more artificial because human bodies were twisted and in different forms where the bodies were unnatural.

- **Virtuosity **- Mannerism artists wanted to show and express their skills in their work instead of producing realistic art. 

- **Strange colors **- Used contrasting and rich colors where deep dark colors were combined against lighter ones.

Specifically, Mannerist paintings are full of **exaggerations**: floating angels, the confusion of illusion and reality, contorted and elongated figures, awkward spatial relationships, and strange lighting effects. One of the iconic Mannerist paintings is ***The Madonna with the Long Neck*** (1535-1540) by Parmigianino. It features the following elements:

- Elegant, stylish, aristocratic, and courtly composition.

- Subject is from a simile in medieval hymns that compares the Virgin’s neck to a great ivory tower or column

- Tall Madonna and large Christ child – looks more dead than asleep - foreshadowing his crucifixion 

- Madonna has a long neck and rubbery fingers

- Her cloth clings to her body – unusually sexual for a Madonna image

He created images that are still potent today by fusing Byzantine, Mannerist, and Venetian Renaissance styles there. He rejected “perfection” and preferred a realistic approach, “warts  and all.”

Born in Flanders, Giambologna (aka Giovanni da Bologna / Jean Boulogne) studied in Rome where he considered Michelangelo a great influence. ## E. The Late Renaissance: The Reformation and Counter-Reformation (1520–1600 CE)

The **Protestant Reformation** (c. 1517–1648) was a movement that divided the Christian Church into the Roman Catholic and Protestant branches. The split had a massive impact on all aspects of European society at the time. It was triggered by **Martin Luther** (1483–1546) posting his** Ninety-five Theses** to a church door on October 31, 1517, in Germany which contained his complaints about the Christian Church. He and several other German priests publicly broke away from church leaders over corruption, greed, and other abuses within the church.

Later on, the **Counter-Reformation (1545–1648 CE)** was the Catholic church’s response to Luther’s Protestant Reformation. The goal was to restore Catholicism's predominance and centrality One of the ways the Church aimed to do this was to support the arts and encourage a new art style that was simple but dramatic, realistic in depiction, and clear in narrative. Ultimately, this led to the **Baroque style** of the 17th century, which will be discussed in the next chapter.

## F. Northern Renaissance (1430–1580 CE)

The “Northern Renaissance” was the **importation of Italian artists and styles to the rest of Europe** as monarchs used riches from the Americas and Africa during the Age of Exploration to expand their wealth and influence, attracting artists and architects to their courts for new building projects and artworks. This is partly a result of the iconoclasm that came from the Protestant Reformation, which changed the face of Northern Renaissance art, leading to humble works, presenting a more toned-down view of everyday reality, and art that was accessible to the new burgeoning merchant classes. As the artists rejected ideas of the Medieval Era, the Northern Renaissance helped to bring Europe out of the Dark Ages. 

Moreover, artists during this period used techniques similar to the Italian Renaissance but did not have the same themes throughout the artwork or tools, which resulted in different styles. Specifically, art during this period displays the following features:	

Jan van Eyck (1385–1441 CE)

One of the distinguished artists during this period was ***Jan van Eyck******, ***a Flemish painter credited with popularizing the use of oil paints and a master of Northern realism. His works include subtle detail and mastery of color, light, perspective, and pictorial space. He is the acknowledged master of Northern realism because of the portrayal of realistic style in his art. One of his notable works is the ***Portrait of a Man*** which many believe to be his self-portrait. A pun on the artist's name, "Als Ik Kan" (which translates to "As best I (Eyck) Can"), is written on the frame. 

His other work, ***The Arnolfini Wedding*** depicts the wealthy merchant Giovanni Arnolfini and his wife. It is famous for its **realism** and **deep symbolism**:

- Height of both figures is the same (gender equality)

- Religious symbolism: single lit candle in the chandelier, stained-glass windows in the background, iconography in background mirror

- Chandelier symbol of merchant’s wealth

Albrecht Dürer (1471–1528)

Another notable artist during the Northern Renaissance is **Dürer** who is seen as the first genuinely humanist artist of the Northern Renaissance. Through his travels and prolific artwork, Dürer helped to bring the Renaissance out of Italy and into Europe. He is renowned for the extensive detail in his paintings, woodcut engravings, and prints. In his ***Self-Portrait *****(1500)**, he portrays himself as Christ-like, including a hand partially raised as if in blessing. Similar to earlier representations of Christ, though more confrontational in its directness and dark, bold tones.
