# Chapter 9: The Baroque Period (1584–1723 CE)

Overview

This chapter will review how the Baroque period first arose and then will highlight the famous Baroque artists and their artworks, as well as the important architecture of the period.

Objectives

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- identify the prominent Baroque artists and their paintings

- discuss the key characteristics of Baroque art and architecture

## A. The Baroque Period

With the Catholic Counter-Reformation and the creations of Italian artists Annibale Carracci and Caravaggio by the late 16th century, a new art movement emerged. Their artworks helped the art world transition from Renaissance pastels to the dark, shadowy Baroque era. The art movement is believed to have originated in Rome at the beginning of the 17th century, but the term "Baroque" is believed to come from the French word "barroque" (irregularly shaped) or Portuguese “barroco” (irregular pearl).

Moreover, the Baroque style can best be described as extravagant beauty. The 17th century was a time when modern science and modern government were developed. As such, palaces, sculptures, and other art in this period was a quest to create immaculate beauty. European countries used money from their colonization and trade exploits to fund their palaces and baroque artwork. Hence, as this new style swept throughout Europe, the Baroque mastery of light and shadow was applied to all aspects of painting while the overall movement impacted everything from literature to music and philosophy.

## B. Baroque Art & Architecture

In terms of style features, the Baroque style **de-emphasized the use of figures** in their painting, and paintings of **still lifes** and **landscapes** gained popularity.  Additionally, Baroque paintings are characterized by the use of **saturated jewel tones** and brilliant light to show a new perspective. Sometimes, elaborate decoration, jewel tones, and glistening light were also seen in baroque paintings. Likewise, baroque artists portray **strong emotions**, such as euphoria, excruciating anguish, or profound despair. The Baroque mastery of light and shadow was applied to every part of the artwork as this new style spread throughout Europe. In the succeeding section, let’s see how this style is expressed in Dutch paintings, the works of Peter Paul Rubens, Rembrandt, Jan Vermeer, and Sir Christopher Wren.

Peter Paul Rubens (1577–1640)

Peter Paul Rubens was a **Flemish** painter known for his Rubenesque style. His paintings are characterized by his experiments with **chiaroscuro** (the interplay of light and dark on the canvas), his work with oils like Caravaggio, and his signature "**Rubenesque**" style. This style features paintings of voluptuous, fleshy, and rounded female figures. This was inspired by other Flemish naturalist painters who chose to depict real-life domestic scenes and women rather than idealized bodies.  In some of his paintings, illuminated figures stand out against dark backgrounds. Additionally, **religious themes**, which were typically court or church commissions for different locations, inspired Rubens’ works. However, Rubens also produced a significant amount of secular art, including paintings of **myths, historical events, portraits, and hunting scenes**. Some of his important works are *Portrait of Marchesa Brigida Spinola Doria *(1606), *Elevation of the Cross* (also called *Raising of the Cross*, 1610), *The Judgment of Paris *(1636), and *The Honeysuckle Bower *(1609).

The Honeysuckle Bower (1609)

This painting is a self-portrait of Rubens and his wife  Isabella Brant. The pair is depicted in the picture as a full-length double portrait while seated in a honeysuckle bower. They are surrounded by **symbols of love and marriage:**  the garden and honeysuckle traditionally symbolize love, while the holding of the right hands signifies marriage. Also, Rubens portrays himself as an aristocratic gentleman holding his sword in his left hand. 

## C. Dutch Baroque (1600–1750)

The Dutch succeeded in capturing the drama and majesty of Baroque painting better than any other region. Black was commonly utilized, dark colors predominated, and these painters were great masters of applying light. *The Night Watch *(1642), Rembrandt's most well-known work, is regarded as the best painting of this movement and, by some, the best Dutch painting ever created. This large piece is approximately twelve feet by fourteen and a half feet in size. The main character stands out in his black clothing even though the bulk of the scene is shaded. 

Additionally, the Dutch used common people as subjects. In his paintings, Vermeer frequently showed common people going about their daily lives. Food and everyday objects, and still lifes were also very popular. Some of the greatest works of Dutch Baroque art are shown below:

Rembrandt van Rijn (1606–1669)

Rembrandt, a Dutch painter and etcher, is renowned for his explorations and manipulations of light in both his portrait and landscape paintings. Rembrandt's style employs the **chiaroscuro **technique, which plays light and dark elements against one another in a painting to express emotion, depth, and movement.  Moreover, he has a **signature angle **for his subjects, which is evident in his portraits. This angle features subjects with faces partially covered by darkness. The lit side of the sitter's face is highlighted by the darkness, emphasizing their expression and compassion. Lastly,  he also established the benchmark for excellence in the **art of etching** (printing from a metal plate with incised lines that have been etched away by acid).

The Storm on the Sea of Galilee (1633)

Rembrandt’s *The Storm on the Sea of Galilee* is a painting that blends elements from modern Dutch fishing settings with the religious subject matter. Each character's particular response to the storm is shown in amazing detail. In this painting, Rembrandt exemplifies his capacity to convey narrative, motion, and emotion. 

Self Portraits (1652)

Rembrandt produced 80-90 self-portraits, and the majority of art historians divide these into **three time periods**: the **1620s**, when Rembrandt was still refining his techniques, such as chiaroscuro; the **1630s and 1640s**, when he frequently portrayed himself as a successful, prosperous artist; and the** 1650s and 1660s** when he was examining the frailties and peculiarities of old age. Researchers wonder about Rembrandt's decision to devote so much time to his paintings and drawings. Here are a few of the speculative causes: 

- He used self-portraits to examine his personality because he wanted to understand himself through his art.

- He only chose himself as a model for rehearsing his depictions of human positions, attitudes, and roles since he was simply polishing his artistic technique.

- He merely produced self-portraits because they were in high demand. 

Nonetheless, his decision could be based on a combination of these three reasons.

      Johannes (Jan) Vermeer (1632–1675)

Dutch painter Johannes Vermeer (also known as Jan Vermeer) was born in **Delft**, Netherlands, where his influence was confined until he gained posthumous fame among younger generations. He is credited with 34 paintings, which tend to emphasize peaceful **home **settings and the **use of gentle, serene light**. His subjects are frequently **ladies **engaging in musical, creative, or relaxing pursuits at home. Furthermore, in his portraits, the positioning of the person and the accessories are very intriguing. He frequently recycled items like apparel, furniture, tapestries, and jewelry, and he often incorporates artworks into his paintings.  Some of his most famous Vermeer paintings are *Girl with a Pearl Earring* (1665), *A Lady Writing* (1665), and *The Art of Painting* (1668). 

The Milkmaid (1657–1658)

*The Milkmaid*, also known as *The Kitchen Maid*, is an oil painting on canvas by Vermeer. A milkmaid, a woman who milks cows and produces dairy goods like butter and cheese, is depicted in the artwork gently pouring milk into a short earthenware container on a table in a basic room. The painting is remarkably illusionistic and conveys not only specifics but also a sense of the woman's and the table's weight. According to art critics, despite the painting’s brightness, it doesn't wash out essential texture or flatten the volume of the maid's thick waist. Meanwhile, the shadow on the woman’s face makes it difficult to interpret whether the downcast eyes and pursed lips of the woman express wistfulness or concentration. 

Girl with Pearl Earring (1665)

Vermeer’s *Girl with Pearl Earring *is a **tronie**, which depicts a particular kind of character and observes the model's facial emotions. Vermeer's use of the **underpainting method** enhances the composition and form, allowing the girl to come to life on the canvas. According to experts, he might have also used a **camera obscura** to help with the placement of the light reflection and the shape of the pearl. This was a small opening in the side of a box or tent with dark walls. The scene would be projected onto the camera obscura's pitch-black wall. 

| **Study Note:** Girl with Pearl Earring The pearl that stood out in the painting was a fake, and  only two paint strokes were used to paint it. At that time, pearls were considered status symbols. |
| --- |

Sir Christopher Wren (1632–1723)

Unlike Rubens, Rembrandt, and Vermeer, **Sir Christopher Wren** was a renowned English architect who is also a mathematician-physicist, anatomist, astronomer, and geometer. After the Great Fire of London in 1666, he was given the job of rebuilding 52 churches in London, including St. Paul's Cathedral on Ludgate Hill (1710). This is considered to be his masterpiece. Others in his office, including Nicholas Hawksmoor, are now more frequently credited with having had the primary creative responsibility for a number of the churches. Wren also designed the south front of Hampton Court Palace, the Old Royal Naval College in Greenwich, and the Royal Hospital Chelsea. 

St. Paul’s Cathedral (1675–1710)

The English Baroque and Neoclassical styles are combined in the construction of Saint Paul's Cathedral in London.   Its structure is modeled after an ancient basilica. The West Front of the cathedral features an impressive entrance, a dramatic dome, a nave, a transept, a quire, and an apse, as well as exquisite interior embellishments. The major gathering place for worshipers is the nave. Although the cathedral also features Neoclassical, ancient, and medieval characteristics, its overall design is English Baroque.

# Chapter 10: The Rococo Style and Neoclassicism

Overview

This chapter will begin by detailing how the Rococo style significantly deviated from the Baroque period and will then explain how, in response to Rococo, the Age of Enlightenment gave rise to Neoclassicism.

Objectives

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- identify the famous Rococo and Neoclassical artists and their artworks

- discuss the key characteristics of Rococo and Neoclassical styles

## A. The Rococo Style (1702–1780)

Rococo was an artistic style characterized by a mixture of grand intricacy with lighthearted frivolity, which discards the grand manner of the Baroque period. Rococo favors peaceful, pastel-colored scenes with dreamy atmospheres. Specifically, Rococo artworks often:

- Appear lighter and more delicate

- Have lovely textures that signify opulence or great expense

- Have feathery foliage and fantasy landscapes

- Associated mostly with decorative arts: pastel colors; irregular, curvilinear shapes (based on plant forms), delicate lines, and soft textures.

- Use sensuous colors, fluid forms, and lively movement

- Treated with a lighter touch, thereby appearing light-hearted or light-headed

- Enjoyed by pleasure-loving aristocracy

- Known for benign scandalous and decadent

Considering these qualities and emphasis on salon decor, this style primarily aimed to impress one's guests or onlookers. Note that this style originated in 18th-century France with a culture based on Paris’ salons, which held weekly social gatherings with dining and entertainment sponsored by wealthy women. Consequently, Rococo painters often depict leisure and love in their artworks.

Jean-Honoré Fragonard (1732–1806)

Fragonard was a French Rococo painter regarded as the father of the Rococo movement and the first Rococo artist. He also popularized the **fête galante** style, a style depicting the themes of fun, play, celebration, and light-heartedness. Specifically, his works display scenes that rejected typical ideas of morality for playful hedonism, lust, and irresponsibility. Some of his key artworks include the *Pilgrimage to Cythera* (1717), *Embarkation to Cythera* (1717), *Pierrot* (1718-19), *The Italian Comedians* (1720), *The French Comedy* (1714), *The Pleasures of the Ball* (1717), and *Merry Company in the Open Air* (1716-19). Likewise, his famous paintings are shown below.

## B. Neoclassicism (c. 1660–1850) 

Age of Enlightenment (1685–1815)

An influential aesthetic that permeates several media is **neoclassical art**. It reached its zenith of acceptance during the **Age of Enlightenment**. The French Revolution and the neoclassical painting movement were both influenced by the Age of Enlightenment, which encouraged the pursuit of knowledge via science and reason. During this time, **deism**, the belief that God created the universe to operate by rational laws became popular. People believed that everything has a cause and all ideas come from experience. Similarly, it was also widely believed that human knowledge was perfectible through reasonable thinking and reason, and human progress was inevitable but was mainly hindered by social intolerance and injustice. Thus, intellectuals and philosophers used writings to educate and provoke new thought.  Consequently, these beliefs permeated the art world and condemned Rococo art for being immoral and indecent, thus calling for a new, moral style of art—**Neoclassicism**. 

Characteristics of Neoclassicism

In contrast to the lavishly ornate rococo style that predominated French painting in the 18th century, Neoclassicism emphasized clear lines, a harmony of solid-looking shapes and logical space, crisp clarity, and harmonious proportions.  Moreover, Neoclassical art usually has a somber tone and aims to evoke the order of ancient Greece and Rome, harmony, and reason. Neoclassical painters often portray ancient historical scenes, and they made an effort to dress their figurines in historically appropriate garb. Generally, they included Classical themes in their works, but they did not adhere to Classical forms as closely as other artists did. In sum, neoclassical artists modernized Greek and Roman Classical subjects and forms.

Additionally, **Neoclassical architecture **was pushed by numerous modern politicians, such as **Napoleon Bonaparte**, as a method to associate themselves with Rome’s power. Additionally, many Neoclassical artists, such **Jacques-Louis David**, employed Classical motifs and historical references to illustrate **patriotism**. Generally, Neoclassical works are characterized by:

- Abstract and moral

- Imposed universal ethical principles

- Depicted scenes from ancient history

- Versatile (at different times it used to revive the grandeur of Versailles to demonstrate the good tastes of the middle class, and to educate and civilize the unsophisticated)

- Sculptors focused on realistic and idealized forms painted or carved in marble, while painters did not emulate ancient forms as much as subjects.

In the next section, let’s see how Napoleon coordinated with the painter Jacques-Louis who led the neoclassical movement in painting.

Jacques-Louis David (1748–1825)

Jacques-Louis David was the most famous French neoclassical painter of his generation and was central to the French Revolution (1789–1799), during which he expressed the ideals of democracy in his paintings. Following the French revolution, Napoleon encouraged David and gave him commissions for his paintings. In 1812, Napoleon invaded Russia aiming to defeat them. When Napoleon lost control, David fled to Brussels and continued to paint there until his death. Through exact proportions, excellent composition, and careful use of light and **dark**, David united the influences of the Renaissance, the Baroque, and Roman Antiquity to express subjects dramatically. Hence, his works had Roman influences while embodying the **leading principles of neoclassicism**: 

- Clean lines

- A balance between solid-looking forms and logical space

- Harmonious proportions

- Sharp clarity

Moreover, David used a severe classical sculptural style in his paintings to revive antique art and provide nobility to images of the French Revolution and Napoleon’s empire. 

Throughout his career, David created numerous outstanding works of art, including politically charged historical paintings like the *Oath of the Horatii *(1784), *The Death of Socrates *(1787),* Belisarius Asking for Alms* (1781), and *The Intervention of the Sabine Women *(1799).

Oath of the Horatii (1784)

David’s *Oath of the Horatii *painting depicts a scene from a Roman legend about a dispute between two warring cities and stresses the importance of patriotism and masculine self-sacrifice for one's country. It also signifies the ending of the corrupt aristocracy and returning to the democratic republic ideals. 

Death of Socrates (1787)

*Death of Socrates *is a painting by David in which Socrates' suicide is framed as a heroic and admirable deed in yet another tale of stoic self-sacrifice and dignity. The muscular body of the elderly philosopher, depicted in the stark setting of his prison cell, is designed to convey his moral and intellectual stamina. Without any doubt or second thoughts, he sits up straight and prepares to gulp down the bowl of lethal hemlock; he would rather die than deny his beliefs. His students exhibit a range of emotional reactions to his execution as he continues to lecture with his arm raised in an oratory gesture until he is killed. Plato's account of the event is referenced in David's picture, connecting it to a classical source; yet, David uses artistic license to change the setting for a more dramatic impact. 

| **Fun Facts about Neoclassical Art** Neoclassical art is a style of art that emerged in the mid-18th century and was influenced by the classical art of ancient Greece and Rome. Neoclassical artists were interested in reviving the ideals of classical art, such as balance, proportion, and simplicity. One of the most famous neoclassical artists was Jacques-Louis David, who is known for his paintings of historical and mythological subjects. Neoclassical art was often used to convey political messages, as it was seen as a more serious and dignified style than the more frivolous and ornamental rococo style that preceded it. Neoclassical art was popular in Europe and North America during the late 18th and early 19th centuries, and it influenced the development of other artistic movements such as Romanticism. Some famous neoclassical works of art include David's *T****he Death of Socrates ***(1787), Canova's ***Pauline Borghese as Venus Victrix ***(1808), and Thorvaldsen's ***Agamemnon's Fight with Achilles ***(1804). |

# Chapter 11: Romanticism (c. 1780–1850)

Overview

This chapter will first discuss how the Age of Revolution gave rise to Romanticism, and how the values of Romanticism differ from the Enlightenment values. We will then explore the famous figures of Romantic Art and their artworks.

Objectives

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- differentiate Romanticism from the Enlightenment

- identify the famous Romantic artists and their artworks

## A. The Age of Revolution (c. 1775–1848)

In the 18th century, the Industrial Revolution (1750–1840) modernized the economy with the proliferation of industries and advanced machines and technology. These changes did not only revolutionize the economy, but also the way of living at that time. In response to major political and industrial changes of the time,  a spirit of revolution spread across much of Europe and the world in the 18th century.  One of the notable revolutions then was the **American Revolutionary War** (1775–1783), part of the **American Revolution** (1765–1791), an ideological and political revolution in British America. This revolution emerged from the competition of European nations to colonize parts of the Americas to capitalize on their natural resources. Inspired by the win of the Americans there, the French also started the **French Revolution **(1789–1799). It caused the death of King Louis XVI and was concluded when Napoleon Bonaparte rose to power. Ultimately, this abolished the monarchy and established a democratic nation. All this movement for change embraced a dedication to the principles of equality, reason, and representative government, which were also expressed in succeeding art movements.

## B. Romanticism

The Romantic century (1798–1850) is deemed as a counter to the perception of the Enlightenment values of an orderly, systematic, and rational approach that had dominated western thought for more than a century. See the following differences between Enlightenment and Romanticism:

| Enlightenment | Romanticism |
| --- | --- |
| Followed Classical Greek and Roman | Followed Medieval Gothic |
| Valued order and structure | Valued imagination, emotion, and expression |
| Upheld reasoned reasoning | Upheld spirituality: mysticism, the occult, and nature |
| Advancement of modernism | A refusal of modernity |
| Modern society leads to happiness | Happiness can be discovered in the simple and primitive. |

Moreover, romantic art was influenced by the **French Revolution **and Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s philosophy called **The Social Contract. **The latter became the conceptual foundation for the desired social and political freedoms of the time. However, the popular conception of the romantic is different from the **romantic era **(1798–1850); the romantic era was not about romance but rather a conviction that the use of **emotions is as significant as the rational scientific method**. Thus, romantic art has a distinctive appearance due to the following: 

- The **landscapes **represent various regions of the globe. 

- Artists were inspired by their **national pride**. 

- Artists valued **imagination** and exercised their** freedom of expression**.

Since the Romantic movement encouraged artistic freedom to convey national pride, it is not known for any major architectural innovations. Hence, the best way to describe this period is as a philosophical movement that places a strong emphasis on emotion and imagination by utilizing the following elements:

- The process of producing dramatic effects through  light and shadow

- The use of the sublime in paintings to elicit a stronger emotional response

- The painting of pensive figures, historical ruins, demons, and monsters to explore the darker side of existence

Lastly, the sublime served as a tool for romantic writers and artists to elicit reactions from their readers. The theory contends that fear and inspiration are both present in a person's sense of relief after fleeing a scary circumstance, and one makes use of that amazing sensation to increase their level of enjoyment. In the succeeding section, let’s see how Goya, Constable, and Delacroix applied these techniques in their artworks.

## C. Romantic Artists

Francisco Goya (1746–1828)

Francisco José de Goya y Lucientes is a Spanish painter and engraver regarded as the **precursor of Romanticism**. Similar to how romanticism is influenced by emotions and imagination, a glorification of the past, exploring a deeper life, and a return to the origins, the subjects of Goya’s paintings and the impulse behind their creation are **desperation and melancholy**, the idea to "fight against the darkness" and the return to the source. However, his works changed as a result of his vicissitudes, illnesses, deafness, and all social changes. For example, his ***Los Caprichos ***(1798) painting uses satire to depict the foolishness and irrationality of Spanish people and the elite.  Similarly, his ***The Third of May 1808*** (1814) aimed to testify and denounce violence and war after **Napoleon Bonaparte **invaded Spain. Later, he relocated to Quinto del Sordo outside Madrid where he painted the ***Black Paintings ***(c. 1819–1823), which reflected his loneliness and desperate circumstances.

John Constable (1776–1837)

John Constable is an English painter and draftsman frequently regarded as the greatest "**naturalist.**" People say that he only painted locations that he was familiar with, which other artists tended to overlook. During his time, his single-mindedness in portraying a narrow range of locations made him unique, whereas his excellence in oil sketching was unmatched by his peers. Some of his important works are  *The White Horse *(1819; see image to the right), *The Hay Wain* (1821, and *The Leaping Horse* (1825).

Eugene Delacroix (1798–1863)

French painter Eugène Delacroix became well-known as the founder of French Romanticism in his later years. Throughout his career, Delacroix employed several painting techniques that significantly affected his paintings, most notably **bold brushstrokes and color splashes**. He painted violent, chaotic, and sexually explicit situations because he wanted to challenge his audience. This approach would eventually result in his masterwork ***Liberty Leading the People**** *(1830; image to the left). Here, he used a **triangle **as the core of his composition, and the fighters' dead bodies are placed at the bottom of the canvas.  Some of his other famous paintings include *The Barque of Dante *(1822), *Massacres at Chios* (1824), and *Death of Sardanapalus* (1827).

Jean-François Millet (1814–1875)

French painter Jean-François Millet is well known for his works depicting **peasants** working in rural settings with **religious undertones**. With fellow artist Théodore Rousseau, he co-founded the Barbizon school in Normandy, France, close to Fontainebleau. His works exhibit the following elements: 

- Old Testament Book of Genesis 3:19 as subtext

- Depiction of peasant class

- Larger spaces for shepherds and farm laborers

- Integration of religious and mythological imagery

- Looser, more gestural brushwork

- Strong emotions reminiscent of romanticism 

Additionally, his personal beliefs, Naturalism-inspired work, and unromanticized imagery paved the way for modern art movements.  Some of Millet’s important works are *The Sower* (1850), *The Angelus *(1857-59), and *Bird's-Nesters* (1874).

# Chapter 12: Modernism in Art (c. 1800–1945)

Overview

This chapter will first explain the breakthroughs of the 19th and 20th centuries and the policies that greatly influenced modernism in art. Then, it will detail the different art movements that arose as modernist approaches continued evolving in response to a changing world.

Objectives

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- state the major 19th-  and 20th-century breakthroughs that shaped modernism in art

- list and describe the famous 19th-  and 20th-century architectural styles and structures

- identify the different art movements under Modernism and their notable artists

- discuss the key characteristics of each modern art movement

## 19th-Century Modernism in Art

The 19th century  is a period filled with a mixture of breakthroughs in art, science, and technology as well as controversial policies. For instance, the **Industrial Revolution** and its technological advances peaked across much of Europe and the Americas. In the sciences, **Charles Darwin **published *On the Origin of Species* (1850) detailing the theory of evolution, and **John and Harriet Mill **wrote *The Subjection of Women* (1869) arguing for women’s rights. Meanwhile, the **Victorian Era** (named after Queen Victoria, the reigning monarch of Great Britain at the time) was marked by advancements in science and technology but also colonialism, imperialism, child labor, and the exploitation of the lower classes. At the same time, Romanticism, Realism, Impressionism, and Modernism also became popular in literature, music, art, photography, and architecture.

## A. 19th Century Architecture

One of the results of the Industrial Revolution is making iron and glass construction more feasible, which allowed for the building of railway stations, shopping arcades, exhibition halls, and more.  The aesthetic possibilities it allowed were seemingly endless. Hence, architecture saw several stylistic changes during this period. National pride and empire expansion led to the revival of styles from each nation’s heritage.

Robert Mills (1781–1855)

One of the prominent architects that capitalized on these construction developments is Robert Mills. He was an American architect best known for creating the **Washington Monument** in Washington, DC. His fusion of the Palladian, Georgian, and Greek Revival styles helped create a unique Federal style of architecture.

Washington Monument (1848–1884)

Mills’ Washington Monument* *in Washington, DC  serves as a memorial to honor **George Washington**, the **first president **of the United States of America. By modeling the monument to the classic **Egyptian** **obelisk **and showing a keen interest in all things Egyptian, Mills aimed to dazzle.  The monument, which is still the world's highest obelisk, was topped with the biggest piece of aluminum ever cast at the time and stands as the tallest free-standing stone structure. The construction of the monument was* *initially conceived and funded by the **Washington National Monument Society**. However, it took 40 years to build it as the group went bankrupt. Hence, the monument has three colors because the original marble quarry ran out of stone.

Soon after, other countries also built grand structures symbolizing their power. One example is **The Crystal Palace** designed by Joseph Paxton in London. It was a 1,851-foot-long exhibition hall built for the 1851 international Great Exhibition event in London  for nations to show off their industrial innovations. It was made of iron and plate-glass, and all parts were pre-fabricated and quickly assembled in the location. Tragically, a fire in 1936 caused it to burn down. 

Similarly,  the **Eiffel Tower** was built for the 1889 World's Fair. It is the tallest structure in Paris at 986 feet tall, even considered the tallest man-made structure in 1889. It is known for being a **lattice tower**, a freestanding construction made of strips of crisscrossing metal. It also displays the proud use of undecorated iron. It was named after Gustave Eiffel, the owner of the engineering company that designed the tower. Like the Crystal Palace, the Eiffel Tower signifies the role of the Republic of France in advancing industrial progress for the world.

## B. Realism (1840 – 1880)

Realism in art emerged in France in the 19th century from the Enlightenment and Industrial Revolution. The Realism art movement rejected the grandiosity of **Romanticism** (which overemphasized the emotion and scale of life) and the fanciful depictions and methods of other ancient arts. Hence, realist painters, musicians, and writers aimed to focus on the individual and depict the world as it was, as opposed to the highly ornamental form of Romanticism. 

Furthermore, Realism art is often confused today with Naturalism art. Although the two share some similarities, the main difference is seen in the **subject matter**. For instance, realism frequently portrays poverty and working-class life, but naturalism usually features landscapes. 

French painter **Gustave Courbet** is often referred to as the father of Realism in art, and his paintings influenced many famous artists from the 19th century and on. Some of the famous artworks in this movement include Courbet’s *Jo, the Beautiful Irish Girl (*1866), Rosa Bonheur’s *Plowing in the Nivernais *(1849), and Jean-François Millet’s *A Woman Baking Bread *(1854). Although Realism began in painting, it later influenced other kinds of art, including literature.  Realism in literature ensured **verisimilitude **or the appearance of reality while still producing engaging narratives, characters, and stories.

## C. Modern Art (1860s–1970s)

Modern art is the art world's reaction to the rationalism of the new lives and concepts bolstered by the **technological advancements** of the industrial age, which led to a different way of life. The novelty of modern existence was something that artists tried to depict in creative and acceptable ways. In terms of style, modern art is distinguished by the artist's desire to depict a subject **as it exists in the world**, based on their **unique point of view**, and by a **rejection of traditional assumptions about Western art**. Although Realism's introduction can be seen as the beginning of modern art (around 1860), modernist approaches and styles of painting continuously evolved throughout the 20th century. 

- **Early Modern artists** painted what they envisioned as the epitome of their subject

- Industrial revolution led to innovations like **photography**

- **Realist artists** aimed to portray people and situations objectively

- **Romantics **depicted landscape as they saw and felt it

- Beginning of **abstraction in the visual arts **in the 20th century

- **Modern Art themes and concepts** were lewd, controversial, even downright ugly

Within the modern period and even in each art movement in it, there are various movements such as Impressionism, Post-Impressionism (Pointillism and Fauvism), Art Deco, Expressionism, Cubism, Dadaism, Harlem Renaissance, Surrealism, and Modern Architecture. Before we dig deeper, let’s learn about the mother of American modernism. 

Georgia O’Keeffe (1887–1986)

Georgia O'Keeffe is an American painter known for her sensual paintings of magnified flowers. She is regarded as the **mother of American modernism**, which is distinguished by its alienation, self-consciousness, and break from realism. She is renowned for her **large-scale floral paintings **whose centers appear magnified. Most people often interpret these as a depiction of female genitalia. However, O'Keeffe herself disapproved of these interpretations and declined to label her work as feminist art. Towards the end of her career, she had a solitary life, and the barren and alluring **New Mexican terrain **became the main subject of her artwork. This place is now called Ghost Ranch, a famous education and retreat center. 

Light of Iris (1924)

*Light of Iris* is one of O’Keeffe’s famous paintings. Gynecological terminology is often used to explain the flower's enlargements and abstractions. Such explanations, which are under the lens of Sigmund Freud’s psychoanalysis, are increasingly being used in feminist interpretations of the flower. Although it may seem outdated at that time, O’Keeffe didn't intend for her painting to titillate or anger her audience. Rather, she desired to:

A. Distinguish herself from the American masculine drawing of the 20th century, or

B. Stand out from her contemporary male painters by creating drawings that would appear both intrinsically feminine and audaciously sexual

Additionally, some art historians contend that O'Keeffe was drawn to women and that her paintings of Georgia flowers should be seen as a continuation of an 18th-century lesbian tradition. 

Petunia No. 2 (1924)

One of O'Keeffe's earliest large-scale depictions of a flower, *Petunia No. 2*, marks the start of her investigation of a motif that would define her career. She enlarges the flower's form in this picture to draw attention to its **style and hue**. Like her other floral paintings, *Petunia No. 2 *is also often analyzed using a feminist lens. Since the petunia's anatomy is so intricate, O'Keeffe may have been highlighting the **androgyny of the reproductive organs** to refute the notion that her subject matter was somehow related to her gender.  Although American and European artists had been experimenting with abstraction for at least 10 years, she was the only artist to constantly employ flowers as a motif.

Jack-in-the-Pulpit series (1930)

O’Keeffe’s *Jack-in-the-Pulpit series *is a set of six paintings that each include a jack-in-the-pulpit. The series starts with a well-crafted rendering of a striped and hooded bloom, moves on to gradually more abstract and sharply focused images, and ends with the essence of the jack-in-the-pulpit, a haloed black pistil standing by itself against a field of black, purple, and gray.  ***Jack-in-the-Pulpit No. IV ***serves as the halfway point in this sequence of escalating specificity and decreasing abstraction. O'Keeffe consistently regarded **nature **to be her greatest source of inspiration, and she held that the immanence of nature could be found in and through the perfection of form. Hence, in the painting series, **abstraction **serves as a metaphor for and an equivalent to **knowledge**: the flower's closest view produces an abstract image, and the subject's in-depth knowledge reveals its abstract shape. 

## D. Impressionism (1862–1892)

Impressionism is a style of art that places less emphasis on accuracy. It first emerged in France in the **second half of the 19**th** century**. A group of artists, the **Anonymous Society of Painters, Sculptors, Printmakers**, etc., engineered the art form opposing the strict academic standards of painting promoted by France’s Académie des Beaux–Arts. Thus, Impressionists used blurry lines and non-traditional colors and hues to evoke deep emotional responses. They opted to use modern painting technology and new techniques to create lovely **landscapes and scenes of everyday people**. Instead of painting idealized landscapes, several Impressionists went to **suburbs and city parks **to paint commonplace landscapes as they appeared in real life, utilizing significantly more vivid colors than their predecessors. Overall, Impressionists are known for their spontaneity of technique, scientific detachment, and innovations in pictorial design. Some of the famous Impressionists are Claude Monet, Edgar Degas, Pierre-Auguste Renoir, Auguste Rodin, and Édouard Manet. Oftentimes, Impressionists displayed their artworks together.

Édouard Manet (1832–1883)

Édouard Manet is a French painter who worked during the transitional period between realism and impressionism in the 19th century. He typically depicted human studies or Parisian street scenes in his paintings. Like other Impressionists, his works were influenced by Gustave Courbet.  As he frequently preferred to paint **en plein air **(the act of painting outside with the artist's subject in full view), his techniques emphasized **rough brush strokes and naturalistic lighting**. Moreover, the subjects and styles of Manet's artwork, such as *Olympia *(1863), scandalized certain people. His other major works are *A Bar at the Folies-Bergere* (1882) and *Luncheon **o**n the Grass *(1863). Manet’s *Luncheon on the Grass* shocked many in its time for its depictions of nudity and non-standard subject matter. He updated traditional paintings with modern subjects, and many disapproved of how he violated these traditions.

Edgar Degas (1834–1917)

Edgar Degas (born Hilaire-Germain-Edgar De Gas) is a French painter regarded as one of the **founding fathers of impressionism**. However, he usually objected to the label and referred to himself as a realist. Like other French artists,  he was inspired by the compositional strategies of Japanese prints. He enjoyed achieving spontaneity by portraying his themes from odd angles and with characters that appeared to be chopped off at the edge by accident. Nonetheless, **isolation, nudity, prostitution, **and **beauty **are the major **themes **of his work. Meanwhile, **movement, history, France**, and **portraits **are his frequent **subject matters**. Among these, he is famous for his paintings of France, dancers, historical figures, and horses. He also produced numerous **sculptures of ballerinas** and was popular for his ability to capture the **darkness and isolation of the human condition**. Some of his most famous works are *The Rehearsal of the Ballet Onstage** *(1874), *Glass of Absinthe* (1876), and *Place de la Concorde* (1875).

Claude Monet (1840–1926)

Claude Monet is a French painter whose painting *Impression, Soleil levant (*translated as *“Impression, Sunrise”) *(1872) coined the term Impressionism. It also helped establish the art movement. His early experience **en plein air** painting outdoors influenced his impressionistic style, which he used as a starting point for both **natural and urban landscapes**. This en plein air technique is exhibited in his *Women in the Garden* (1866) painting, which also displays his **realist **roots. His **gardens in Giverny **appeared repeatedly in later paintings. Additionally, his approach to impressionism was further accentuated by the effect of **cataracts **on his eyesight as he aged, which led to the development of a particular style of paint layers and textures applied with loose brush strokes that conveyed seemingly blurred pictures.  Some of his other famous works are *Gare St. Lazare *(1877), *The Japanese Footbridge* (1899), *San Giorgio Maggiore at dusk *(1908–1912) as well as different perspectives of Rouen Cathedral and haystacks. 

| **Did you know? ** Notice the subtle changes in color and light in the two different versions of *San Giorgio Maggiore At Dusk* (1908–1912). Like Pierre Renoir, Monet’s works sought to capture the fleeting effects of light and color with rapid, sketchy brushstrokes. He often painted many versions of the same subject hoping to capture each as it was altered by changing light. |
| --- |

Pierre Renoir (1841–1919)

Like his friend Monet, Pierre-Auguste Renoir was a French painter regarded as a founding member of the Impressionist movement. Unlike Monet, however, Renoir’s art is considered** more lyrical and less bound to the empirical facts** of perceptions. Also, his most well-known paintings are revered for their **vibrant style** and use of** color** and **light**. He is renowned among the Impressionists for his portrayals of Parisian city life, his use of brilliant and powerful color, and his **female beauty **as subject matter. For example, his painting ***Dance at ******Le moulin de la Galette***** **(1876) exhibits a range of colors, variations in dress, and patterns. His other distinguished paintings are discussed below.

Two Sisters On the Terrace  (1881)

Renoir’s *Two Sisters on the Terrace* is an oil on canvas painting done from the top terrace of Restaurant Fournaise in the Parisian town of Chateau on the banks of the Seine. Despite the title, the subjects are not related to each other. Jeanne Darlot, who subsequently went on to become an actress, played the role of the older sister. Around this time, Renoir started to move away from Impressionism, and this separation of subject and background became more obvious. This painting skillfully showcases the **serene facial expression and flawless youthful complexion** of the subjects.

Luncheon of the Boating Party (1881)

The *Luncheon **of the Boating Party* is a painting by Renoir aiming to depict a typical Impressionistic scene of people enjoying a pleasant lunch together on a bright afternoon. It is set on a balcony at the Maison Fournaise restaurant overlooking the Seine river in Chatou, outside of Paris. The modernity of the event is confirmed by a sight of a recently constructed railway bridge in the distance, as well as by the relaxed attitude and casual attire of some of the attendees. This painting illustrates Renoir’s mastery in capturing the effects of light.

By the Water, Near the Lake (1880)

Renoir’s painting *By the Water, Near the Lake *features a canotier (anyone who engages in the sport of rowing), or perhaps just a man costumed as a canotier, conversing with a young girl along the Lower Lake in the Parisian park Bois de Boulogne. These gentlemen frequently appeared in Renoir's paintings during this time. Meanwhile, the youngster’s presence gives the scene a sense of innocence and joy.  One of several paintings by Renoir that show people enjoying leisurely outdoor pursuits is this one. This continues an earlier practice when landscapes employed humans to set the setting in context, particularly in French Rococo paintings from the 18th century. 

Auguste Rodin (1840–1917)

François-Auguste-René Rodin, also known as Auguste Rodin, was a highly esteemed French sculptor renowned for his use of realism. For Rodin, **art was more private and subjective** than shared with all of society. 

***The Gates of Hell ***(1880–1917), a huge bronze cast based on Dante's* Divine Comedy *(1321), was Rodin's first significant commission and inspiration for Rodin’s later works. For instance, *The Thinker *(1880), Rodin's most well-known sculpture, was also originally depicted among the individuals toiling in the inferno. Likewise, *The Kiss* (1884) depicts two figures that were first discovered in miniature in *The Gates of Hell*. Some of Rodin's works have been produced numerous times and are on display all over the world because he mostly used **bronze **castings in his work. However, His work was widely criticized and even condemned as an insult to France for venturing too far from convention. 

Pallas (Athena) with the Parthenon (1896)

This sculpture by Rodin exhibits **Athena**, the goddess of craft and wisdom to whom the Parthenon temple was dedicated, whose epithet (descriptive nickname sometimes offensive) was Pallas. Rodin's interest in Greek mythology is evident in the bizarre composition, which depicts a miniature Parthenon perched like a crown atop the woman's bouffant hair. It alludes to the scene when Zeus swallowed Metis, the mother of Athena, after tricking her into becoming a fly, and Athena emerged from Zeus' head. Athena's beautiful skin is softly polished and softened with a "**sfumato**" look, in stark contrast to the coarseness of her hair and attire, as Rodin emulates the shape and finish of ancient sculptures. In his various pictures and sketches, as well as in his sculptures, Rodin's unique respect for the fragment is evident. 

## E. Beyond Impressionism

Post-Impressionism

The chaotic movement Post-impressionism arose as a response to the Impressionism style that dominated the art world of the 1800s and was heavily influenced by Japanese art and culture (Japonism). Although they did not claim to be, Paul Cezanne, Georges Seurat, Vincent van Gogh, and Paul Gauguin are famous painters who are currently regarded as the movement's founders. Since the movement’s first deviance, other factions and methods of creating art have also emerged, and the variety of paintings that belong under the Post-Impressionism umbrella makes it difficult to define. 

For instance, concepts like **Pointillism**, the use of tiny dots to create a full image, were born from the foundation of **Synthetism**, the approach that combines a natural picture with the artist's interpretation and choice of color and line. The movement also influenced many painters who identified as "**Les Nabis**" to use painting as a means of expressing their mysticism and spirituality. Despite the variations within the movement, the post-impressionist style is still characterized by a few distinctive features:

- **Subjectivity:** Unlike  Impressionists who tried to capture the world as they saw it, Post-Impressionists incorporated the artist's **subjectivity** or interpretation and reflection into the painting.

- **Real-life subjects:** These subject matters refer to scenes that artists saw with their own eyes, which Post-Impressionist painters feature in their paintings.

- **Color or geometric design manipulation:**  Instead of merely capturing the world as if shooting a snapshot, Post-Impressionism painters add interpretation and emotion to the landscape or figure by manipulating color and shape.

Japonism (1854–1920)

Japonism was a 19th-century art movement influenced by the opening of Japan's borders to the Western world for trade. Consequently, exotic goods and Japanese arts and crafts flooded European markets. Post-Impressionists became obsessed with the flat, intense colors and bold lines of **Ukiyo-e** (Japanese woodblock prints) and applied these techniques when painting Western subjects. Both Impressionists and Post-Impressionists, particularly Vincent Van Gogh, collected Japanese prints and were greatly influenced by this art form.

Japanese Ukiyo-e (1672–1880s)

Although Japan is home to many popular woodblock painters, the art of making **mokuhanga** (woodblock prints) was originally brought to Japan from China in the 8th century. A significant component of the **ukiyo-e (floating world images)** is Japanese woodblock prints created during the **Edo period** (17th–19th centuries). Most woodblock prints were created in the Middle Ages (12th–16th centuries) using black ink, but the Edo period improved the use of color pigments, leading to vibrant woodblock prints known as **nishiki-e** (brocade images). 

In terms of process, the **nishiki-e** process required numerous blocks in addition to the key block to finish a colorful work of woodblock art since color had to be added in layered phases. When creating numerous multi-colored prints, **kento **(guide marks) were required to maintain alignment and consistency. With Kento, the precise color application was possible over countless numbers of subsequent printing. The woodblock method allowed the ukiyo-e art culture to flourish and was a major factor in the lower classes' social and economic ascent throughout the Edo era. Even in the 21st century, there are still collections and markets for Japanese woodblock prints. 

Many Japanese artists also employ the Nishiki-e style. The first person to introduce the intricate use of color in woodblock prints was Harunobu Suzuki. Additionally, **Hiroshige Utagawa** is popular for painting urban and rural themes, whereas **Katsushika Hokusai** produced the famous woodblock print known as ***Great Wave off Kanagawa***.  

Hokusai Katsushika (1760–1849)

Given his breakthroughs in subject and composition, Hokusai is regarded as one of Japan's best artists and is credited with modernizing traditional print techniques. His art viewed Japan as a single country by showing a variety of settings and activities connected by common symbols and narratives. He was one of the first artists to both be shaped by and shape globalization, incorporating elements from across the world before being accepted by artists in Europe. Apart from the *Great Wave off Kanagawa, *he also created a block-print, realism-based art book called *The Hokusai Manga* that focuses on landscapes, flora and fauna, everyday life, and the supernatural. The term “manga” here means “sketches”, but would go on to inspire modern Japanese comic books also called manga.

Moreover, the following are his most notable achievements: 

- He integrated the **European perspective into Japanese printmaking**. He employed various framing techniques to highlight these focal points and add depth to his images.

- Hokusai altered the Ukiyo-e genre, which depicts  ephemeral pleasures, from traditionally emphasizing people to focusing on **landscapes and the changing seasons**.

- Hokusai used a variety of techniques to depict **Mount Fuji**, which served as a major theme in his works. The various scenes of Japanese life that the artist represented became more cohesive as a result of this repetition. 

## F. Post-Impressionists

James AM Whistler (1834–1903)

James Abbott McNeill Whistler was an American painter in London known for advocating "**art for art's sake.” **His pastels, etchings, and paintings are the perfect example of this. Additionally, this signifies one of the first transitions from classical representational art to **abstraction**, which is at the core of much modern art. His most notable accomplishments include: 

- Demonstrating a novel compositional strategy** **that highlighted the painting's **flat, abstract character**

- Titling or (re-titling) his works with **"****symphony,****"**** ****"****arrangement,****"**** **and **"****nocturne****"**** **to imply a connection between musical notes and variations in color tone, which were used to draw the viewer's attention to the artist's use of paint instead of the real subject matter

- Redefining beauty by incorporating the **Japanese aesthetic **into his imaginative compositions and using unconventional models reminiscent of **Pre-Raphaelite figures **(a group of English 19th-century artists who consciously sought to emulate the simplicity and sincerity of the work of Italian artists from before the time of Raphael, an Italian painter and architect of the High Renaissance).

- Establishing the so-called **Anglo-Japanese fine art style **in England and America and using **unconventional models**

- Inspiring modern artists, like the Impressionists, to **search outside of traditional art organizations for exhibition space and financial support** after Whistler filed a libel suit against John Ruskin and took other defensive actions against critics who disagreed with his artistic philosophies. 

Some of his notable artworks are *Harmony in Blue and Silver: Trouville* (1865), *Arrangement in Grey and Black No. 1: Portrait of the Artist's Mother* (1871), and *Nocturne: Blue and Gold - Old Battersea Bridge *(1875).

Paul Cézanne (1839–1906)

Paul Cézanne was a French painter deemed the **father of modern art **who used Impressionism's lessons to emphasize the importance of the artist's **subjectivity**. He deviated from realistic proportions and relationships when shaping and contouring his figures, and he chose colors based on the composition's overall harmony. Moreover, he influenced Impressionists to emphasize **shapes**, which would become a hallmark of painting during the following century. Throughout his career, his style shifted from focusing on landscapes and solitary figures and using artificial lines to emphasizing more on the** shapes and geometries** in his pieces and restricting **artificial lines** to situations in which they could be mistaken for shadows. Similarly, he transitioned to **still art **almost completely in his later years after realizing that it was the ideal medium for this investigation. Some of his famous works are *Montagne Saint-Victoire* (1890), *The Large Bathers* (1906), *Still Life with Onions* (1898), and *The Basket of Apples* (1926). 

Vincent van Gogh (1853–1890)

Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch Post-Impressionist painter whose work was often driven by a religious sympathy for the harsh realities of rural peasant life.  He is also known as an artist struggling with seizures and other mental health issues. He is now highly acclaimed for his **portrait art,** which includes self-portraits, still-lifes, and landscapes.  His early works feature dark, crude images, and realistic images of the poor. Meanwhile, his later works display bright, colorful images and appear bold, careful, and formal. His works attempted to express the terrible passions of humanity and the quiet innocence of the village and countryside.  

Additionally, Van Gogh is known for thickly applying paint, often with a palette knife, and creating bold, Japanese-influenced pieces. Aside from his most famous painting *Starry Night *(1889), he is also known for his drawing of *Chair *(1888),* The Night Café* (1888), *Fourteen Sunflowers in a Vase* (1888), *Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear *(1889). The last one displays his appearance after cutting off one of his ears. 

Amedeo Modigliani (1884–1920)

Italian-Jewish painter and sculptor Amedeo Modigliani helped apply modernism to Western Art. He is most known for **three different kinds of art**.

**Portraits**, such as *Jacques and Berthe Lipchitz* (1916), exhibit slightly abstract, mask-like faces that represent the subject's personality more than just their physical attributes.

**Nudes**,  like *Nude Sitting on a Divan* (1917), presented brash figures contrasted with flat backgrounds, which fuse modernism and traditional motifs.

**Sculptures**, such as  *Tete* (1922), display how heavily traditional **African art **influenced his approach. 

Louise Nevelson (1899–1988)

Louise Nevelson, originally Leah Berliawsky, was an American feminist painter and sculptor who was largely influenced by Cubism and other abstract movements and translated them into massive free-standing wall sculptures (with wooden boxes, filled with **objets trouvés **stacked on top of each other at different angles). Although her subject matters encompassed her thoughts about an uprooted childhood, conflicting cultures, and nature's divinity, **feminine biography** dominated her artworks. Her sculpture** *****Sky Cathedral*** (1958) is her response to the massive **Abstract Expressionist **paintings by primarily male artists that captured the public's attention in American art throughout the 1950s. Her first** artist retrospective**, featuring pieces from all stages of her career, was held at the Whitney Museum in 1967. 

## G. Pointillism (1880–1890)

Together with Van Gogh, George Seurat, Paul Cezanne, and Paul Gauguin are seen as artists who intensified the impressionists’ deviation from tradition and took a step toward a modernist style. One of these steps to modernity is expressed in **Pointillism**. It was the prevailing technique in the **late 19**th** **or early 20th-century art that prospered during the Post-Impressionist period. In this technique, small unmixed pigment dots were sequentially put onto the canvas to create a larger image. The dots appeared as various colors up close, but from a distance, the human eye saw them as blending into a single color. Artists who used pointillism used **oil **as the primary medium and **optics**, the study of color and light. Similarly, they frequently used unmixed pigments in vivid, saturated hues. They also used **chromoluminarism**, which enhances the appearance of the canvas's white showing through the color dots, and gave Pointillist paintings their distinctive luminosity. After 1910, pointillism's appeal began to decline, although it continued to have an impact on 20th-century art styles like Fauvism, Cubism, and Pop Art. 

Georges Pierre Seurat (1859–1891)

French painter Georges Seurat is renowned for being the **father of pointillism** and for being an expert in** chromoluminarism** and **pointillism**, two key Post Impressionism techniques. His painting *Sunday on La Grande Jatte* (1886) is usually identified as the most popular example of Pointillism.  He chose to convey life through **color **rather than shape or motion. His works are characterized by more vibrant colors and an artificial appearance, which made him stand out from Impressionist painters since they highly valued shape.  Some of his other known artworks are *Gray Weather, Grand Jatte* (1888), and *The Circus *(1891).

Paul Signac (1863–1935)

Signac was a French Neo-Impressionist painter who was influenced by Seurat and popularized pointillism. This led to the **Fauves movement**, which included artists who made use of vivid coloring and claimed Signac as an inspiration. In his art, Seurat practiced **divisionism**, a technique that is based on **color theory**, or how the eye interprets color. The *Portrait de Félix Fénéon* (1890), *Capo di Noli* (1898), and *Port de Marseilles* (1907) are some of his famous works.

## H. Fauvism (1899–1908)

Fauvism is often seen as one of the first movements focusing on **abstraction**. **Les Fauves, **a movement based on **Post-Impressionism**, aimed to alter how artists viewed color, perspective, and emotional impact. An art critic used to describe it as “Fauves” meaning “**wild beasts**” because of the use of unnatural colors.  Generally, Fauvism is distinguished by the following characteristics:

- emphasis on two-dimensional flatness

- saturation of colors, color separated from representation and reality

- emotional resonance of color and composition

Inspired by Paul Gauguin, the Fauvists employed **colors **to create an emotional language. Furthermore, the** goal** of the Fauvist movement was to** deviate from Impressionism's obsession with representational art** and toward non-representational depictions that better reflected the individual emotion and vision of the artist. Later on, the emphasis of Fauvism on two-dimensionality and flatness, as seen in Henri Matisse's *The Dance* (1910) influenced the **Cubist** movement that followed.

Henri Matisse (1869–1954)

Henri Matisse was a prominent French artist recognized as a key figure in the Fauvist movement. He rivaled Picasso in influence and ability.  He believed that the color used in such boldly decorative arrangements created its pictorial structure. For Matisse, art should be a means of **expression **and therapy.

Vibrant colors and strong brushstrokes are characteristics of Matisse's artistic style. For example, the unusual use of** vibrant colors** in* Femme au Chapeau (The Woman with a Hat)* (1905) shocked viewers. Similarly,  he often used **bold outlines with one color** as in* Bonheur de Vivre* (The Joy of Life) (1906). Even decades after his passing, Matisse's renowned works of art continue to inspire artists with their creativity and expression. 

## 20th-Century Modernism in Art

The 20th century included several technological milestones such as the moon landing and the invention of airplanes and nuclear technology, among others. However, it was also an era of war as these milestones also coincide with World War I and II, the Cold War, the Vietnam War, and more. Thus, tension, devastation, and a desire for change became the themes of the 1900s. Similarly, socio-political forces, such as communism, nazism, mass media propaganda, and capitalist material consumerism greatly influenced people’s lives. Given all these global societal changes, there was an increase in psychological understanding and awareness of environmental and social issues.

Consequently, the vast and sudden global changes throughout the 1900s urged many artists, writers, architects, philosophers, and more to seek new ways of expressing themselves thereby establishing a style we loosely define as 20th-century Modernism and Postmodernism. This includes the following:

- Art Deco

- Expressionism

- Cubism

- Dadaism

- Harlem Renaissance

- Surrealism

- Regionalism

- Abstract Expressionism

- Pop Art

## A. Expressionism (1905–1933)

Initially, expressionism appeared in **1905** when four German architecture students named Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, Fritz Bleyl, Karl Schmidt-Rottluff, and Erich Heckel founded the group **Die Brücke **(The Bridge). From around 1905 to 1920, the Expressionist movement's golden era flourished across Europe. Moreover, German cities simultaneously experienced the emergence of expressionism, which is thought to have been named by **Czech art historian Antonin Matejcek**.Expressionism developed alongside **formal abstraction** (another branch of modernism) and focused on communicating feelings and states of mind directly and intensely. Thus, most artworks here display pictorial subjects, typically conventional  landscapes, portraits, and city scenes. Some of the significant expressionist artworks are Wassily Kandinsky’s *Der Blaue Reiter* (1903),  Ernst Ludwig Kirchner‘s *Street, Berlin *(1913), and Erich Heckel’s *Portrait of a Man* (1919).

## B. Cubism (1907–1922)

Cubism, an early **Modernist** movement,** **had a remarkably brief existence yet had a significant influence on the rest of the art world. Cubism broke from realism and explored multifaceted perspectives of a subject. The definition of Cubism might be summed up as a style that turns objects and space into **geometric shapes and colors**. Using abstraction and **collage** for the first time, cubist artists like Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque simplified their subjects with subdued hues and geometric patterns. 

Moreover, unlike earlier artists who added depth to paintings using methods like foreshortening and chiaroscuro, cubist artists were more interested in creating **a world of their own **unrestricted by reality. Because cubists disagreed with the idea that art should reflect nature, their work was more inspired by imaginative abstraction. Hence, there are two types of cubism. 

First, **Analytical Cubism **(1907–1912)** **frequently had a more **muted color scheme**, jagged and cloistered appearance, two-dimensional, and a lack of texture, such as Picasso's *Le Demoiselles D'Avignon *(1907). Meanwhile, **Synthetic Cubism **(1912–1914)** **used non-art materials in highly-textured, brightly-colored simple collages, utilizing a more reality-bending stance, greater boldness, and emphasis on layering, and constructing forms instead of disassembling things in real life. An example of this is Braque's* Rhum et Guitare *(1918). 

Pablo Picasso (1881–1973)

Pablo Picasso, a prominent Spanish painter, is credited with founding the avant-garde Cubism movement. Although he had many distinct artistic phases, including the **Blue, Rose, and African-Influence Periods**, he is more known for **Cubism**. He created two-dimensional drawings of the natural figures he had studied in his Analytical Cubism movement. He used additional textures and components to his two-dimensional drawings to create a collage in Synthetic Cubism, which expanded the style of Cubism. Most of his later works, which included paintings, sculptures, and drawings that seemed twisted and surreal, were associated with the Surrealist Movement. His most well-known piece, ***Guernica ***(1937), which is on display in Madrid, demonstrates this. Some of his other noteworthy works are * Les Demoiselles d’Avignon *(1907)*, Three Musicians* (1921), *Ma Jolie* (1912), and *Maquette for Guitar* (1912). Later on, his focus on disassembling and reassembling materials, as well as his integration of indigenous art from Africa and the Pacific inspired other artists.

African Art: Dan Masks, Picasso, & Cubism

Picasso's African-influenced period was followed by the style known as Cubism, which developed from *Les Demoiselles d'Avignon. *This painting depicts the angular characteristics of African masks. Artists Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque expressed reality in their art in a new way by blending items or individuals creating paintings with pictures that appear fragmentary. It represents the image by “flattening” it on the canvas, and then “dismantling” it in its different components, which are simplified and geometrized and can be seen from different points of view at the same time. Henri Matisse's display of a mask from the Dan region in 1907 piqued Picasso's curiosity. 

Moreover, African African art dates back before written records and many of the significant African works can be found in **Central** and **West African arts**. Natural materials like wood from bark, plant extracts, raffia, ivory, shell, clay, and feathers are also used in their art. 

African arts reflect their religions and traditions and are used in celebrations, grieves, ceremonies, and honoring dead ancestors. Geometrical patterns and different bright colors are visible in their art forms. Many great artists like Picasso and Matisse were influenced by African art, especially masks, and sculptures. Aside from Cubism, African Art also inspired Fauvism such as Henri Matisse’s French ivory art. 

The Dan People

The Dan are a Mande ethnic group from Liberia and the northwest Ivory Coast.  They believed that their world is split into the **human domain** (the village and its people) and the **spiritual domain** (the forest and its spirits). They are known for their art, notably  wood sculpture, including a huge variety of masks, each with unique forms and purposes.

|  | **Study Note:** African Dan masks One of the most famous African art forms is the **Dan masks,** which are **sacred objects**. They are used for protection and as a channel for **communication with the spirit world.** Dan masks have a typically **high forehead**, **pouting mouth,** and **pointed chin.** They also sometimes have scarification marks like the line that divides the forehead and nose in the left image. These are carved in wood and stained with a brown dye. When a **dancer wears a Dan mask he becomes the spirit of that mask** and speaks in the language of the spirits which is then interpreted by a wise man. |

Sir Jacob Epstein (1880–1959)

British sculptor Jacob Epstein is revered as one of the foremost **modern** sculptors.  He is known for linking the act of sexual expression and artistic creativity, for incorporating influences from the Pacific Islands, Native American, Indian, and African cultures, and as one of the most significant **Direct Carving** practitioners (the sculptor works directly on the material of choice without sketching first). He referred to this approach as "**truth to material**" and emphasized that his material selection was an integral component of the creative process.  Some of his noteworthy works are *Rock Drill *(1913),  **portrait busts** (a sculpted or cast image of the upper body that includes the head, neck, and some portion of a person’s chest and shoulders) of *Paul Robeson* (1928) and *Albert Einstein *(1933), as well as *Genesis *(1929).

## C. Dadaism (1916–1924)

Dadaism was an anti-art, anti-war movement that directly followed the First World War (1914–1918). It was devoted to the idea that since logic and reason caused the war, society should accept the** absurd, senseless, and irrational**. Hence, many dadaists rejected the idea of fine art itself. In dadaism, the **meaning of the physical form **of the artwork is more valuable than the visual content. It embraced a degree of** anarchy** never previously seen in art, challenging the idea of what constitutes art. They did this, among other things, by depending on** chance**. They saw chance as: 

- Anarchy

- Rejecting the social norms that had caused world war to erupt

- Restoring art to a personal, deep, and mystical experience

For example, artists like** Jean ****"****Harp****"**** Arp** let chance decide how their pieces were to be designed. In his *Collage with Squares Arranged According to the Laws of Chance *(1917), he tore up pieces of paper and dropped them, attaching them where they landed. Others, such as **Kurt Schwitters**, were more conscientious about the design but left the materials to chance, utilizing anything they happened to come across, including trash. The message in Schwitters' "**Merz 19**" is that an object is only art if you consider it to be such.  A Dada artist must then concentrate on pushing the boundaries of art through its purpose and function rather than honing the visual abilities and techniques that are normally required. Some of the other popular Dada artworks are Marcel Duchamp’s *Fountain* (1917) and *LHOOQ* (1919).

## D. Harlem Renaissance (1920–1940s)

The Harlem Renaissance, also known as the** ****"****New Negro****"**** movement** of the 1920s, was a cultural and intellectual revolution that took place in the predominantly black area of New York City. African Americans came together in support of this famous figure because he represented an idealized vision of the development of a new racial identity.  One of the factors that sparked this is **The Great Migration**, the movement of millions of African Americans from rural areas in the rural South to urban centers in the North and Midwest between 1910 and 1930. Through this, the Southern diaspora came into contact with the political and cultural environment of New York City.The Harlem Renaissance, which was championed by influential personalities like W.E.B. Du Bois, Langston Hughes, and Duke Ellington, had a significant impact on society and the arts. For instance, an innovative kind of **jazz poetry**, a rhythmic prose form that anticipated the beat poetry of the 1960s, also mirrored the popularity of blues and jazz music. **Mural paintings** also became known venues for artists who covered entire buildings and walls with common themes like portraits, folklore, and street scenes. Overall, the art of the Harlem Renaissance brought black artists together through the merging of arts and culture rather than having a distinctive aesthetic all its own. One of the prominent works here is Aaron Douglas’s *Aspects of Negro Life: The Negro in an African Setting *(1934). 

## Mid-Century Modernism in Art (c. 1900–1940s)

## A. Surrealism (1924–1966)

The anti-art movement, Dada, that emerged immediately after the First World War and allowed members to use their art to attempt and make sense of what they had seen, gave rise to Surrealism in the 1920s. **Surrealism**, formed by Paris-based writers and painters, sought to break free from the limitations of formal Enlightenment thought to access and glorify the **unconscious **mind and adopted Sigmund Freud’s ideas on it. They Sought to release unconscious images and words in their art. To express the inner workings of the mind, surrealist artists did not attempt to show actual sights or landscapes. 

Instead, they highlight the following **characteristics**:

- Subconscious mental expressions

- Art intended to challenge and cross boundaries

- The liberty of thought and language, including liberation from sexual taboos

- Randomness, chance, and unpredictability

All of these factors combined to create extremely original and odd pieces of art. They also entail the use of the following** techniques**:

- **Automatism:** Drawing, painting, or writing as spontaneously or without thought as possible to create visuals that were ambiguous and open to a variety of audience interpretations while also releasing the unconscious mind

- **Combined images:** Collages, mixed media, and other methods that combined pictures you wouldn't typically see together

- **Symbols:**  Things that have one appearance yet represent another

- **Exquisite Corpse:** A painting created by numerous artists in which each person adds a new body component to a creature

These are employed by some of the famous surrealists like **Salvador Dali** (the face of modern surrealism), **Max Ernst** (used **frottage and grattage**, methods where Ernst would scrape away parts of an image to create a textured effect), and **André Breton**, author of *Surrealist Manifestos*. Eventually, surrealism inspired later movements like absurdism and postmodernism. 

Joan Miró (1893–1983)

Miró was a Spanish artist known for his work in Surrealism, Abstract Expressionism, and other modern art movements. Miró’s work transitioned from the depiction of objects in the physical world to the depiction of concepts in the mental world. Some of his distinguished works are *The Farm* (c. 1922), *Harlequin's Carnival* (c. 1925), and *Dona i Ocell* (1982).

Alexander Calder (1898–1976)

Calder was an American artist and engineer whose wide variety of work included sculptures, airplane and automobile illustrations, jewelry, paintings, printmaking, and theatrical productions. His most well-known works of art were his “mobiles”, kinetic sculptures with organic shapes which involved being hung from wires and gaining motion through motors or air power. Two of his key artworks are the *Three yellow, two blue polygons and brass on red *(1958) and *Les Masques *(1971).

Salvador Dali (1904–1989)

Spanish artist Salvador Dalí was a forerunner of the** Surrealist **movement and is known for both his eccentric, dramatic behavior, and his appearance. He had ties with celebrities like  John Lennon, Alfred Hitchcock, and Elvis Presley. In his paintings, he usually used symbols and images from the **unconscious **and dream experiences. Dali called his paintings “**hand-painted dream photographs**” and he combined minute details with bizarre images and vividly painted landscapes. 

Surrealists were influenced by Freud’s earlier *The Interpretation of Dreams* (1899). He deepened his investigation into Freudian philosophy by creating the **Paranoiac Critical methodology**. In this methodology, he would hypnotize himself and then paint what he saw when he came out of it. Just like many other Surrealists, he painted employing a visual language of symbols, bones, bodies, natural elements, and desolate, twisted landscapes that served as the outward expression of his psyche. Like other painters, he also had a muse, **Gala Eluard** (later known as his wife Gala Dalí) who is the subject of his painting *Eggs on a Plate Without the Plate *(1932), which features a couple of fried eggs.

Un Chien Andalou (1929)

The film does not have a conventional plot, instead using a Freudian-inspired, “free association” dream logic narrative flow with a disjointed chronology that skips to seemingly unrelated scenes.

Gala Dali was a Russian school teacher, but she is more popular in the art world as the spouse of French poet Paul Éluard and, later, as Salvador Dali's muse and wife. ## B. Regionalism (1928–1943)

American Regionalism was an art movement aiming to **paint scenes of America** realistically. It flourished from the 1920s to the 1940s. The Regionalists rejected **abstraction**, which was popular in Europe at the time. They also intended to create art that reflected the lives of **working-class Americans **rather than focusing on the upper classes as art had previously done. Along with comprehensive pictures of people, American Regionalist art frequently depicted households, farms, and landscapes. 

One recurring theme in American Regionalist portraits was a **lack of clarity** in the emotional interiority of the subjects. Many of these photos appear quite enigmatic, allowing viewers to read different meanings into them based on their own experiences. Grant Wood painted the most famous piece of American Regionalist art, ***American Gothic***. Other notable paintings are John Steuart Curry’s ***Baptism in Kansas**** *in 1928 (showing images of rural life in the American Midwest) and Thomas Hart Benton’s public mural ***Achelous and Hercules**** *(1947), which is displayed in a Kansas City store. In literature, **Mark Twain** is dubbed the first regionalist writer. Because it was thought to be too close to Second World War propaganda art, regionalism eventually lost popularity. 

Grant Wood (1891–1942)

American painter Grant Wood led the Regionalist movement in America and painted the *American Gothic, *a key piece of Regionalist art. His artistic style was largely influenced by the Flemish painter** Jan van Eyck**. Wood is renowned for his subtle artistic style and use of rhythmic lines in his paintings. It is a technique that integrates the work artistically. 

American Gothic (1930)

*American Gothic* is Wood’s painting exhibiting **rhythmic lines** as seen in the lines of the pitchfork, the lines on the man's shirt, and the lines on the house all being related. Grant was inspired to paint it after seeing a white farmhouse with Carpenter Gothic window design in Eldon, Iowa. He then requested his** sister and dentist** to serve as models for the folks he imagined in front of the farmhouse. The painting intends to convey the strength of rural Americans. It is now displayed at *The Art Institute of Chicago.*
