Johann Sebastian Bach (1685–1750)

Johann Sebastian Bach was a German composer whose music has two known elements:

- An elaborate counterpoint (a mixture of two or more equally important melodies)

- A pronounced bass line that harmonically carried other lines (called a basso continuo)

Aside from these elements, he also utilized a **continuo **(an accompanying part that enhances harmony and serves as a bassline for the other sections) to produce a harmonic ground. He emphasized the melody with an ongoing **ritornello** (a recurring refrain in a concerto that is played by the full orchestra and alternates with solo portions). Bach also created choral works known as **cantatas **for the church. Some of his famous works are *Brandenburg Concertos *(1721), *The Well-Tempered Clavier *(1722), *Concerto for Two Violins *(1731), and *Mass in B Minor *(1749).

Bach: Musical Compositions & Techniques

Additionally, Bach created a new method for composing music containing the following: 

- An** eighth-note octave scale** divided into seven intervals, which are arranged by whole and halftones.

- A **tonic **(the primary pitch of the key) as the core of the composition

- A **prelude **(a free form to show the player’s abilities)

- A **fugue **(musical form in which a theme is created)

Bach is also often associated with the **Baroque Counterpoint**, a trademark of music from the Baroque era. Counterpoint is the distinct melodies that are powerful enough to stand alone as melodies, yet they were placed in a superb composition, "point against point." The use of counterpoint can be heard in fugues or the more improvisational forms found in dance suites and preludes. Many genres from the period have interwoven melodies, which is one of the single most essential aspects of the time.  The fugue is a common example of counterpoint from the Baroque era. A fugue is a composition that strictly follows the guidelines of species counterpoint. Bach is arguably the most well-known fugue composer, and his **Fugue in G Minor **(1707) is among the most popular.

Furthermore, Bach composed the “**Toccata and Fugue**” in D minor, a piece of** organ music**. The date it was written is still being debated, which ranges from c. 1704 or as late as the 1750s. The composition largely adheres to the traits thought to be typical of the north German organ school of the Baroque era with different artistic influences, such as south German traits. 

Brandenburg Concertos (1721)

The *Brandenburg Concertos* (originally titled Six Concerts à Plusieurs Instruments in French or Six Concertos for Several Instruments) is a  collection of six instrumental pieces that Bach gave to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt. Some of them combine several solo instruments. They are frequently cited as some of the greatest orchestral works of the Baroque period. 

The Well-Tempered Clavier (1722 and 1742)

Bach composed two sets of preludes and fugues for the keyboard in each of the 24 major and minor keys for his *Well-Tempered Clavier*. In the era of the composer, the term "clavier" (French for "keyboard") applied to a wide range of musical instruments, usually the harpsichord or clavichord. In 1722, Bach made a book entitled *Das Wohltemperirte Clavier *containing preludes and fugues in all 24 keys, major and minor. Twenty years later, Bach created *The Well-Tempered Clavier, Part Two*, a second book of the same genre (24 pairs of preludes and fugues).  

## E. Enlightenment Music

With the Enlightenment values of pursuing knowledge through science and reason, the musical world experienced an explosion of musical ingenuity, particularly through the operas and symphonies of Franz Joseph Haydn and Wolfgang Mozart.

The Classical Period  (1750–1820)

Operas and Symphonies

Two of the most important Enlightenment-era composers were Haydn and Mozart. They were part of the explosion of musical genius now called the **Classical period**. They composed music for court events, religious services, and public concerts. 

Franz Joseph Haydn (1732–1809)

Franz Joseph Haydn, an Austrian composer, is regarded as the **Father of Symphony**. Symphony is an orchestral composition usually in four movements (or sections). It typically opens with the ‘**sonata**’ form, followed by a slow and lyrical tempo (**adagio**), then a graceful dance in a moderate tempo (**minuet**), and concludes with a fast, animated tempo (**allegro**). Each movement is written in a specific formal pattern.

His 106 symphonies and 83 string quartets reflect his upbeat and jovial outlook on life. Hadyn also taught other composers like Mozart and Beethoven. Additionally, Haydn gained the moniker "Papa" for his enormous heart and propensity to look out for his students and friends.  Inspired by Handel's *Messiah *in London, he composed *The Creation (1798)*. Some of his other well-known compositions are *Symphony No. 94*, and the *Trumpet Concerto (1796)*. 

Surprise Symphony (1791)

While residing in London in 1792, Haydn wrote his *Symphony No. 94 *(now referred to as *Surprise Symphony*). Haydn surprised his audience by defying their preconceived notions of what a symphony should sound like with his *Surprise Symphony. *The piece follows a four-movement structure typical of Haydn's symphonies and the surprise comes near the beginning of the second movement. It earned its moniker because a sudden, very loud chord shocks the audience during a quiet portion of the composition.

| **Did you know?** According to legends, Haydn allegedly added the loud chord on the spot while conducting because he wanted to wake up a listener who was snoring, but Haydn insisted that this was untrue. |
| --- |

Classical Symphonies

During the 18th century, four-movement symphonies became the popular musical style.  A symphony is an extended musical composition in classical music, consisting of an orchestral arrangement and multiple distinct sections (or movements), with the first movement in sonata form. Terms often used in symphonies are:

- An **opening sonata** - a musical structure generally consisting of three main sections (exposition, development, and recapitulation)

- **Adagio** - the Italian word for "slowly," indicates slow with great expression tempo

- **Allegro**: fast, quick, lively, and bright

- **Largo**:  	very slow and broad with 40-60 beats per minute

- **Andante**: at a walking pace, moderately slow 

- A **minuet** or **scherzo with trio** - a contrasting part of the movement usually in AB form; 

- **Rondo** form - musical structure in which a main theme alternates with other contrasting themes.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756–1791)

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was an Austrian composer revered for his mastery of blending music and drama in his operas. He displayed his mastery of the **gallant style**, perceived as clear, energetic, and "natural" by listeners at that time.  He composed and performed based on the preferences of his audiences. His creations also combine wisdom and sophistication with the rococo's frivolity and gaiety.  He and Haydn were the first important Enlightenment-era composers and began an explosion of musical genius now called the **Classical period**. Some of Mozart's more well-known compositions are *Don Giovanni *(1787), *Eine Kleine Nachtmusik *(1787), *Requiem *(1791), *String Quartet in D Minor *(1785), *Symphony No. 41 *(1788), *The Magic Flute *(1791), and *The Marriage of Figaro *(1786)—the latter of which is regarded as a humorous musical work. 

Così Fan Tutte (1790)

*Così fan Tutte, ossia La Scuola degli amanti (All Women Do It, or The School for Lovers)* is a two-act opera buffa (comedy or humorous opera) by Mozart employing the theme "fiancée swapping.” **Così  fan Tutte**, the abbreviated title, literally translates to "So do they all," utilizing the feminine plural (tutte) to denote females. The standard English translation is "Women are like that." This melodic phrase is also used in the opera's overture and is sung by the three men in act 2, scene 3, shortly before the finale. The opera is a bittersweet meditation on women's faithfulness against a backdrop of disguises, false goodbyes, and deceptions. Contrary to popular belief, **Antonio Salieri**, a contemporary of Mozart, attempted to set the text but abandoned it before Mozart did. This suggests that Cosi fan Tutte was **not **written and composed at Emperor Joseph II's recommendation. 

The Magic Flute (1791)

*The Magic Flute* is a German opera or more accurately, a **singspiel **since it is performed in German and contains spoken conversation interwoven with sung arias (a self-contained song for one vocal, with or without musical or orchestral accompaniment). The libretto was written by Emanuel Schikaneder, while the music was composed by Mozart. It narrates the story of Prince Camino, his bird-catching buddy Papageno, their magic flute, and bells, as they embark on the journey to rescue **Pamina**, the **Queen of the Night's daughter**, from Sarastro. Eventually, they discover that the Queen, who represents irrationality, is the real villain, not Sarastro. It attracted well-known classical musicians like **Antonio Salieri **and Joseph Haydn. It is a significant piece in the history of **classical music** and is heavily shaped by the Enlightenment and the Freemasonry movements. 

## F. Late Modern Period (1800–1945)

Romantic Music and Theater (c. 1780–1850)

The 18th century experienced tumultuous events that transformed people’s lifestyles. For instance, the Industrial Revolution modernized the economy and technology. There was also the American Revolution, which inspired the French Revolution. Hence, no wonder that many of the epic poems, operas, and other musical pieces then are related to these events.

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749–1832)

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was a leading figure in German romanticism. His works include plays, poetry, literature, and aesthetic criticism as well as treatises on botany, anatomy, and color. He was also the founder of the **Sturm und Drang**** **(or **Storm and Strife**) movement and writing style. This has themes of uncontrollable emotion, disrespect for logic, and desire for impossibly impossible action. His writings feature dramatic emotion, the significance of the individual experience, nature, and explorations of color theory and biology. Aside from *Faust *(1790), one of his important works is *The Sorrows of Young Werther,  *an epistolary novel (i.e., literary works that take the form of letters or other documents).

Faust (1790)

*Faust* is a two-part epic poem considered a play featuring Doctor Faustus, a scientist who strikes a deal with the devil. The first section of* Faust* deals with a wager made by the Lord to the devil Mephistopheles that he cannot corrupt his preferred pious scientist, Faust is extremely prosperous yet unhappy with his life, which prompts him to make a deal with the Devil when he is at a crossroads. He trades his soul for limitless knowledge and worldly luxuries. To get anything he wants, the demon fools Faust into giving up his soul, which causes a chain of unpleasant events to occur in his life. Ultimately, Faust has everything he desires in life and is sucked up to harness the power of nature. Overall, *Faust* depicts the romantic desire to burst free of constraints and indulge in all aspects of the human experience.  

Johann Christoph Friedrich von Schiller (1759–1805)

One of the most prolific and well-known writers of the **Romantic**** **era was the German Friedrich von Schiller. Using his plays, poems, and philosophical writings, he propagated his vision of an ideal community free from tyranny, where peace and universal love may bloom. His poems are often based on **ballads **as they are simple to memorize and speak aloud.  His works often reveal themes of human freedom and the struggle between good and evil.

| **Did you ****know****?** Schiller’s “Ode to Joy” (1785), set to music by Beethoven in his *Symphony No. 9* (1824), was adopted as the anthem of Europe by the Council of Europe in 1972 and later by the European Union in the mid-1980s. The piece also features in the football scene of *Dead Poets Society* (1989). |
| --- |

Ludwig van Beethoven (1770–1827) 

Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer and pianist known for being a musical innovator, expanding the possibilities of sonatas and symphonies, and encapsulating the originality and emotion of Romanticism. Beethoven is most known for his **symphonies**, which are lengthy orchestral compositions separated into parts. Some of these are *Eroica (****Symphony No. 3****) *and ***Symphony No. 5***, which opens with a powerful four-note sequence that follows a **short-short-short-LONG pattern** and is arguably his most well-known composition. Lastly, his ***Symphony No. 9*** is unique because it involves a **choir **whereas past symphonies had previously only been written for orchestra. This symphony is also known for a melody that can be heard throughout called ***Ode to Joy***,** **which was written by Schiller in 1785.  

Georges Bizet (1838–1875) 

Georges Bizet was a French composer known for his opera, *Carmen. *Although Bizet's subsequent musical career spanned several genres, his operas are what made him most famous. Other than *Carmen*, he was also recognized for *Les Pêcheurs de Perles (*or *The Pearl Fishers; *1863*) *and *Djamileh *(1872).

Carmen (1875)

Based on Prosper Mérimée's 1845 book of the same name, Bizet collaborated with librettists (Henri Meilhac and Ludovic Halévy) to create the four-act opera *Carmen*, which premiered at the Paris Opéra-Comique. Carmen is a young** Romani lady** who works in a **cigarette factory** and has a tragic love affair with Don Jose. Bizet incorporated Spanish-inspired melodies and musical idioms to accurately reflect the feel of the country. He used **chromatic scales**, which include the 12 notes that make up an octave in Western music, and traditional Spanish rhythms in the **Habanera** aria, which bears the name of **Cuban dance**. Now, Carmen is viewed as the best example of the French **opéra comique **style (the French form of opera wherein a self-contained musical number alternates with spoken dialogue). It influenced the **dramatic realism **of succeeding opera verismo composers. Verismo is an opera style portraying ordinary people and their daily emotions, especially their darker aspects.  Giacomo Puccini (1858–1924)

Giacomo Puccini is a renowned Italian opera composer. His magnificent orchestrations and lavish operatic melodies have yielded some of the most beloved and exquisite opera music. Some of his famous works are *La Bohème* (1830), ***Manon Lescaut****** ***(1893; his first big hit), *Tosca *(1900), and ***Madama Butterfly**** *(1904). The last one examines the issue of imperialism. Puccini frequently wrote in the **verismo**, a realist style common in Italian opera of the late 19th and early 20th centuries that uses realistic portrayals of average people and events rather than mythology. He also used **leitmotifs, **compositional devices to highlight particular characters and feelings. His operas are thoroughly constructed, with the musical shape and structure evolving continuously rather than repeating significant components. Using the theme of a **tragic heroine giving everything up for love**, Puccini wrote 12 operas.

# Chapter 19: Performance Arts from the 19th Century to Present

Overview

This chapter examines the more recent examples of performance art since the 19th century. This includes the popularity of realist theaters and the evolution of music and opera, dances, film, and theater into the contemporary forms we know today.

Objectives

At the end of this chapter, you should be able to:

- describe the characteristics of realist theater and its famous playwrights

- name the major performance artists and explain their contributions to music, opera, dance, film, or theater into the present era

## The 19th Century

While there are many developments arising from the Industrial Revolution, the Victorian Era, and other influential thinkers, there were also many social issues that emerged. Thus, many plays, operas, and other forms of performance arts during this time tackle these social issues or tried to deviate from conventional standards.

## A. Realist Theater: Chekhov & Ibsen

Realism in playwriting brought European theater back to prominence after a decline in popularity during the romantic era. Realist theater was based on strict rules of plausibility and was often written in a highly-logical prose style. Similarly, the sets were carefully designed and used curtains and electric lights to make them appear more realistic. Two of the leading realist theater artists are Henrik Ibsen and Anton Chekhov.

Henrik Ibsen (1828–1906)

Henrik Ibsen was a  Norwegian dramatist known as the **father of realism. ** He examined the inner conflicts of middle-class society. He also tackled topics of social and philosophical interest such as venereal disease, marriage, and the role of women. For instance, *The Wild Duck* (1884) and *Hedda Gabler* (1891) used powerful, ambiguous symbols to probe beneath middle-class appearances. 

Additionally, he is renowned for plays such as *Peer Gynt *(1867), *A Doll's House* (1879), and *Ghosts *(1881)*.* His difficult upbringing can be seen in the recurring theme of **alienation and isolation **in his plays. Additionally, his plays were renowned for their discussion of contentious issues like women's rights and Norwegian independence.

Peer Gynt (1867)

*Peer Gynt *is a** satirical verse play** (any play that features a considerable amount of verse and is presented to an audience by an actor like Shakespeare’s works) based on the Norwegian folktale of the same name. It is also one of the most widely performed Norwegian plays. It tells the story of overconfident Peer Gynt who leaves home to seek his fortune and has several disastrous misadventures. He thinks that his final conflict is between **hell and nothingness**. He meets, impulsively abducts, and then abandons a bride-to-be, **Solveig**, who also falls in love with him. Several adventures later he has wealth and fame but not happiness. The five-act play was intended to be read aloud rather than performed because it was conceived as a **closet drama **(a drama that is best read aloud rather than performed).

A Doll’s House (1879)

Ibsen’s *A Doll’s House* is a realist play that follows the fate of a married woman (Nora) who seeks self-fulfillment in a male-dominated world after realizing she is expected to act like a doll to take care of her husband (Torvald Helmer). One day, Nora tries to hide a secret forgery from her husband that could threaten their marriage. Meanwhile, Torvald treats her as a pretty plaything (a “doll”) by regularly referring to Nora as his "**little lark**" and "squirrel," insinuating that she overspends, simply enjoys playing at home, and is unintelligent. Eventually, she leaves him to pursue her freedom in the play's shocking conclusion.

Due to its instant impact on theater and the subsequent controversy, the play's last scene is frequently referred to as "**The Slam Heard 'Round the World**." The epilogue cemented realism as a serious genre, inspiring many to follow in Ibsen's footsteps. The incident was contentious because many people believed it was improper for a lady to leave her husband and children. This is a great illustration of how Ibsen used **social issues **as the focal point of the production.  

Anton Chekhov (1860–1904)

Anton Chekhov was a 19th-century Ukrainian former doctor, playwright, and author recognized for his short stories and the play *The Cherry Orchard*. Originally, he published humorous short stories. Later on, he incorporated his medical expertise into his writing. The common themes in Chekhov's plays and stories include "illness" and "untimely death," which is similar to Chekhov's struggles with tuberculosis in the years leading up to his untimely death at the age of 44. His characters either feel deflated or full of hope after his short works. 

The Cherry Orchard (1904)

The fundamental theme of*** The Cherry Orchard*** by Chekhov is **social mobility** and change at the start of the 20th century in Russia. **Mrs. Ranevskaya **represents members of the upper class who are currently bankrupt and trying to survive. As a result of her child’s death and the abuse by her partner, she is unable to heed the wise counsel of **Lopakhin, **who has become wealthy as a trader after rising from the peasant class.  He advised her to destroy her cherry orchard and lease the property to save her position, but she cannot part with the orchard as it is a remnant of her noble upbringing. When the estate is eventually sold at auction, Lopakhin purchases both the cherry orchard and the entire property for himself, signifying the full amount of Mrs. Ranevskaya's loss and the demise of her aristocratic way of life. The sound of the cherry trees reflects the uncertainty of the family members' future in this new world as they part ways at the end.

Giuseppe Verdi (1813–1901)

The Italian composer Giuseppe Verdi is regarded as the hero of 19th-century Romantic Italian opera. His musical adaptations of various sources, including the Bible and literature, were frequently used in his opera compositions. Verdi was in high demand as a composer after the success of his first opera, *Nabucco *(1839). He composed at least 25 operas, and his most known work is the song “La Donna e Mobile” from *Rigoletto *(1851), which was sung by the modern opera tenor, Pavarotti. His Shakespearean adaptations, which include *Macbeth (1847)*, *Otello *(1887), and *Falstaff *(1893), are among his best-known works. Verdi’s last opera was *Falstaff*, which drew from Shakespeare's *Henry IV, *part of *Henriad*, a history play that features Prince Harry—who would later become Henry V—as its principal character. Overall, his use of **parlando**, the combination of orchestra music and sung speech, defines his unique style and influences his successors.

Richard Wagner (1813–1883)

Richard Wagner was a German composer and musical theorist recognized through his operas, which he called **music dramas**, and for popularizing Known for **two operatic concepts: **leitmotif and Gesamtkunstwerk. The German word **Gesamtkunstwerk** (total work of art or artwork combining different art forms) describes Wagner's all-encompassing artistic style. He attained Gesamtkunstwerk by enriching his music to incorporate drama.  Most of Wagner's later works were inspired by **German legends**. He also used **leitmotifs  **(musical name tags) to convey thematic movements and alert the listener to the musical portrayal of specific characters. *The Ring Cycle *(or *Der Ring des Nibelungen; *1869-1876), an opera made up of four music dramas, is Wagner's best piece. Some of his other famous works are *Lohengrin* (1850), *Tristan and Isolde* (1859), and *Parsifal *(1882).

## B. Atonality Writers

Any musical composition that lacks a tonal center or key and deviates from conventional Western standards of harmony, key, or mode is considered **atonal music**. At the end of the Romantic era, several composers felt frustrated that music had reached its peak. Hence, they experimented with breaking the rules of the tonal hierarchies of typical European music. Some of the famous atonality writers are Claude Debussy (1862–1918), Alexander Scriabin (1871–1915), Béla Bartók (1881–1945), Igor Stravinsky (1882–1971), Edgard Varèse (1883–1965), Sergei Prokofiev (1891–1953),  and Paul Hindemith (1895–1963). 

Claude Debussy (1862–1918)

Achille-Claude Debussy or simply Claude Debussy was an atonality, romantic-early modern composer who explored new harmonic relationships and exotic tone colors. The following characteristics best describe his work: 

- Using** timbre** (the individual sound of an instrument or voice that distinguishes it from other instruments or voices) and **modality** (a note’s pattern on a certain pitch)

- The impact of Richard Wagner, Russian music, and the Indonesian music percussion instrument, *Gamelan*

- Using non-Western whole tones, octatonic, and pentatonic scales

His works are often considered **Impressionist** (linking them to the painting style of Monet) as the subject matter was expressed with vague suggestion rather than precise representation. He composed 141 pieces for voice, chamber, opera, and orchestra. One of his most famous pieces was “Clair de Lune” (1905). Others are “La Damoiselle Élue” (1888), “Deux Arabesques” (1890), “Prelude a L'apres-midi d' un Faune” (1902), “La Mer” (1905), and “La Plus Que Lente” (1910). Generally, his works are often considered Impressionist (linking them to the painting style of Monet) as the subject matter was expressed with vague suggestions rather than precise representation.

Béla Bartók (1881–1945)

Béla Bartók was a 20th-century Hungarian composer widely regarded as the founder of **ethnomusicology**, the study of music in its social and cultural context. According to legend, Bartok became interested in **folk music** after hearing a** Transylvanian **woman sing a traditional song and recorded folk tunes on an **Edison phonograph**. Thus, he incorporated many elements of folk music and produced works that were rhythmically and tonally complex. 

Specifically, the music of Bartok examined **non-tonal **or pentatonic harmonies and complicated rhythms within a framework of Hungarian nationalism by fusing classicism, romanticism, nationalism, and his work in ethnomusicology. Some of his works are, “Duke Bluebeard's Castle” (1911),  “Cantata Profana” (1930), and “Music for Strings, Percussion, and Celeste” (1936).

## C. Composers

Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky (1840–1893)

Tchaikovsky was a Russian composer who paved the way for Russian musical nationalism typically associated with Eastern Europe in the late 1800s. He celebrated the people and the beauty of his homeland. He often incorporated native folk music and programmatic musical descriptions (representational and based on other forms of art or nature) into his work. One of his most famous pieces is the “1812 Overture” (1880) and the ballet *The Nutcracker* (1892). His most famous works were composed for ballets popular in czarist Russia and are associated with famous Russian ballet choreographer, **Marius Petipa**.

The Nutcracker (1892)

*The Nutcracker* is a two-act ballet that tells the tale of Clara, a little girl whose toys suddenly come to life during Christmas, and the nutcracker is her most significant toy.  Even though *The Nutcracker* was not well received when it was first performed or while Tchaikovsky was alive, the ballet has become the most often performed ballet ever, 

Richard Strauss  (1864–1949)

Richard Strauss is one of the last great German composers who brought the Romantic period ideals into the modern age. The three genres for which he is most known are **tone poems, opera, and Lieder** (German art ballads for voice and piano solos). In each genre, he ensured adherence to the expressive aspirations of the Romantic era. **Tone poems** (or symphonic poems are compositions for orchestra that illustrate a concept or tell a tale) were Strauss' first successful excursion into professional composition. Some of his famous works are *Till Eulenspiegels Lustige Streiche *(1895), *Don Juan *(1889), *Also Sprach Zarathustra *(1896), *Don Quixote *(1897), and *Elektra* (1909), which is deemed as his most musically and thematically modern work. Others are  *Morgen *(1894; lieder) and *Der Rosenkavalier* (opera) (1910).

Don Juan (1889)

Strauss created the tone poem Don Juan for an orchestra. The piece is based on **Don Juans Ende**, a drama that was inspired by Nikolaus Lenau's incomplete 1844 retelling of the Don Juan legend, which first appeared in Spain during the Renaissance. Three drama passages were reproduced by Strauss in his score. According to Lenau's depiction, Don Juan's proclivity is a result of his desire to find the ideal woman. He eventually gives in to melancholy and wishes for his own death since he loses hope of ever seeing her.

Also Sprach Zarathustra (1896)

Friedrich Nietzsche's philosophical work *Thus Spoke Zarathustra*, which was published between 1883 and 1885, served as the inspiration for Richard Strauss' tone poem *Also Sprach Zarathustra. *After being used in Stanley Kubrick's 1968 film *2001: A Space Odyssey*, the original fanfare—dubbed "**Sunrise**" in the composer's program notes—became well-known.  

Scott Joplin (1868–1917)

African American composer and pianist Scott Joplin became known as the **father of ragtime music**, a brand-new genre distinguished mostly by its "ragged" rhythm. In large part because of Joplin's published works, particularly the book he self-published in 1907 titled *School of Ragtime*, ragtime became a new musical genre in the early 1900s. Even though there are still numerous gaps in our knowledge of Joplin's life, we do know that he was a composer, musician, and conductor of contemporary music. Since the dates and records were not always exact, it is difficult to say with certainty when certain of his songs were released, but here are some of his famous works:

- *Maple Leaf Rag *(1899)

- *The Entertainer *(1902)

- *A Guest of Honor  *(1903)

- *Fig Leaf Rag *(1908)

- *Treemonisha *(1911)

After Joplin’s death, his music and ragtime, in general, declined in popularity as other musical genres like **jazz **and **novelty piano **came into being. Nonetheless, his legacy lives on through musical styles such as jazz and frequent revivals of the ragtime style.

## The 20th Century

The 20th century witnessed several technological breakthroughs as well as wars across the globe. Additionally, many socio-political forces greatly altered people's lives. All these breakthroughs, wars, and socio-political forces filled the period with feelings of tension, devastation, and a desire for change, leading to increased psychological understanding and awareness of environmental and social issues.

## A. Music and Opera

Charles Ives (1874–1954)

American experimentalist composer Charles Ives was a leader of the early 20th-century modernist movement and a pioneer of polytonality and spatial music. Early musical and familial influences on Charles Ives influenced his use of avant-garde sounds and compositional methods, including:

- **Polytonality**: Using two or more time signatures or tonal centers simultaneously

- **Polyrhythms**: Simultaneously employing various, contrasting rhythms in similar musical context

- **Quotation of American musical vernacular**, including parlor ballads, circus music, marching bands, fiddle tunes, and patriotic songs

- **Spatial music**: Music composed with distinct sound source locations in mind, such as two instruments playing simultaneously in different portions of a theater

| **Did you know?** Ives and his family were also quite active in the New England region's abolitionist movements as well as their local community, which also influenced his works. |
| --- |

His exposure to American music styles shaped his works. He wrote several of his most known pieces during the height of the abolitionist movement, including The Unanswered Question (1908), one of the best-known uses of spatial methods in Charles Ives's music, Three Places in New England (1911–14), Holidays (1913), and Fourth Symphony (1916).

Three Places in New England (1914)

The *Three Places in New England* is a three-movement orchestral composition. The piece is praised for its use of musical paraphrasing and quotation. The movements are made in a slow-fast-slow order, with the longest movement coming first and the smallest movement coming last. Ives used layered textures with various, often simultaneous melodies, many of which are identifiable hymn or march themes, masses of sound, including tone clusters, and abrupt, sharp textural contrasts. These are all characteristics of his style that are present in this composition. 

Origin of Jazz

Jazz is a music of popular melodies played with improvisational invention and a characteristic “swing” rhythm developed in America in the early 1900s. Together with **Dixieland jazz**, it emerged in the city of **New Orleans**. Dixieland is a jazz musical genre that is frequently linked to New Orleans' jazz pioneers but also describes slightly later musical genres from the Chicago area.  Brass bands, slave songs, and the blues all influenced the development of jazz music. Early jazz music featured a front line that included the** clarinet, trombone, and trumpet**. Later on, more instruments including the piano, saxophone, horn instruments, and others were added to jazz music ensembles. Ragtime, bebop, and swing/big band were further popular jazz musical genres. Additionally, the origin and rise of jazz stem from the **Harlem Renaissance**, a cultural and intellectual revolution in the African American community in the 1920s. Two of the prominent figures in jazz are Buddy Bolden and Louis Armstrong.

Buddy Bolden (1877–1931)

African American cornetist Charles Joseph "Buddy" Bolden was recognized by his contemporaries as a pivotal player in the evolution of jazz or New Orleans ragtime music. He was called"King" Bolden and was famous for his loud sound and improvisational prowess. Bolden is also credited with creating the "**Big Four**," a rhythmic innovation on the marching band beat that allowed for considerably more freedom for individual improvisation in the formative stages of jazz. One of his famous songs is "Funky Butt," which became known as "**Buddy Bolden's Blues**." 

Louis Armstrong (1901–1971)

One of the most well-known jazz musicians of the 20th century, Louis Armstrong was also a gifted singer and skilled player of horn, trumpet, and cornet. He widened the horn's conventional tone and range in jazz music. One of his significant contributions to jazz was the switch from collective to solo improvisation. 	 

Aaron Copland (1900–1990)

American composer Aaron Copland produced numerous notable pieces of music. He was greatly affected by the music of fellow composer and Neoclassical composer **Stravinsky **when he returned to America. Early Copland compositions were influenced by the jazz era, but he later developed a more condensed, straightforward, and powerfully evocative approach. Among Copland's famous compositions are *Billy the Kid* (1938), *Fanfare for the Common Man *(1942), and *Appalachian Spring* (1944).

Billy the Kid (1938)

On Lincoln Kirstein's request, Copland wrote the ballet *Billy the Kid*, while Eugene Loring created the choreography for Ballet Caravan. It is most well-known for its use of many cowboy ballads and American folk songs. Despite being based on the life and exploits of Billy the Kid, it is more of an interpretation of the "Wild West," in which characters like Billy played prominent roles.

Rodeo (1942)

*Rodeo* is a ballet composed by Aaron Copland in 1942 and later arranged as an orchestral suite called *Four Dance Episodes from Rodeo*. It tells the story of a cowgirl who tries to win the heart of a rancher but is ignored because of her rough appearance. The music combines American folk tunes, lively rhythms, and open harmonies that reflect the Western landscape. The four movements, *Buckaroo Holiday*, *Corral Nocturne*, *Saturday Night Waltz*, and *Hoe-Down*, each show a different part of the story. *Hoe-Down* is especially famous and often used in advertisements. The ballet was choreographed by **Agnes de Mille**, and the third movement is notable for its softer sound and use of a smaller group of instruments.

Appalachian Spring (1944)

The Appalachian Spring is Copland’s musical composition choreographed with modern dance style by Martha Graham depicting a 19th-century American village's celebration of the building of a new farmhouse.  The moving plot of Appalachian Spring is combined with exquisite settings, costumes, and music in the film. With its joyful sections, Appalachian Spring shows both the underlying tension and worry of the villagers as well as this steadfast hope. The spectator is reminded that these people had no idea what would happen to their families in this new country by the joyful leaps and partnerships that are interspersed with longing looks into the distance. 

Celia Cruz (1925–2003)

One of the most celebrated Latin musicians of the 20th century was Celia Cruz, whose real name was Ursula Hilaria Celia de la Caridad Cruz Alfonso. Cruz gained notoriety in Cuba in the 1950s as a guaracha singer, gaining the moniker "La Guarachera de Cuba." Guarachas is a style of Cuban music with rapid tempo and comic lyrics. As a result of her contributions to Latin music in the ensuing decades, she rose to fame as the "**Queen of Salsa**" on a global scale. Some of her hits are "Quimbara" and "Bemba colorá." Her slogan "¡**Azúcar**!" ("Sugar!") has grown to be one of the most known salsa music trademarks. Some of her hits include *Bemba colorá* (1960) and *Quimbara* (1974).

Joan Alston Sutherland (1926–2010)

Joan Alston Sutherland or Dame Sutherland was an Australian **dramatic coloratura soprano** (someone who specializes in music that stands out for its swift dashes, leaps, and trills). She made significant contributions to the revival of the** bel canto repertoire** from the late 1950s to the 1980s. Although music critics disliked her weak diction, she had a voice that combined quickness, accurate intonation, pinpoint staccatos, a trill, and a strong upper register. 

| **Did you know?** Sutherland, who received the 1961 Grammy Award for Best Classical Performance - Vocal Soloist (with or without orchestra), was the first Australian to win the award. |
| --- |

Philip Glass (1937–present)

American composer Philip Glass is regarded as a **pioneer of minimalism** (focus on simple consonance, repeated phrases, and a continuous beat or tone; frequently described as hypnotic or meditative). Glass is known for his long, frequently repetitive pieces that integrate synthesizers, classical instruments and styles from various cultures, and occasionally sacred texts and chants. His music incorporates influences from rock, ambient music, electronic music, and world music.  His composition *Music in Twelve Parts *(1971–1974) demonstrates his minimalist methods, whereas *Glassworks* (1981) is his only album to get a commercial release, Lastly, his *The Voyage* (1991) opera was written to commemorate the 500th anniversary of Christopher Columbus' first voyage to the so-called New World. 

Pablo Casals (1876–1973)

Pau Casals I Defilló was a Spanish-Puerto Rican cellist, composer, and conductor better known by his Castilian Spanish name **Pablo Casals** in English. He is widely considered one of the greatest cellists of all time and the** foremost cellist of the first half of the 20**th** century**. He is probably best known for the recordings of the **Bach Cello Suites** he did between 1936 and 1939. In 1963, President John F. Kennedy bestowed upon him the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Yo-Yo Ma (1955–present)

Yo-Yo Ma is a Chinese-American cellist who has received 19 Grammy nominations and has released over 90 albums. In addition to recordings of the mainstream classical repertoire, he recorded a variety of folk music, such as Brazilian music, traditional Chinese music, the tangos of Argentine composer Astor Piazzolla, and American bluegrass music. He is known for his smooth, rich tone, soulful lyricism, and virtuosity.

## B. Dance

Serge Pavlovich Diaghilev (1872–1929)

Sergei Pavlovich Diaghilev, a Russian ballet impresario, art critic, and patron, founded the **Ballets Russes**.  Diaghilev was an expert at luring talent, which helped the Ballets Russes become a success. 

| **Did you know?** Diaghilev collaborated with recognized designers and artists like Coco Chanel, Pablo Picasso, Joan Miró, and André Derain, giving them a platform for fresh ideas, which also sustained the fame of Ballets Russes even in turbulent times. |
| --- |

Ballets Russes (1909)

The Ballets Russes displayed choreography and costuming art directly resembling Russian culture and style. It also utilized avant-garde artists to create set pieces and costumes, which reflect the idea of **total art **or  **Gesamtkunstwerk** (total work of art or artwork combining different art forms). As a result, it veered away from the usage of graceful movements, leaps, and traditional pirouettes. It used stomping, jumps, turns, and stamps of the foot. Thus, it changed the way dancers, choreographers, and audiences saw ballet as dancers had to move, connect with music, and portray a story visually. The Ballets Russes was based primarily in Paris, France but toured Europe, and North and South America.

Igor Stravinsky (1882–1971)

Igor Stravinsky was a Russian ballet composer and atonality  who used multiple meters within a passage, and beats were frequently changed from one measure to the next. He employed the novelties of **polytonality**, or the simultaneous use of two or more musical keys, and **polyrhythm**, the simultaneous or rapid succession of different time signatures. 

The Firebird (1910)

***The Firebird*** is Stravinski's first significant symphonic composition, while **Michel Fokine  (1880–1942)**** **created the choreography. *The Firebird* is a mythical creature inspired by Russian folklore. The story is based on iconic figures like the evil sorcerer Koschei and handsome Prince Ivan to develop a theatrical drama that differentiates the life of humans and the world of mythological creatures like the magical Firebird. To make this contrast more visible, Stravinsky applied **chromaticism**** **(incorporation of notes from outside the diatonic scale to generate a variance in musical tone and interrupt the expected pattern of notes) to match more discordant musical tones and rhythms with the scenarios involving the Firebird and Koschei, which aims to convey the unfamiliarity of their world.  

The Rite of Spring (1913)

*The Rite of Spring* (1913) was written for Diaghilev's Ballet Russes and tells the story of the return of spring and the renewal of the Earth through the sacrifice of a virgin chosen to dance herself to death. It was considered controversial as it used the dissonant sounds of early modernism and the avant-garde as a way to shock and thrust the audience into prehistoric pagan Russia – even causing a riot from audiences at its first showing.

Martha Graham  (1894–1991)

Martha Graham was an American dancer and choreographer considered to be a **pioneer of Modern Dance **in the mid-20th century and the **Picasso of her art form**.** **While modern dance is undoubtedly influenced by ballet, it differs from it in that it is more improvised and less formal in terms of costume, with most modern dances being performed barefoot rather than on pointe shoes. Graham and other choreographers of the new generation linked the movement to emotion to develop the Modern Dance style. She often starts with the body's center, then moves on to contractions and releases of muscles during motion. Ultimately, her method is known for its foundation in breath rhythms, sharpness, and accuracy.  

Aleksandra Danilova (1903–1997)

Aleksandra Dionisyevna Danilova was a Russian-born prima ballerina, who brought both classical Russian and modern Diaghilev training in American ballet. Upon moving to the US, she was quickly hired as a dancer by **Sergei Diaghilev**, the founder of Ballets Russes. After Diaghilev’s death, Danilova and  Frederic Franklin established **Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo**, one of the most illustrious ballet collaborations of the 20th-century wit. Danilova in ***Gaîté Parisienne*** (1938) became one of the attractions of the Ballet Russe de Monte Carlo. Gaîté Parisienne (1938). She also performed in *Song of Norway *(1944) and *Oh, Captain!* (1958), and she also published her autobiography *Choura*, which bagged the  1986 de la Torre Bueno Prize.

Gower Champion (1919–1980)

Gower Carlyle Champion was an American actor, theatrical director, dancer, and choreographer. He performed as a choreographer and solo dancer on Broadway in the late 1930s and early 1940s. His most notable choreographic pieces include: *Make a Wish* (1951), *Bye Bye Birdie* (1960), *Hello, Dolly!* (1964), and *42**nd** Street* (1980).

Twyla Tharp (1941–present)

Twyla Tharp is an American choreographer, dancer, and author who established the Twyla Tharp Dance company in 1966. Her first choreography was Tank Dive (1965). She frequently incorporates jazz, classical music, and contemporary pop music. Tharp then created the dance ***Deuce Coupe***** **in 1973 set to The Beach Boys' music, and it is considered to be the **first crossover ballet**. Meanwhile, her ***Push Comes to Shove***, which she choreographed and featured Mikhail Baryshnikov, is currently regarded as the **best crossover ballet**. In 2001, Tharp had the Chicago premiere of her dance musical *Movin' Out*, which has words and music by Billy Joel, which received ten Tony nominations, and Tharp won Best Choreographer. Her other notable choreographies are  *The Fugue *(1970) and *Baker’s Dozen* (1979).

Mikhail Baryshnikov (1948–present)

Baryshnikov is a Soviet Latvian-born Russian-American dancer, choreographer, and actor who was the preeminent male classical dancer of the 1970s and 1980s. He has initiated his artistic endeavors and is known as one of the key contributors to promoting modern dance. He joined the American Ballet Theatre (ABT) in 1974 during which he re-choreographed the Russian classics *The Nutcracker* in 1976 and *Don Quixote* in 1978. He starred as Yuri Kopeikine in the movie *The Turning Point *(1977), which earned him nominations for both the Golden Globe and the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor in the same year. He also had a recurring role in *Sex and the City*'s final season and also acted in the film *White Nights *(1985).  As a result of his success as a dramatic actor in theater, film, and television, he is now arguably the **most famous dancer in contemporary ballet**.

## C. Film

Fascination with capturing and controlling movement as well as the invention of the **kinetoscope**, the original motion picture machine, led to the creation of the film. The United States, which did not suffer the post-World War I as severely as it affected European nations, dominated the making of movies. In 1910, many film companies moved to Hollywood, a small town in Los Angeles, California where many of the influential American filmmakers discussed below flourished.

DW Griffith (1875–1948)

DW Griffith was an American film director who pioneered many aspects of film editing and expanded the art of narrative film. His most famous black-and-white silent film, ***The Birth of a Nation *****(1915)**, though a technically ground-breaking film and a commercial success, is a profoundly racist movie that glorifies white supremacy and the **Ku Klux Klan**. Based on the novel *The Clansman* (1905), the historical-fiction plot is that the Ku Klux Klan saved innocent white southerners from anarchy when radical Reconstructionists temporarily gave power to undeserving and incapable Black men after the Civil War. However, the movie's racist stereotypes were denounced by the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) when it was released.

Influential American Filmmakers

John Ford (1894–1973)

John Ford was an American filmmaker mostly known for his **Westerns**, where the **landscape itself almost becomes a character **as Ford was an expert at using** long shots that capture the power of the environment**. Ford was also famous for **powerful and insightful dramas**** **which have all become classics. Some of his notable films are *The Informer* (1935), *Stagecoach* (1939), *The Grapes of Wrath* (1940), *How Green Was My Valley* (1941), and *The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance* (1962).

Alfred Hitchcock (1899–1980)

Alfred Hitchcock was a London-born film director turned Hollywood director popular for his thriller movies. He is dubbed as the **Master of Suspense** and is known for using **MacGuffins**, unimportant incidents that propel the plot ahead. His movies probe the deep, dark corners of the human mind in a way that keeps viewers on the edge of their seats. They are full of tension and suspense relayed through a **fast-paced style** with **twisting plots**,** clever camera angles**,** startling point-of-view shots**, and **abrupt sounds**. Some of his recognized films are *The 39 Steps* (1935), *Rear Window* (1954), *Vertigo* (1958), *Psycho* (1960), and *The Birds *(1963).

Orson Welles (1915–1985)

Orson Welles is another influential American filmmaker also revered for his mastery of suspense. His dramatic 1938 radio broadcast of ***The War of the Worlds*** (1938) terrified listeners who thought that the earth was really being invaded by Martians!  His first film,** *****Citizen Kane ***(1941), is a classic known for its unique use of the **'deep focus' lens**, vivid filmography, layered story elements, and deep character development. Welles created other film masterpieces, such as *The Magnificent Ambersons* (1942), *Touch of Evil* (1958), and *Chimes at Midnight* (1965).

Francis Ford Coppola (1939–present)

Francis Coppola is acclaimed for creating **powerful characters** in his films. From the 1970s, he revived popular genres and characters from Hollywood's earlier days, including **war films** like ***Patton**** *(1970) and ***Apocalypse Now**** *(1979), and gangster movies such as ***The Godfather*** trilogy (1972–1990). His other distinguished films are *The Outsiders* (1983) and *Bram Stoker's Dracula* (1992).

## D. Theater

Theater is a collaborative type of performance art in which live actors or actresses perform in front of a live audience in a particular setting, frequently a stage, to portray the experience of a real or imagined event. To communicate this experience to the audience, the performers may make use of gestures, song, voice, music, and dance. Let’s turn to the succeeding paragraph and discover the foremost playwrights and how they used theater as a means to entertain, express imagination, or tackle social issues, among others. 

George Bernard Shaw (1856–1950)

George Bernard Shaw is most commonly known as a playwright, but he was also a literary and social critic, reviewer, novelist, and screenwriter. He was also considered a subscriber of **evolutionary socialism**,** **which advocates for peaceful forms of expression through intellectual and creative discourse as opposed to violent ones. Shaw has a history of using comedy and irony to criticize society in both his fiction and nonfiction writing. Thus, his works illustrate critiques against the British social class, language as a class barrier, transformation, appearance, identity, and femininity. Shaw is famous for writing *Man and Superman *(1903), *Pygmalion* (1912), and *Saint Joan *(1923)*. Saint Joan* is also the drama that earned Shaw the Nobel Prize in Literature. Additionally, *Pygmalion* also inspired the musical  *My Fair Lady* (1956), which centers on Eliza Doolittle and Professor Higgins.

Pygmalion (1912) 

*Pygmalion *is probably the most well-known and widely-read drama by Shaw. In the play, the character Professor Henry Higgins figuratively sculpts the character Eliza Doolittle into the "ideal woman," echoing the ancient Greek legend of King Pygmalion (from where the play gets its name) who fell in love with a statue of a woman he carved. Higgins, a professor of phonetics, wagers that by coaching and dressing up the appearance of a lower-class flower girl, he can pass her off as an upper-class duchess. Shaw criticizes the social class of the British people. *Pygmalion *served as the basis for the musical ***My Fair Lady*** and popularized this story, which can be seen in films and television. 

Lorraine Hansberry (1930–1965)

African American playwright Lorraine Hansberry was a major force in American theater. She became the youngest and first African American to ever win the New York Drama Critics’ Circle Award through her famous work, *A Raisin in the Sun*. This deals with the themes of **African liberation and the African American experience**. It was the first Broadway production of a play written by an African American woman. Hansberry went on to produce highly regarded pieces like* The Sign in Sidney Brustein's Window* (1964) and* Les Blanc (1970).*

A Raisin in the Sun (1959)

Hansberry’s* **A Raisin in the Sun* was the first play produced for Broadway by an African American woman. The play takes place in a Chicago neighborhood of African Americans in the 1950s. Three generations of the **Younger family** live in a small, dilapidated apartment that serves as the setting for the entire play. When Walter, the family patriarch, dies, the family members argue with one another throughout the play about their own goals and objectives while coping with the challenges of being a Black family in the time **before the Civil Rights movement**. The Younger family decides to pursue their goals with conviction, dignity, and freedom at the play's end. The play's three main themes are **addressing racial injustice, the value of family, and the power of dreams**. 

Dale Wasserman (1914–2008)

American playwright Dale Wasserman is arguably best known for writing the *Man of La Mancha* script. He also adapted Ken Kesey's novel *One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest *(1962) into a play of the same title, which ran for many years in San Francisco and other states.  

Man of La Mancha (1965)

*Man of La Mancha* is an adaptation of Wasserman's non-musical teleplay *I, Don Quixote (*1959), which was influenced by Miguel de Cervantes' ***Don Quixote ***** (1605)**. *Don Quixote* tells the story of the "mad" knight Don Quixote as a play within a play, performed by Cervantes and his fellow prisoners as he awaits a hearing with the Spanish Inquisition. Don Quixote is considered the very first modern novel upon its publication in the early 1600s. It has its roots in Arthurian-era tales of chivalry. Additionally, *Man of La Mancha*’s lead tune is "The Impossible Dream.” 

Stephen Sondheim (1930–2021)

American Broadway composer and lyricist Stephen Sondheim is regarded as one of the major figures in musical theater of the 20th century. He was an apprentice of Oscar Hammerstein II and made his Broadway debut with the show** West Side Story**, which has the famous song “I Feel Pretty.”  In collaboration with **Harold ''Hal'' Prince**, he created *A Little Night Music*, which includes one of his most well-known songs, “Send in the Clowns” (1973). He also produced the musical *Company *(1970) and *Sweeney Todd* (1979). 

A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum (1962)

Stephen Sondheim wrote the music and lyrics for the musical *A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum*. The musical tells the bawdy tale of a slave named Pseudolus and his efforts to win his freedom by assisting his young master to woo the girl next door.** **The plot features numerous traditional farcical elements, such as puns, door-slamming, situations of mistaken identification (sometimes involving persons posing as one another), and sarcastic remarks on socioeconomic class. 

| **Did you know?** The title originates from the phrase "a funny thing happened on the way to the theater," used frequently by vaudeville (a form of entertainment featuring mixed specialty acts such as burlesque comedy and song and dance comedians to open a story. |
| --- |

Sweeney Todd (1979)

Stephen Sondheim composed the music and lyrics for the musical play *Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street*  (or simply "*Sweeney Todd*"). It is based on Christopher Bond's 1973 drama of the same name. The musical play is about the legendary barber who returns from wrongful imprisonment to 1840s London, bent on revenge for the death of his wife. He kills multiple people and gives the bodies to his partner,  Mrs. Lovett, who bakes the bodies into pies. 

Tony Kushner (1956–present)

Tony Kushner is an American writer who frequently discusses the struggles faced by minority groups in America while drawing on his own experiences as a gay Jew. Many of his works were profoundly influenced by the** Civil Rights Movement** and other political events of the 20th century. He also wrote a play called *A Bright Room Called Day *(1991), which compares the experiences of a group in 1930s **Germany** to those of marginalized people in 1980s America. In 2003, he also created the musical *Caroline*, *or Change *(2003)*,* which shows a black maid whose financial and personal difficulties are not alleviated by significant societal developments like the Civil Rights Movement.

Angels in America (1991)

It is a two-act play with a running time of almost seven hours. The majority of the action in the play takes place between 1985 and 1986, with the final scene taking place in 1990, all in New York City. Prior Walter, a gay guy in his 30s, receives an AIDS diagnosis in the narrative. The play is a passionate investigation of a wide range of subjects, all centered on politics during the **Reagan administration** and the effects of the AIDS crisis on the LGBT community.
